FINDINGS: The analysis identified distinct ECT-modulated structural and functional networks. The structural network primarily involved subcortical regions (hippocampus, amygdala), ventral attention areas (insula, operculum, temporoparietal junction), and somatomotor regions (precentral and postcentral gyrus). The functional network mainly implicated the default mode network (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex).

INTERPRETATION: This is a meta-analytic and network-mapping study, not a primary clinical trial, so causal inferences about ECT’s antidepressant effects cannot be drawn. The strength lies in integrating heterogeneous neuroimaging data to propose a network-level mechanism, but the clinical relevance of these structural/functional changes remains uncertain. The dissociation between structural and functional networks is intriguing but preliminary; replication in larger, longitudinal cohorts with clinical outcome data is needed.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study suggests ECT may exert its antidepressant effects through network-specific brain changes, but it does not yet inform treatment decisions. Clinicians should note that ECT’s mechanisms likely involve distributed brain networks rather than isolated regions, but this remains a research finding until linked to patient outcomes.

articles.title: Acceptability and Experience of Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Adult ADHD: A Systematic Review With Narrative Synthesis.
articles.authors: Sobolak R, Aho B, Hunter MS, et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is a first-line psychosocial treatment for adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). While its clinical efficacy has been the focus of considerable research, the acceptability of CBT for ADHD remains under-studied. This is a critical gap, as core ADHD deficits may impact on acceptability and, therefore, utility. This review evaluates CBT acceptability for adults with ADHD using the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability (TFA). METHOD: Five databases (Scopus, PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science and PsycINFO) were systematically searched in February 2026. Twenty-one studies including randomised controlled trials, pilot, feasibility, qualitative and mixed-methods studies, were included. Data were integrated and mapped to the seven TFA domains. RESULTS: Across studies, CBT acceptability in adults with ADHD most strongly explored the domains of affective attitude, intervention coherence, perceived effectiveness and self-efficacy. Acceptability was driven by skills training, psychoeducation, therapeutic support, accountability strategies, individualisation and diverse materials. Burden was linked to homework, cognitive load and treatment intensity, while opportunity costs and ethicality were rarely reported. Group and digital formats were generally acceptable but dependent on facilitation quality, accessibility and therapeutic presence. CBT for adult ADHD is most acceptable when it enhances affective response, understan
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review with narrative synthesis examined the acceptability of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for adults with ADHD, addressing a gap in understanding how core ADHD symptoms may influence treatment engagement and satisfaction. The review included 21 studies (RCTs, pilot/feasibility trials, qualitative and mixed-methods studies) and mapped findings to the seven domains of the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability (TFA).

FINDINGS: Acceptability was most consistently assessed in the domains of affective attitude, intervention coherence, perceived effectiveness, and self-efficacy. Positive drivers included skills training, psychoeducation, therapeutic support, accountability strategies, and individualisation. Burden was primarily associated with homework demands, cognitive load, and treatment intensity. Group and digital formats were generally acceptable but depended on facilitation quality, accessibility, and therapeutic presence. Ethicality and opportunity costs were rarely reported.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is heterogeneous, combining diverse study designs and measures, which limits firm conclusions. However, the synthesis suggests that CBT for adult ADHD is most acceptable when it enhances engagement, understanding, and perceived benefit while minimising burden. The review highlights the importance of intervention content and delivery style over format alone. Key limitations include the lack of standardised acceptability measures and underreporting of ethical and opportunity-cost domains.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should prioritise structured, flexible CBT interventions that incorporate psychoeducation, skills training, and accountability strategies to improve acceptability. Attention to homework load and cognitive demands may reduce treatment burden. Further research using standardised acceptability measures is needed to refine delivery approaches.

articles.title: Outcomes of Mindful Mood Balance for Moms, online mindfulness-based cognitive therapy for perinatal depressive relapse prevention in the USA: a two-arm, single-blind, pragmatic randomised clinical trial.
articles.authors: Dimidjian S, Gallop R, Goodman SH, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Effective and accessible approaches to prevent depressive relapse and reduce symptoms are crucial for addressing the major public health problem of depression among perinatal women. We aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of Mindful Mood Balance (MMB) for Moms plus usual care (hereafter MMB for Moms)-a web-based mindfulness-based cognitive therapy programme customised for perinatal women-compared with usual care only, in reducing depressive relapse and symptoms. METHODS: This single-blind, randomised clinical trial was done across the USA, in euthymic pregnant women with recurrent depression who were on recent or current antidepressant medication. Recruitment occurred from March 7, 2019, to July 8, 2020 (data collection was completed Sept 12, 2021). Participants were randomly assigned to MMB for Moms, or usual care. Primary outcomes were reduction in depressive relapse risk and symptom burden, assessed using the Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview and Patient Health Questionaire-9, respectively, across the study period. Outcomes were assessed from baseline until 6-months postpartum in three phases (intervention, end of intervention to delivery, and postpartum). The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03623620, and is complete. FINDINGS: Participants were recruited between March 7, 2019, and July 8, 2020. Data from 500 randomly assigned participants (mean age 32 years [SD 4·5] and mean 11·5 [2·8] weeks gestation), were analysed as the intentio
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study evaluated whether adding an online mindfulness-based cognitive therapy programme (Mindful Mood Balance for Moms) to usual care reduces depressive relapse and symptom burden in euthymic pregnant women with recurrent depression in the USA, using a two-arm, single-blind, pragmatic RCT.

FINDINGS: In 500 participants (mean age 32 years, mean 11.5 weeks gestation), MMB for Moms reduced relapse risk over 6 months postpartum (33% vs 44%; hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.56–0.99; p=0.045). Symptom burden decreased more during the 12-week intervention (average PHQ-9 reduction 0.75 vs 0.31), but not across the full trial period (0.61 vs 0.54).

INTERPRETATION: The trial suggests a modest reduction in relapse risk and short-term symptom improvement with MMB for Moms versus usual care. Strengths include pragmatic design and low attrition (77–78% follow-up). However, the effect on relapse is modest (HR ~0.74), the CI approaches 1, and symptom benefits did not persist postpartum. Funding from NIH/NIMH supports credibility, but generalisability to non-academic settings or outside the USA is uncertain.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: MMB for Moms may offer a non-pharmacological adjunct for perinatal relapse prevention, particularly during pregnancy, but the clinical impact appears limited and not sustained postpartum; integration should be cautious pending replication and cost-effectiveness data.

articles.title: Effects of EEG neurofeedback in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review of randomised and non-randomised studies.
articles.authors: Rotkiewicz M, Yachou Y, Charef S, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pharmacotherapy is recommended as the first-line treatment for adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), yet some individuals show partial or inadequate response associated with adverse effects. These limitations have prompted interest in adjunctive or alternative interventions. Electroencephalography (EEG) neurofeedback is a non-pharmacological intervention for ADHD, which enables self-regulation of neural activity. This systematic review synthesised clinical, cognitive, and electrophysiological outcomes of EEG neurofeedback in adult ADHD, and examined standard versus personalised training protocols. METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, four databases (PubMed, ScienceDirect, Ovid, Web of Science) were searched from 1960 to October 2025 for this PROSPERO-registered review (ID: CRD420251020898). Eligible studies included adults (≥ 18 years) with a formal ADHD diagnosis undergoing EEG neurofeedback. Outcomes comprised symptom severity, cognitive performance, electrophysiology, and adverse events. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and ROBINS-I V2. RESULTS: Seven studies (three RCTs, four non-randomised; n = 390) met inclusion criteria. Protocols included theta/beta (n = 1), slow cortical potential (n = 1), alpha downregulation training (n = 1) and personalised approaches guided by individual alpha peak frequency (n = 3) or QEEG profiles (n = 1). Naturalistic and personalised studies reported large symptom reductions, whereas RCTs revealed small, gen
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined whether EEG neurofeedback improves symptoms, cognition, or brain activity in adults with ADHD, comparing standard and personalised training protocols. Seven studies (three RCTs, four non-randomised; n = 390) were included.

FINDINGS: RCTs showed small, generally non-significant effects on ADHD symptoms versus controls (effect sizes not reported). Non-randomised studies reported larger symptom reductions, but with high risk of bias. Cognitive gains were inconsistent and likely due to practice effects. Protocol-specific EEG changes were observed without convergence across studies. No treatment-related adverse events were reported.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by small samples, heterogeneous protocols, variable controls, and risk of bias. RCTs do not currently support efficacy over placebo. Non-randomised studies suggest potential benefit but are prone to confounding. High-quality, blinded RCTs with standardised outcome measures are needed to determine clinical utility.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: EEG neurofeedback cannot be recommended as an evidence-based treatment for adult ADHD based on current data. Clinicians should discuss this uncertainty with patients and consider established treatments while awaiting better trials.

articles.title: Undertreatment of Wernicke encephalopathy in alcohol-related clinical contexts: a scoping review of diagnosis, thiamine regimens, and clinical management.
articles.authors: Goldani AAS, Feitosa G, Colchete EV, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Wernicke encephalopathy (WE) is a potentially reversible neurological emergency that remains frequently missed and undertreated in patients with alcohol use disorder (AUD). Although thiamine is widely accepted as the cornerstone of prevention and treatment, diagnostic uncertainty, limited comparative evidence, and heterogeneous clinical recommendations contribute to substantial variability in real-world management. This scoping review aimed to map the available evidence on the diagnosis and clinical management of WE in patients with AUD or clinically significant alcohol use, with particular attention to practice variability, undertreatment, and clinically actionable gaps in care. METHODS: We conducted a scoping review in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidance. Electronic databases and trial registries were searched for studies addressing the diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of WE in populations with AUD or clinically significant alcohol use. Eligible sources included randomized controlled trials, observational studies, clinical audits, and implementation-focused reports. Data were charted and synthesized thematically. RESULTS: A total of 26 studies were included. The evidence base was limited and heterogeneous. Only two randomized controlled trials evaluated thiamine regimens, and no consensus emerged regarding optimal dosing. Diagnostic criteria for WE varied widely across studies, with inconsistent use of formal criteria such as the Caine criteria. Across observ
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Wernicke encephalopathy (WE) is a preventable neurological emergency in alcohol use disorder (AUD) that is often missed or undertreated due to diagnostic uncertainty and heterogeneous management. This scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) mapped evidence on diagnosis and thiamine regimens in AUD or clinically significant alcohol use, focusing on practice variability and undertreatment.

FINDINGS: Only 26 studies were included, with only two RCTs on thiamine regimens; no consensus on optimal dosing emerged. Diagnostic criteria varied widely, and observational studies consistently reported undertreatment, including delayed initiation and frequent use of oral thiamine in high-risk scenarios. Protocolized, guideline-concordant care was associated with earlier parenteral thiamine use in suspected/confirmed WE.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited, heterogeneous, and underpowered, with no clear optimal thiamine regimen. While diagnostic variability and undertreatment are well-documented, the strength of conclusions is constrained by the lack of high-quality trials and inconsistent diagnostic criteria. Early recognition and parenteral thiamine in high-risk cases remain plausible but unproven strategies to reduce morbidity.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should prioritize early suspicion of WE in AUD patients, use parenteral thiamine in high-risk cases, and follow local protocols where available, while acknowledging the lack of definitive evidence for optimal dosing or regimen.

articles.title: Protocol for a parallel-group superiority randomized controlled trial comparing Sage- a couple psychotherapy- to supportive individual psychotherapy for borderline personality disorder.
articles.authors: Fitzpatrick S, Arunagiri V, Traynor JM, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Although borderline personality disorder (BPD) is associated with substantial mortality and morbidity, frontline BPD interventions are difficult to access and have suboptimal efficacy. Therefore, there is a pressing need to develop and test brief, optimized BPD interventions. BPD is associated with disrupted intimate relationships, and recent theoretical models suggest that such disruptions may play a central role in driving BPD pathology. This led to the development of Sage, a protocolized, conjoint psychotherapeutic intervention delivered to people with BPD and their intimate partners to treat BPD and simultaneously improve relationship conflict and intimate partner's mental health. While preliminary research supports the efficacy of Sage, a key next step is identifying whether Sage is more efficacious compared to standard care in improving its targets. This manuscript outlines the study protocol for a single-blind, parallel two-arm randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing Sage to a supportive psychotherapy that is delivered separately to people with BPD and their intimate partners. METHODS: Couples wherein one member has BPD (target N = 152 couples) are actively being recruited. After eligibility and baseline assessments are complete, couples are randomized to Sage or Supportive Individual Psychotherapy. Weekly supervision meetings are held for both conditions by independent supervisors to ensure intervention adherence and prevent drift. Primary (BPD symptom
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) carries high mortality and morbidity, and frontline treatments are often inaccessible or only partially effective. Sage is a novel, protocolized couple psychotherapy for BPD that targets both patient symptoms and relationship conflict, but its superiority over standard supportive care has not yet been tested in a rigorous trial. This is a single-blind, parallel-group RCT protocol comparing Sage to supportive individual psychotherapy in 152 couples where one partner has BPD.

FINDINGS: The trial randomizes couples to 16 weeks of Sage (couple-based) versus supportive individual psychotherapy (separate sessions for patient and partner). Primary outcome is BPD symptom change; secondary outcomes include relationship conflict and partner mental health. Assessments occur at baseline, mid-treatment, post-treatment, and 1-, 3-, and 6-month follow-ups. Primary analysis will use intent-to-treat generalized mixed linear models. No results are reported yet.

INTERPRETATION: This is a well-designed, adequately powered RCT with masked assessors and independent supervision to prevent drift, which strengthens internal validity. However, as a protocol paper, no outcome data are available, so efficacy, effect sizes, and safety remain unknown. The design addresses an important gap—testing whether adding a relationship-focused component improves outcomes—but generalizability may be limited by the requirement of a stable intimate partner and the exclusion of individuals without one.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Until results are published, clinicians should view Sage as an experimental intervention. Standard evidence-based treatments for BPD (e.g., DBT, MBT) remain first-line while this trial is ongoing.

articles.title: [Efficacy and tolerability of co-administration of clozapine with atypical antipsychotics in patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, comorbid with chemical addictions].
articles.journal: Zh Nevrol Psikhiatr Im S S Korsakova
articles.authors: Selivanov GY, Bokhan NA, Shushpanova TV, et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To compare the efficacy and tolerability of combination therapy with clozapine and atypical antipsychotics for patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, comorbid with chemical addictions. MATERIAL AND METHODS: A clinical study was conducted from 2018 to 2026 in various psychiatric departments in the North-Western, Siberian, and Ural regions of the Russian Federation. The study included a total of 470 male and female participants diagnosed with therapeutically resistant paranoid schizophrenia, comprising individuals with and without concomitant chemical addictions: n=80 without addictions; n=390 with unrelated chemical addictions (opioid, cannabinoid, psychostimulant, and ethanol dependence). Participants were randomly allocated into six treatment groups receiving distinct combinations of medications: clozapine with cariprazine (n=84), lurasidone (n=84), aripiprazole (n=78), risperidone (n=84), olanzapine (n=70), or brexpiprazole (n=70). The clinical status of patients was assessed at weeks 2 and 6 of the therapeutic regimen. RESULTS: A comparative analysis of treatment efficacy indicated significant differences between therapy groups across various psychometric scales (p<0.05). The co-administration of clozapine with cariprazine, and to a lesser extent with lurasidone, demonstrated the most pronounced therapeutic effect within a 42-day treatment period (p<0.05), specifically in alleviating psychotic symptoms and reducing the negative symptoms characteristic
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study compared six clozapine-plus-atypical-antipsychotic combinations in 470 adults with treatment-resistant paranoid schizophrenia, 83 % of whom also had a comorbid substance use disorder. It is a six-arm, open-label RCT conducted across multiple Russian psychiatric centres (2018–2026).

FINDINGS: After 42 days, combinations with cariprazine and, to a lesser extent, lurasidone produced significantly greater reductions in positive and negative symptoms than the other four regimens (p < 0.05). The cariprazine group also had the longest subsequent outpatient treatment duration. No adverse events were attributed to the combinations.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and of low internal validity: randomisation method and allocation concealment are not described, raters were unblinded, and no adverse-event monitoring protocol is mentioned. The 42-day horizon is short for a chronic disorder, and the lack of placebo or clozapine-monotherapy arms precludes firm conclusions about incremental benefit. Effect sizes and confidence intervals are not reported, so statistical versus clinical significance cannot be judged.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings do not yet justify changing practice. Clozapine plus cariprazine may be considered on a case-by-case basis when negative symptoms dominate, but clinicians should await larger, longer, and better-controlled trials before adopting this strategy routinely.

articles.title: Complex post-traumatic stress disorder in refugees, asylum seekers, and internally displaced people: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Melkam M, Xu C, Maccallum F, et al.
articles.abstract: Background: Forcibly displaced populations, including refugees, asylum seekers, and internally displaced persons, are frequently exposed to severe, prolonged and repeated trauma from which escape is difficult or impossible. Such exposures increase the risk for complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD), defined by core PTSD symptoms alongside disturbances in self-organisation (DSO), including affective dysregulation, negative self-concept, and relational difficulties. However, the prevalence of CPTSD in forcibly displaced populations has not yet been quantitatively synthesised, and the added value of the CPTSD construct over PTSD in this population has not been examined.Methods: This systematic review and meta-analysis searched five databases from inception to January 2026. A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted to estimate pooled CPTSD prevalence, with pre-specified subgroup analyses, meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses.Results: Twenty studies met inclusion criteria, representing 17 independent samples (n = 12,504). Reported CPTSD prevalence varied from 3.0% to 74.6%. The random-effects pooled prevalence, retained as a descriptive summary of the included studies, was 20.9% (95% CI [12.6%, 32.6%]), the 95% prediction interval was [1.7%, 80.3%]. Between-study heterogeneity was very high (I² = 98.3%). Recruitment context was strongly associated with prevalence: estimates averaged 10.6% in community-based samples and 55.2% in treatment-seeking samples. Asylum see
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified the prevalence of complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD) in forcibly displaced populations (refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced people) and assessed whether CPTSD adds clinically meaningful information beyond classic PTSD in this group. Twenty studies (17 independent samples, n = 12,504) were synthesised.

FINDINGS: Pooled CPTSD prevalence was 20.9 % (95 % CI 12.6–32.6 %), but heterogeneity was extreme (I² = 98.3 %; 95 % prediction interval 1.7–80.3 %). Prevalence was 10.6 % in community samples versus 55.2 % in treatment-seeking samples. Asylum seekers showed higher rates than refugees. Across four studies, post-migration living difficulties correlated more strongly with disturbances in self-organisation (DSO) than with core PTSD symptoms.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is large but highly heterogeneous and geographically uneven. The pooled estimate should be treated as a descriptive summary rather than a generalisable prevalence. The stronger link between ongoing adversity and DSO supports the clinical relevance of the CPTSD construct in displaced populations, but causal inferences are limited by cross-sectional designs and inconsistent reporting of confounders.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: CPTSD appears common in forcibly displaced people, especially among asylum seekers and those seeking care, suggesting routine screening and trauma-focused interventions are warranted; however, local prevalence may vary widely, so services should adapt to local post-migration stressors rather than rely on a single global estimate.

articles.title: Caution before canonisation: a clinical and implementation science perspective on psychedelics.
articles.authors: Paris A, Thoma F, Velentza A, et al.
articles.abstract: Recent advances in psychedelic research have renewed interest in the potential therapeutic role of psychedelic-assisted interventions in psychiatry. Early clinical trials suggest that compounds such as psilocybin and MDMA, administered within structured therapeutic frameworks, may produce rapid symptom improvements for conditions including depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and substance use disorders. While these findings are scientifically promising, the current evidence base remains characterized by methodological and translational limitations. Many studies involve small samples, short follow-up periods, functional unblinding, and heterogeneous safety reporting, which complicate causal interpretation and generalizability. In the present paper, we examine psychedelic therapies through clinical, methodological, ethical, and implementation science lenses. We argue that current trials primarily demonstrate proof-of-concept efficacy under controlled conditions rather than readiness for large-scale clinical adoption. Responsible translation therefore requires stronger evidence regarding durability, safety monitoring, comparative effectiveness, and real-world implementation. Psychedelic therapies represent an important emerging research direction, but continued rigorous evaluation and improved implementation of established evidence-based interventions remain central to addressing mental disorders.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review critically appraises the emerging evidence for psychedelic-assisted therapies (e.g., psilocybin, MDMA) in psychiatry, focusing on their therapeutic promise and methodological limitations. It synthesizes early clinical trials across depression, PTSD, and substance use disorders to assess readiness for routine care.

FINDINGS: Early trials report rapid symptom improvements under controlled conditions, but many suffer from small sample sizes (often <50 per arm), short follow-up (weeks to months), functional unblinding (due to psychoactive effects), and inconsistent safety reporting. The evidence base is preliminary, heterogeneous, and lacks comparative effectiveness against established treatments.

INTERPRETATION: The review highlights proof-of-concept efficacy but emphasizes major translational gaps: durability of effects, standardized safety protocols, and real-world feasibility. The lack of robust, long-term data and methodological rigor limits causal inference and generalizability. Ethical and implementation challenges (e.g., training, access) further complicate adoption. The findings are promising but not yet definitive.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Psychedelic therapies remain experimental; clinicians should await larger, longer, and methodologically rigorous trials before considering integration into routine care. Current evidence supports continued research but not routine use outside specialized settings.

articles.title: A combined study of whole-exome sequencing and structural neuroimaging markers in bipolar disorder.
articles.authors: Park SW, Han KM, Oh EY, et al.
articles.abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a highly heritable psychiatric disorder. An increasing number of whole-exome sequencing (WES) studies have been conducted on psychiatric research. However, few studies have investigated the association between single nucleotide variants (SNVs) in WES and structural brain changes in patients with BD. We conducted WES on 93 patients with BD and 161 healthy controls (HCs) to detect germline variants and copy number alterations (CNAs), as well as the gene-based effects of rare variants on BD. The impact of genetic factors on structural neuroimaging markers, including cortical thickness and white matter tract integrity, was examined using neuroimaging-genetic association analysis. We identified 382 BD-related genes, including SYNE1, PKHD1L1, FRAS1, and ZFHX4, from a systematic review, and the most frequently mutated genes. We identified a new gene, GNB3, which harbors a significant burden of rare nonsynonymous variants that affect BD. By integrating WES and structural neuroimaging data, we found that the single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) rs56850341 in KMT2C was substantially correlated with structural neuroimaging measures, including cortical thickness and white matter tract integrity. In the present study, we suggest that rare nonsynonymous variants in GNB3 may be involved in the pathophysiology of BD, and that highly contributing heritable genetic variant in KMT2C may influence brain structural changes.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study explores whether rare genetic variants identified via whole-exome sequencing (WES) in patients with bipolar disorder (BD) are associated with structural brain changes, addressing a gap in understanding the genetic underpinnings of BD using neuroimaging-genetic association analysis.

FINDINGS: WES was conducted on 93 BD patients and 161 healthy controls (HCs). The study identified 382 BD-related genes, including SYNE1, PKHD1L1, FRAS1, and ZFHX4, and highlighted a novel gene, GNB3, with a significant burden of rare nonsynonymous variants linked to BD. Additionally, the SNP rs56850341 in KMT2C was found to be substantially correlated with cortical thickness and white matter tract integrity in BD patients.

INTERPRETATION: This is a small, exploratory case-control study combining WES with neuroimaging, which limits generalizability and causal inference. The findings suggest potential genetic contributors to BD and brain structural changes, but the sample size is modest, and the associations require replication in larger, longitudinal cohorts. The clinical significance of these genetic variants remains uncertain without further functional validation or larger-scale studies.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Currently, these findings do not directly inform clinical practice, as the genetic variants identified are not actionable for diagnosis or treatment. Further research is needed to determine if these associations are reproducible and clinically meaningful.

articles.title: A novel digital hybrid care model for maternal mental health: preliminary findings from a matched retrospective cohort study.
articles.authors: Calvert E, Chen K, Moon KC, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Perinatal mood and anxiety disorders are among the most common complications of pregnancy and the postpartum period, while access to timely, evidence-based mental health care remains limited. Although smartphone applications may help extend access to care, recent research highlights notable limitations, including variable quality and unclear effectiveness. Hybrid care models, which integrate asynchronous app use with synchronous clinician-delivered care, have therefore emerged as a promising alternative. This study examined one such model, the Digital Clinic, to assess its potential to help bridge this treatment gap by analyzing clinical outcomes among peripartum women receiving care for anxiety and depressive symptoms. METHODS: Pregnant and postpartum women referred for anxiety and depression of peripartum onset received 8 weeks of synchronous, virtual, evidence-based CBT from a trained clinician. This treatment was complemented by the asynchronous use of the mindLAMP app, providing digital phenotyping, psychoeducation, and CBT skills, with the support of a Digital Health Navigator. Preliminary clinical outcomes were assessed by comparing GAD-7 and PHQ-9 scores from intake to the completion of the treatment course. RESULTS: This preliminary matched retrospective cohort study included 13 peripartum and 39 matched non-peripartum patients receiving care through the Digital Clinic. Among the peripartum cohort, GAD-7 scores decreased from 14.4 (SD = 5.0) at intake to
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Peripartum mood and anxiety disorders are common but often undertreated due to access barriers. This matched retrospective cohort study evaluated a hybrid digital care model (Digital Clinic) combining clinician-delivered CBT with app-based support for peripartum women with anxiety/depression.

FINDINGS: The peripartum cohort (n=13) showed a large reduction in GAD-7 scores from 14.4 (SD 5.0) to 5.5 (SD 4.3), mean change −8.9 points (p < 0.01; d = −1.91, 95% CI −2.89 to −0.93). PHQ-9 scores fell from 9.3 (SD 5.9) to 5.6 (SD 4.8), mean change −3.7 points (p = 0.055; d = −0.68, 95% CI −1.41 to 0.05).

INTERPRETATION: The study’s retrospective design, small peripartum sample, and lack of a concurrent control group limit causal inference. The large anxiety effect is statistically robust but based on a tiny cohort; depressive symptom change was not statistically significant. Funding sources and blinding status were not reported, raising potential bias risks. Larger, adequately powered RCTs are needed to confirm effectiveness and generalisability.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These preliminary findings suggest a hybrid digital model may reduce anxiety symptoms in peripartum women, but current evidence is insufficient to change routine practice; further rigorous trials are required before recommending widespread adoption.

articles.title: Clinical and genetic correlates of a circadian subtype of depression in the Australian Genetics of Depression Study.
articles.authors: Tonini E, Crouse JJ, Shin M, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Although commonly accepted depressive subtypes reflect phenotypic differences, there has been minimal progress in identification of discrete pathophysiological pathways, biomarkers or differential therapeutic approaches to effectively guide clinical management. AIMS: To test the biological validity and clinical utility of a circadian subtype of depression on the basis of clinical course, differential medication response (self-reported) and genetic risk profile. METHOD: Cross-sectional data were drawn from the nationwide Australian Genetics of Depression Study. Participants were classified as having a 'circadian' or 'non-circadian' subtype of depression on the basis of meeting criteria for at least three binary circadian-associated features: social jetlag, seasonality, delayed sleep midpoint, evening chronotype, morning tiredness and hypersomnia. Clinical course characteristics were compared. Associations with response to commonly prescribed antidepressants and polygenic risk scores for mental disorders and sleep, circadian, metabolic and inflammatory traits were investigated using logistic regression models. RESULTS: A total of 2604 participants (23%; 80% female; mean age 37.87 ± 13.62 years) had a circadian subtype. They reported an earlier age at onset (P < 0.001), more severe clinical features including (hypo)manic-like and psychotic-like experiences, suicidality, psychological distress and somatic complaints (all P < 0.001), weight gain during depressive episo
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study from the Australian Genetics of Depression Study examined whether a circadian subtype of depression—defined by ≥3 circadian features—differs clinically, pharmacologically, and genetically from non-circadian depression in 2604 adults (80% female, mean age 37.9 years).

FINDINGS: The circadian subtype (23% of participants) showed earlier onset (P<0.001), more severe symptoms (including suicidality and psychotic-like experiences, P<0.001), greater weight gain during episodes (P<0.001), and poorer self-reported response to SSRIs (OR 0.88 [95% CI 0.82–0.94]) and SNRIs (OR 0.89 [95% CI 0.83–0.97]). It was associated with higher polygenic risk for ADHD, depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, metabolic traits, inflammatory markers, and later chronotype (all P<0.05).

INTERPRETATION: The study’s cross-sectional design and self-reported outcomes limit causal inference. Selection bias (female-predominant, online-recruited sample) and lack of clinician-rated outcomes reduce external validity. The small effect sizes (ORs ~0.88–1.15) suggest limited clinical predictiveness at present. Genetic associations are hypothesis-generating and require replication.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No immediate treatment change is warranted; the circadian subtype may flag higher symptom burden and lower SSRI/SNRI response, but evidence is preliminary. Future longitudinal studies with objective measures and clinician-rated outcomes are needed before considering tailored interventions.

articles.title: From Protective Factors to Mechanisms: Charting the Neurobiology of Schizophrenia Resilience.
articles.authors: Bittner RA, Barnes-Scheufler CV, Reif A, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND HYPOTHESIS: Elucidating the neurobiological and psychological mechanisms that promote resilience to the adverse effects of schizophrenia's genetic and environmental risk architecture may reveal new avenues for advancing treatment and prevention. Identification of genetic loci associated with schizophrenia resilience enables links between protective polygenic variation, non-genetic resilience factors, and intermediate phenotypes. This approach may help identify protective traits and delineate potentially evolutionarily shaped resilience mechanisms that attenuate schizophrenia pathophysiology across biological levels. STUDY DESIGN: This narrative review integrates current concepts in psychiatric resilience research with findings from schizophrenia resilience genetics and evolutionary medicine. Within a decompositional, dimensional framework, we summarize evidence for trait-level resilience factors that may be linked to schizophrenia resilience variants and discuss candidate neurobiological mechanisms. STUDY RESULTS: Schizophrenia's substantial fitness costs and evolutionary dynamics may have favored common genetic variants that buffer elevated polygenic liability and promote resilience to the disorder. Existing evidence implicates protective traits across obstetric, immunological, cognitive, and visual-system domains as candidate mediators of resilience to schizophrenia pathophysiology. CONCLUSIONS: Current findings suggest that common genetic variants may confer
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review explores neurobiological and psychological mechanisms that may promote resilience to schizophrenia, integrating genetic, evolutionary, and phenotypic evidence to identify potential protective factors and pathways that could inform future prevention and treatment strategies.

FINDINGS: The review highlights that common genetic variants may confer resilience by enhancing neural plasticity, fluid intelligence, and visual cognition. Candidate protective traits span obstetric, immunological, cognitive, and visual domains, though direct links to specific resilience variants remain unestablished. Evolutionary pressures may have shaped these adaptations to buffer polygenic liability for schizophrenia.

INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this work synthesizes emerging but preliminary evidence rather than definitive findings. The lack of direct causal links between resilience variants and mechanisms limits conclusions. The evolutionary framing is speculative, and many proposed pathways (e.g., immune or obstetric) require further validation. The discussion of neural plasticity and cognition is plausible but not yet supported by robust empirical data.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review does not yet change clinical practice but suggests future research directions, such as targeting neural plasticity or cognitive resilience in early intervention strategies. Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting these hypotheses until mechanistic and translational evidence emerges.

articles.title: Dynamic gene expression signatures predict psychotherapy response in PTSD.
articles.authors: Xu C, Bader HN, Flory JD, et al.
articles.abstract: Static blood-based biomarkers provide limited insight into psychiatric illness and recovery, largely because they capture only a single, unperturbed snapshot of inherently dynamic biological systems. In this study, we applied a dynamic, longitudinal dual-state approach to characterize peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) transcriptional trajectories associated with psychotherapy outcomes in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). PBMC transcriptional profiles were generated for veterans with PTSD (n = 46, 21, and 17, respectively) and controls (n = 26, 26, and 23) at pre-treatment, post-treatment, and follow-up. The PTSD cohort with profiles across all three timepoints was divided into responders (n = 6) and non-responders (n = 11) based on their Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5 (CAPS-5) trajectories. All subjects were profiled in both unstimulated and dexamethasone-stimulated states. At pre-treatment, unstimulated responders and non-responders exhibited pronounced transcriptional differences exceeding those observed between PTSD and controls. Longitudinally, unstimulated responders showed a marked shift toward control-like profiles, whereas non-responders retained persistent divergence. Pathway analyses identified a prominent temporal signal within Class C/3 G-protein-coupled receptor pathways driven largely by bitter taste receptors (TAS2Rs), along with subgroup-specific regulation of GABAB, opioid, and NMDA receptor signaling. Dexamethasone-induced responses
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study investigated whether dynamic, longitudinal changes in gene expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) could predict psychotherapy response in veterans with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). It used a dual-state approach (unstimulated and dexamethasone-stimulated) to assess transcriptional trajectories in PTSD patients (n=17 with complete data) and controls (n=23) at pre-treatment, post-treatment, and follow-up.

FINDINGS: At pre-treatment, unstimulated responders (n=6) and non-responders (n=11) showed pronounced transcriptional differences, exceeding those between PTSD patients and controls. Longitudinally, responders shifted toward control-like gene expression profiles, while non-responders retained persistent divergence. Pathway analyses highlighted Class C/3 G-protein-coupled receptor pathways (e.g., bitter taste receptors, TAS2Rs) and subgroup-specific regulation of GABAB, opioid, and NMDA receptor signaling. Dexamethasone-induced responses further differentiated subgroups, suggesting glucocorticoid sensitivity as a predictor of treatment outcomes.

INTERPRETATION: This is a small, exploratory cohort study (n=17 PTSD patients) without randomization or blinding, limiting causal inference and generalizability. The dynamic dual-state approach is innovative but requires validation in larger, more diverse samples with standardized psychotherapy protocols. The observed transcriptional shifts in responders are intriguing but not yet clinically actionable due to the small sample size and lack of replication. The study highlights potential biomarkers (e.g., TAS2Rs, glucocorticoid sensitivity) but does not establish their predictive utility or mechanistic role in PTSD recovery.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings are preliminary and do not yet change clinical practice. They suggest that dynamic gene expression profiling *might* one day help predict psychotherapy response in PTSD, but further research is needed to confirm these signals and their clinical utility. For now, treatment decisions should rely on established clinical assessments (e.g., CAPS-5) rather than gene expression markers.

articles.title: Investigating the role of drama-based strategies in addressing psychological trauma: a systematic review.
articles.authors: Oliver E, Grummitt L, Ewing R, et al.
articles.abstract: Background: Drama-based techniques have been increasingly implemented with trauma-exposed populations. However, the evidence base remains conceptually and methodologically heterogeneous, with substantial variation in how trauma is defined, how interventions are described, and which trauma-related outcomes are assessed.Objective: This review aimed to synthesise empirical studies examining drama-based interventions for individuals exposed to trauma. The review describes the characteristics of drama-based interventions, the types of trauma addressed, the pattern and range of trauma-related psychological outcomes assessed, and the methodological quality and certainty of the available evidence.Methods: A search was conducted across Scopus, PsycINFO, MEDLINE, and Web of Science Core Collection databases on 29 October 2025. Studies published in English within the past 20 years were eligible if they examined a drama-based intervention in a trauma-exposed population and reported trauma-related psychological outcomes. Methodological quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE.Results: Twenty-six studies met inclusion criteria out of 1,461 screened papers. Interventions were grouped as psychodrama, dramatherapy, applied theatre, other drama-based psychotherapeutic interventions, and other. The most commonly examined outcomes were depression, anxiety, and PTSD symptoms. Across intervention types, some studies reported im
articles.summary: Background: Drama-based techniques have been increasingly implemented with trauma-exposed populations. However, the evidence base remains conceptually and methodologically heterogeneous, with substantial variation in how trauma is defined, how interventions are described, and which trauma-related outcomes are assessed.Objective: This review aimed to synthesise empirical studies examining drama-based interventions for individuals exposed to trauma.

articles.title: Addressing heterogeneity in trauma responses in research and clinical practice: reflections and recommendations from early career researchers.
articles.authors: Dasen L, Alison Büeler L, Kemmere B, et al.
articles.abstract: Background: There is considerable heterogeneity in how individuals respond to potentially traumatic events (PTEs). Recognising and addressing this heterogeneity has become an increasingly important focus within psychotraumatology, leading to the development of diverse research and clinical approaches. Yet, there remains an opportunity to further integrate these developments into research and clinical practice.Objective: This letter critically reflects on recent developments in psychotrauma research and practice and discusses complementary methodological and clinical approaches that may further account for heterogeneity in trauma-related responses.Methods: Drawing on current literature and reflections from a recent international early career researcher networking event, we present reflections and practical recommendations across five domains: conceptualisation, sampling and eligibility, measurement and outcomes, analysis, and intervention.Results: We identify several promising developments and opportunities for further advancing the field: (1) complementing categorical diagnostic frameworks with transdiagnostic and adiagnostic approaches; (2) broadening eligibility criteria to include comorbid, subclinical, and diverse trauma-exposed populations; (3) expanding outcome assessment beyond PTSD symptom reduction to include transdiagnostic, culturally sensitive outcome measures valued by patients; (4) incorporating person-centered analytic strategies to better capture within-sample
articles.summary: Background: There is considerable heterogeneity in how individuals respond to potentially traumatic events (PTEs). Recognising and addressing this heterogeneity has become an increasingly important focus within psychotraumatology, leading to the development of diverse research and clinical approaches.

articles.title: The effectiveness of meaning-based interventions in reducing suicide-related vulnerability: A systematic review.
articles.authors: Gwon TK, Jung HO
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Existential factors such as loss of meaning play a central role in suicide-related vulnerability, yet most prevention interventions target symptom reduction. We aimed to systematically review the effects of meaning-based interventions on suicide-related outcomes and characterize the mechanisms through which these effects operate. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Six databases (PubMed, Web of Science, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Research Information Sharing Service, and Korean Studies Information Service System) were searched from inception to April 2026. Studies were included if they evaluated meaning-based interventions and reported suicide-related outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 for randomized trials and RoBANS for nonrandomized studies. Given heterogeneity across populations, interventions, and outcomes, findings were synthesized narratively by domain. RESULTS: Ten studies were included (7 randomized controlled trials, 2 quasi-experimental studies, and 1 secondary analysis). Meaning-based interventions most consistently improved existential outcomes, including meaning in life, spiritual well-being, and quality of life. Emotional outcomes showed partial and heterogeneous effects. Suicide-related outcomes, including hopelessness, demoralization, and suicidal ideation, generally showed reductions, although effects varied across studies. Mechanistically, most studies showed patterns of indirect pathways, whereby imp
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The review asks whether meaning-based interventions (e.g., meaning-centered therapy, dignity therapy) reduce suicide-related vulnerability (ideation, hopelessness, demoralization) and how any benefits are mediated. Ten heterogeneous studies (7 RCTs, 2 quasi-experimental, 1 secondary analysis) were synthesized narratively.

FINDINGS: Across studies, meaning-based interventions consistently improved existential outcomes (meaning in life, spiritual well-being, quality of life) with moderate effect sizes. Emotional outcomes showed mixed and smaller effects. Suicide-related outcomes (hopelessness, demoralization, suicidal ideation) generally decreased, but results varied by population and intervention; no pooled effect sizes were reported.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small, methodologically mixed, and lacks meta-analytic pooling, limiting certainty. Most studies were at moderate risk of bias; heterogeneity in populations (e.g., advanced cancer, veterans, general psychiatric outpatients) and interventions precludes firm conclusions. The pattern suggests potential benefit via existential pathways, but causal mediation remains unproven. Larger, preregistered RCTs with standardized outcomes and mediation analyses are needed.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify wholesale adoption of meaning-based interventions for suicide prevention outside research settings. Clinicians may consider adjunctive meaning-centered approaches for patients with existential distress, while monitoring suicide-related outcomes closely and integrating with evidence-based treatments.

articles.title: Vitamin D Supplementation and Improvement in Insomnia Symptoms Among Malaysian Women With Vitamin D Deficiency: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.authors: Puspitasari RM, Mohamad Noor Z, Setiawan D, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Insomnia is a prevalent sleep disorder associated with adverse physical, psychological, and functional outcomes. Emerging evidence suggests that vitamin D deficiency may contribute to sleep disturbances. Women are more likely to have lower serum vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D]) levels than men, and they also report a higher prevalence of insomnia. Although several studies have proposed that vitamin D supplementation may improve insomnia symptoms, findings remain inconsistent, and evidence from Southeast Asian populations is limited. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of weekly vitamin D₃ supplementation in improving insomnia symptoms, sleep quality, sleep efficiency, and functional outcomes among Malaysian women with vitamin D deficiency. METHODS: This study is a double-blind, parallel-group, randomized placebo-controlled trial conducted among women aged 19-50 years with serum 25(OH)D levels <20 ng/mL and insomnia symptoms. Participants are randomized to receive either vitamin D₃ capsules (50,000 IU/wk) or placebo (1 capsule/wk) for 9 weeks. The study is conducted in a community setting. Primary outcomes include insomnia severity assessed using the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), sleep quality measured by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and sleep efficiency objectively assessed using actigraphy. Secondary outcomes include daytime sleepiness measured using the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) and functional outcomes assessed u
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Insomnia is common and disabling, and low vitamin D levels may contribute to sleep disturbance, especially in women. This is a double-blind, parallel-group randomized controlled trial (RCT) protocol testing weekly high-dose vitamin D₃ (50 000 IU) versus placebo for 9 weeks in Malaysian women aged 19–50 years with serum 25(OH)D <20 ng/mL and insomnia symptoms.

FINDINGS: Recruitment began December 2023; by July 2026, 42 were screened, 33 enrolled, 22 completed, 4 were still receiving intervention, and 1 withdrew. No efficacy results are yet available because the trial is ongoing and unblinded.

INTERPRETATION: This is a well-designed RCT protocol with clear allocation concealment and validated sleep measures, but no outcome data are available to judge efficacy. The small sample size and single-centre, community-based setting limit generalisability. Until results are published, any claim of benefit remains speculative.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine vitamin D supplementation for insomnia. Clinicians should await trial results before considering vitamin D as adjunctive therapy; CBT remains first-line.

articles.title: Characterizing Behavioral Engagement in Smartphone Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Obsessive Compulsive Disorder: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.authors: Weingarden H, Jonathan GK, Hoeppner SS, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) are increasingly popular for their ability to disseminate evidence-based treatments in a scalable, accessible way. Engagement with digital treatments is critical for effectiveness but remains poorly defined and measured. Most studies rely on subjective self-reports or 1 or 2 objective metrics, overlooking the multidimensional nature of how users interact with DMHIs. OBJECTIVE: This exploratory secondary analysis applied a road map for comprehensive behavioral engagement measurement, developed for a prior smartphone cognitive behavioral therapy program for body dysmorphic disorder, to a 12-week randomized controlled trial of smartphone cognitive behavioral therapy for obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD; N=60). Aims were to (1) comprehensively characterize behavioral engagement using 21 objective app analytics-based variables, (2) identify distinct behavioral engagement profiles via cluster analysis, (3) assess whether profiles were differentially associated with OCD symptom change, and (4) evaluate associations between profiles and pretreatment credibility, expectancy, posttreatment satisfaction, and perceived app quality. METHODS: Behavioral engagement was measured via 21 objective variables derived from app analytics, spanning use volume, frequency, feature usage, session duration, and temporal patterns. Hierarchical agglomerative cluster analysis identified engagement profiles. Associations between cluster membership a
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This secondary analysis of a 12-week RCT (N=60) examined behavioral engagement in smartphone cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for OCD using 21 objective app analytics variables. It aimed to characterize engagement profiles, link them to OCD symptom change, and explore associations with pretreatment credibility/expectancy and posttreatment satisfaction.

FINDINGS: Cluster analysis identified three engagement profiles: high (35%), moderate (52%), and low (13%) users. All clusters showed significant pre- to posttreatment reductions in OCD severity (Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale), with no significant differences in symptom change across clusters. Cluster 3 (low users) reported lower treatment credibility, expectancy, and satisfaction than cluster 2, while app quality ratings were similar across clusters.

INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates feasibility of multidimensional engagement measurement in digital CBT, but the lack of differential symptom improvement across engagement profiles challenges simplistic dose-response assumptions. The findings may reflect true equivalence in effectiveness across engagement levels or be limited by small sample size and insufficient power to detect meaningful differences. Pretreatment expectations appear linked to engagement patterns, suggesting a modifiable target for improving adherence.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These results imply that even low engagement with smartphone CBT for OCD may yield clinical benefit, though expectations may influence engagement and satisfaction. Clinicians should consider addressing pretreatment expectations to enhance participation, but should not assume higher engagement necessarily leads to better outcomes.

articles.title: Mortality Among People With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.authors: Corrigan L, Heywood L, Stewart GR, et al.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with adverse life outcomes and increased mortality. Clarifying the magnitude of mortality risks using international data and the potential association between medication and mortality is essential to inform clinical care and motivate public health strategies to address mortality. OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between ADHD and all-cause and cause-specific mortality and to assess whether mortality risk differs according to ADHD medication use. DATA SOURCES: A comprehensive search of PubMed, Web of Science, PsycINFO, EMBASE, MEDLINE, and CINAHL was conducted from database inception to July 8, 2025. STUDY SELECTION: Eligible studies included quantitative research across all age groups reporting all-cause and/or cause-specific mortality in individuals with ADHD, defined via diagnostic criteria, self-identification, trait measures, or ADHD polygenic risk scores. Exclusion criteria were nonoriginal research, qualitative studies, non-peer-reviewed publications, and studies not reporting mortality outcomes. DATA EXTRACTION AND SYNTHESIS: Data extraction was conducted independently by 2 reviewers. Study quality was assessed by 1 reviewer. Summary data were extracted from published reports, and pooled hazard ratios (HRs) were calculated using random-effects model meta-analysis. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and cause-specific mortality (suicide, unintentional or
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with increased all-cause and cause-specific mortality and whether ADHD medication modifies this risk. The study included 19 observational studies with over 15 million participants.

FINDINGS: ADHD was associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.71, 95% CI 1.31–2.24), suicide (HR 1.89, 95% CI 1.21–2.95), unintentional or intentional injury (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.22–2.00), and natural-cause mortality (HR 1.27, 95% CI 1.16–1.38). Among individuals with ADHD, medication use was associated with lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.64–0.87). Substantial heterogeneity was reported across studies.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests ADHD is linked to higher mortality across multiple causes, with medication associated with reduced risk. However, the observational nature of included studies, substantial heterogeneity, and potential confounding limit causal inference. The association between medication and reduced mortality may reflect confounding by indication or severity rather than a direct causal protective effect.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support timely diagnosis and treatment of ADHD, particularly given the elevated mortality risk. Clinicians should remain vigilant about suicide risk and injury prevention in this population, while recognizing that the protective effect of medication requires further confirmation in robust study designs.

articles.title: Concentrated Exposure Therapy vs Internet-Based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.authors: Jelinek L, Wille L, Scheunemann J, et al.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Given the high prevalence, chronicity, and associated disability of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), optimizing treatment is a global priority. The Bergen 4-day treatment (B4DT), a concentrated exposure-based intervention, may reduce treatment burden and improve access to evidence-based care. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of B4DT compared with internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy (iCBT) in reducing OCD symptom severity. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Single-center randomized controlled trial (1:1 allocation). Between May 8, 2024, and August 8, 2025, adults (aged 18 to 72 years) with OCD were enrolled and were followed up for 3 months. Key exclusion criteria included schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, acute suicidality, substance dependence, and recent psychopharmacological changes. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 6 weeks, 8 weeks (posttreatment), and 3 months (follow-up) by masked evaluators. INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomized to B4DT (including preparatory sessions) or an 8-week unguided iCBT program. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was the change in OCD symptom severity, measured by the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS). Secondary outcomes included self-reported OCD (OCI-R), dysfunctional cognitions, quality of life, depressive symptoms, experiential avoidance, global functioning, self-esteem, and treatment satisfaction. RESULTS: A total of 253 individuals were screened, and 119 were enrolled after 53 were
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This single-center randomized controlled trial (RCT) compared the efficacy of a concentrated 4-day exposure-based intervention (Bergen 4-day treatment, B4DT) with an 8-week unguided internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy (iCBT) for adults with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), assessing outcomes over 3 months.

FINDINGS: 119 adults (mean age 33.5 years, 66.4% women) were randomized to B4DT (n=60) or iCBT (n=59). At posttreatment, B4DT showed a significantly greater reduction in OCD symptoms (Y-BOCS) than iCBT (mean difference -7.9 points, 95% CI -9.7 to -6.0; Hedges g = -1.6). At 3-month follow-up, the difference remained significant but smaller (mean difference -5.6 points, 95% CI -7.8 to -3.4; Hedges g = -1.0). Response and remission rates at follow-up were higher with B4DT (61.4% vs 25.0% and 42.1% vs 13.6%, respectively).

INTERPRETATION: The study provides high-quality RCT evidence that B4DT is superior to unguided iCBT for OCD symptom reduction, with large effect sizes at posttreatment and moderate effects sustained at 3 months. Strengths include masked outcome assessment, intention-to-treat analysis, and clear superiority in both primary and secondary outcomes. However, the single-center design, predominantly female sample, and lack of active iCBT comparator (e.g., therapist-guided) limit generalizability. The concentrated format may improve access but requires replication in diverse settings.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: B4DT may offer a more effective and time-efficient alternative to unguided iCBT for OCD, particularly where rapid symptom reduction is prioritized. Clinicians should consider patient preferences and logistical constraints when choosing between formats, while awaiting broader validation.

articles.title: Home Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation With Gamified Cognitive Control Training for Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.authors: Dechantsreiter E, Padberg F, Benjamini Y, et al.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has emerged as a home-based treatment in major depressive disorder (MDD), although its effects are typically small to moderate and inconsistently observed. Because tDCS may act synergistically with behavioral interventions, combining both approaches represents a promising strategy for developing more effective home-based treatments for MDD. OBJECTIVE: To investigate the feasibility, safety, and efficacy of home-based tDCS and concurrent gamified cognitive control training (CCT) in adults with MDD. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This multicenter, double-masked, parallel-group, randomized clinical trial with follow-up at week 10, masking checks at 2 time points, and expectancy assessments was conducted at 3 university hospitals in Latvia, Germany, and Israel between June 22, 2021, and August 8, 2024. Participants included adults aged 18 to 65 years with MDD, 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores of at least 13, and no or stable antidepressant medication. INTERVENTION: Participants were randomly assigned 1:1 to active tDCS (2 mA; anode F3, cathode F4) plus a gamified CCT or sham tDCS plus a sham game. Participants were asked to complete 30 home treatment sessions (30 minutes each) over 6 weeks with software-assisted electrode positioning. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was feasibility, defined as completing at least 20 of 30 sessions with greater than 50% probability. The secondary outcome
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This multicenter, double-masked randomized clinical trial (RCT) evaluated the feasibility, safety, and efficacy of home-based transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with gamified cognitive control training (CCT) versus sham tDCS plus sham game in adults (18–65 years) with major depressive disorder (MDD). The study addressed whether this combined home-based approach could improve depressive symptoms more than sham treatment.

FINDINGS: Of 111 enrolled participants, 109 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (55 active, 54 sham). Feasibility was met, with 78.9% (lower bound of 1-sided 95% CI, 71.5%) completing ≥20 of 30 sessions. Both groups showed MADRS score improvements at week 6, with no significant difference between groups (difference: 0.89 [95% CI, -1.37 to 3.15]; P = .44; Cohen d = 0.10 [95% CI, -0.15 to 0.34]). Results were consistent at week 10 follow-up. Adverse events were balanced between groups.

INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates that home-based tDCS with CCT is feasible and safe, but it does not show superior efficacy to sham treatment for reducing depressive symptoms in MDD. The small effect size (Cohen d = 0.10) suggests no clinically meaningful difference. Limitations include the lack of an active comparator (e.g., standard tDCS alone) and potential expectancy effects despite masking checks. The population was relatively young and predominantly female, which may limit generalizability. Further research is needed to optimize the combination of tDCS and behavioral interventions.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support the use of home-based tDCS combined with gamified CCT as a superior treatment for MDD over sham. Clinicians should remain cautious about adopting this approach until more robust evidence emerges. Further trials should explore optimal stimulation parameters and cognitive interventions.

articles.title: Assessing the Impact of Metacognitive Therapy on OCD Severity and Beliefs: A Three-Wave Multisite RCT With Panel Mediation Analysis.
articles.authors: Anwar S, Younas R, Deebani W, et al.
articles.abstract: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a chronic and disabling condition, and although exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the first-line psychological treatment, many patients decline it, drop out, or retain residual symptoms. According to Wells' metacognitive model, OCD is maintained less by intrusive thoughts themselves than by metacognitive beliefs about the significance, danger, and control of thoughts, which metacognitive therapy (MCT) targets directly. However, individual MCT has been evaluated almost exclusively in high-income Western settings, and whether metacognitive belief change temporally precedes symptom improvement remains untested. This multisite, assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial (RCT) addressed both gaps in Pakistani outpatient services. Seventy-six adults with OCD were randomized to 12 weekly sessions of individual MCT (n = 38) or documented treatment as usual (TAU; n = 38) and assessed at baseline, post-treatment, and 6-month follow-up; outcomes were analyzed with intention-to-treat (ITT) mixed-effects models and an exploratory three-wave panel mediation model. MCT produced greater reductions in clinician-rated Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale severity than TAU, F(1.81, 134) = 11.30, p < 0.001, with mean differences of -4.00 at post-treatment and -6.92 at follow-up (both p < 0.001) and more frequent treatment response. MCT also reduced Metacognitions Questionnaire-30 belief domains, with gains maintained at follow-up. However, the pr
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This assessor-blinded multisite RCT (n=76 adults with OCD in Pakistan) tested whether 12 weekly sessions of individual metacognitive therapy (MCT) reduce OCD severity more than treatment-as-usual (TAU) and whether changes in metacognitive beliefs temporally precede symptom improvement.

FINDINGS: MCT produced greater reductions in clinician-rated Y-BOCS severity than TAU (F(1.81, 134)=11.30, p<0.001), with mean differences of −4.00 at post-treatment and −6.92 at 6-month follow-up (both p<0.001). MCT also reduced Metacognitions Questionnaire-30 belief domains, maintained at follow-up. However, the prespecified lagged indirect effect through post-treatment beliefs was not supported (β=−0.01).

INTERPRETATION: The trial shows MCT outperforms TAU for OCD severity with moderate-to-large effects at post-treatment and follow-up, supporting external validity in a non-Western outpatient setting. However, the lack of temporal precedence in the mediation analysis weakens claims that metacognitive belief change is a causal mechanism. Limitations include small sample size, single-blind assessment, and absence of active comparator (e.g., ERP), leaving uncertainty about MCT’s superiority to established treatments. Funding sources are not reported.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: MCT may be a viable alternative where ERP is declined or unavailable, but clinicians should note that the mechanism remains unclear and comparative effectiveness against first-line treatments is untested.

articles.title: Structural network alterations and peripheral immune-inflammatory dysregulation define distinct subtypes of major depressive disorder with prognostic implications.
articles.authors: Du W, Yuan M, Gao Z, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Immune-inflammatory dysregulation and cortical structural vulnerability have been increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, how they interact with each other, and whether immune heterogeneity in MDD is systematically organized by structural networks, remain unclear. METHODS: Genome-wide association studies data of MDD, gray matter volume (GMV) phenotypes, and 19 immune-related traits were utilized to assess causal relationships. A prospective cohort comprising 122 patients with MDD and 66 healthy controls underwent structural magnetic resonance imaging and assessment of 40 inflammatory and immune-related markers. Individualized structural covariance network analysis, machine-learning approaches, and survival analyses were used to identify neurobiological subtypes and evaluate treatment outcomes. RESULTS: Genetically predicted MDD was associated with lower levels of circulating IGF-1 (pFDR = 0.013). Levels of IL-5 and leptin were negatively associated with GMV alterations in the right cingulate gyrus and bilateral putamen, respectively (pFDR < 0.05). Structural covariance abnormalities were predominantly localized to connectivity between the default mode and limbic networks and within the limbic network in MDD, and they were classified into a hypoconnectivity subtype (n = 49) and a hyperconnectivity subtype (n = 73). The hypoconnectivity subtype exhibited greater anxiety and anhedonia symptoms, whereas the hyperconnectivity subtype showed
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This study investigated whether immune-inflammatory dysregulation and cortical structural changes in major depressive disorder (MDD) interact systematically, and whether they define clinically meaningful subtypes. It combined genome-wide association data with a prospective cohort of 122 MDD patients and 66 healthy controls who underwent MRI and immune marker assessments.

FINDINGS: Genetically predicted MDD was linked to lower circulating IGF-1 (pFDR = 0.013). Higher IL-5 and leptin levels correlated with reduced gray matter volume in the right cingulate gyrus and bilateral putamen (pFDR < 0.05). Structural covariance network analysis identified two subtypes: hypoconnectivity (n = 49) with greater anxiety and anhedonia, and hyperconnectivity (n = 73) with elevated inflammatory markers and faster antidepressant response (p = 0.032).

INTERPRETATION: The study provides preliminary evidence for immune-brain interaction in MDD and suggests two neurobiological subtypes with distinct symptom profiles and treatment responses. However, the sample size is modest, follow-up is short, and causality cannot be inferred from associations. The clinical relevance of subtype-specific immune markers and the stability of subtypes over time remain uncertain.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings do not yet justify subtype-specific treatment choices but suggest that immune profiling and network connectivity measures might eventually help personalize MDD care. Further validation in larger, longer studies is needed before bedside application.

articles.title: Greater proximity to greenspace is associated with fewer depressive symptoms among urban middle-aged adults.
articles.authors: Li S, Liao J, Cai B, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Understanding the factors that influence depression is crucial for both its treatment and prevention. Residential greenspace has received increasing attention for its potential role in mitigating depressive symptoms. However, traditional statistical methods are fundamentally constrained to evaluating simple bivariate associations between greenspace exposure and depression risk, overlooking the complex interactions among key health-related factors and failing to comprehensively assess the relative importance of greenspace compared to other contributing factors. METHODS: We employed machine learning (ML) methods to assess the effects of multiple factors, including greenspace, on the development of depressive symptoms among 1,542 urban middle-aged adults in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, with depressive symptoms measured using the 10-item Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale. Individual greenspace exposure for each subject was quantified using vegetation indices obtained from the NASA satellite database. RESULTS: Among the five ML models, the Support Vector Machines model achieved the best predictive performance, with an AUC of 0.776. Life satisfaction, EVI250m (a measure of greenspace), social activity, pain, sleep duration, and impairment in instrumental activities of daily living were significant predictors of depressive symptoms. EVI250m, identified by the ML model, indicated that closer proximity to greenspace was associated w
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This observational cohort study used machine-learning (Support Vector Machines) to rank predictors of depressive symptoms among 1,542 urban middle-aged adults in China, asking whether residential greenspace proximity matters more than other health and social factors.

FINDINGS: The best-performing model (AUC 0.776) identified life satisfaction, greenspace (EVI250 m), social activity, pain, sleep duration and instrumental-ADL impairment as significant predictors. Closer greenspace exposure was associated with fewer depressive symptoms; Shapley values placed greenspace among the top influential factors.

INTERPRETATION: The study’s internal validity is limited by its cross-sectional design and reliance on satellite-derived greenspace metrics rather than direct environmental measurements. The ML approach improves variable ranking but cannot establish causality or rule out residual confounding (e.g., unmeasured neighbourhood or lifestyle factors). The reported AUC suggests moderate predictive power, but effect sizes for greenspace proximity are not provided, so clinical significance remains uncertain.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest that urban greenspace may be a relevant—but likely modest—contributor to mental health; they do not yet justify changing practice, but they support further longitudinal and interventional research.

articles.title: Symptom Trajectories and Attendance in Face-to-Face and Online Psychiatric Follow-Up for Major Depressive Disorder and Anxiety Symptoms: Prospective Observational Cohort Study.
articles.authors: Akalın D, Şentürk Cankorur V
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Major depressive disorder is a leading cause of disability, and access to specialist psychiatric follow-up remains limited in many settings. Telepsychiatry may reduce logistical barriers to care, but data on video-based follow-up under routine outpatient conditions in Türkiye are scarce, and comparisons of delivery modalities are frequently limited by baseline imbalance between self-selected groups. OBJECTIVE: The aim of the study is to describe symptom trajectories and attendance over 6 months of routine psychiatric follow-up delivered either face-to-face or online and to examine whether outcomes differed between modalities after adjustment for baseline severity. METHODS: In this prospective, nonrandomized observational cohort study, 120 adults with Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) major depressive disorder were followed for 6 months at a university hospital psychiatry department in Ankara, Türkiye (September 2021 to May 2022). Participants entered face-to-face (n=60) or online (n=60) follow-up according to their own preference.
