Seven sessions were scheduled at approximately 4-week intervals; the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAM-D; primary outcome), the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, and DSM-5 Level 1 and Level 2 measures were administered at baseline and at sessions 1, 2, 4, and 6. Attendance was recorded at all sessions. Between-group comparisons used analysis of covariance adjusted for the corresponding baseline
articles.summary: BACKGROUND: Major depressive disorder is a leading cause of disability, and access to specialist psychiatric follow-up remains limited in many settings. Telepsychiatry may reduce logistical barriers to care, but data on video-based follow-up under routine outpatient conditions in Türkiye are scarce, and comparisons of delivery modalities are frequently limited by baseline imbalance between self-selected groups.

articles.title: Initial Treatment for Acute Low Back Pain and Risk of Opioid Use Disorder and Overdose.
articles.authors: Doan LV, Hung AM, Olfson M, et al.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Guideline-discordant care for acute low back pain (aLBP) is common and has been associated with adverse outcomes. OBJECTIVES: To estimate the incidence of new opioid use disorder (OUD) or overdose diagnosis among opioid-naive patients with Medicaid coverage initiating treatment for aLBP and to evaluate the association between initial treatment modalities and subsequent risk of OUD or overdose diagnosis. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This retrospective cohort study used data from January 1, 2016, to December 31, 2019, with 13 months of follow-up (1-month exposure assessment followed by 12 months of outcome follow-up) from the Transformed Medicaid Statistical Information System Analytic Files from 25 states that expanded Medicaid under the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act by 2014. Participants included opioid-naive, adults aged less than 65 years who received pain treatment within 1 month of diagnosis of aLBP. Data were analyzed from March 1, 2025, to July 31, 2026. EXPOSURES: Initial pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic treatments for aLBP. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: OUD or overdose diagnosis, defined using diagnostic codes for opioid abuse, opioid dependence, opioid-involved overdose, or a prescription for medication for treating OUD. RESULTS: In this cohort of 399 500 Medicaid patients who initiated treatment for newly diagnosed aLBP, the median age was 39 (IQR, 30-50) years, and 237 846 (59.5%) were female. The cumulative incidence of OUD or overdo
articles.summary: IMPORTANCE: Guideline-discordant care for acute low back pain (aLBP) is common and has been associated with adverse outcomes. OBJECTIVES: To estimate the incidence of new opioid use disorder (OUD) or overdose diagnosis among opioid-naive patients with Medicaid coverage initiating treatment for aLBP and to evaluate the association between initial treatment modalities and subsequent risk of OUD or overdose diagnosis.

articles.title: Dual benefit of esketamine-based opioid-free anesthesia on postoperative pain and mental health outcomes in patients undergoing bariatric surgery: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.authors: Huang C, Guan Z, Wang S, et al.
articles.abstract: Patients with morbid obesity are at a high risk of comorbid depressive and anxiety symptoms. While bariatric surgery is an effective treatment, conventional opioid-based anesthesia carries significant perioperative risks. Opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) presents a safer alternative. Esketamine, known for its dual analgesic and rapid antidepressant effects, is a promising component of OFA. However, clinical evidence supporting its simultaneous benefits for both physical and psychological recovery in bariatric patients remains limited. In this double-blind, randomized clinical trial, patients scheduled for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either esketamine-based anaesthesia or opioid-based anaesthesia with remifentanil during surgery. The co-primary outcomes were postoperative pain intensity within the first 24 h and mental health status at three months after surgery. Secondary outcomes included pharmacokinetics of esketamine and adverse events. A total of 84 patients were randomized, with 42 allocated to each group. Seventy-four participants (88.1%) completed the 3-month follow-up. Patients in the esketamine group experienced significantly lower postoperative pain intensity (P < 0.01) and a reduced incidence of moderate-to-severe pain (P < 0.05) within 24 h after surgery. Mental health outcomes at 3 months were also significantly better in the esketamine group, and adverse events rate did not differ significantly. Pharmacokinetic analysis sh
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This double-blind randomized controlled trial (RCT) investigated whether esketamine-based opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) improves postoperative pain and 3-month mental health outcomes in morbidly obese patients undergoing laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, compared to conventional opioid-based anesthesia.

FINDINGS: 84 patients were randomized (1:1) to esketamine-based OFA (n=42) or opioid-based anesthesia with remifentanil (n=42). 74 (88.1%) completed 3-month follow-up. Postoperative pain intensity within 24 hours was significantly lower in the esketamine group (P < 0.01), with fewer patients experiencing moderate-to-severe pain (P < 0.05). At 3 months, mental health outcomes were significantly better in the esketamine group. Adverse events did not differ significantly between groups. Pharmacokinetic analysis confirmed rapid esketamine metabolism to active (S)-norketamine.

INTERPRETATION: The study suggests esketamine-based OFA may offer dual benefits for acute pain and longer-term mental health without increasing adverse events. Strengths include the double-blind RCT design, clear co-primary outcomes, and pharmacokinetic confirmation. However, the sample size is modest, follow-up is limited to 3 months, and the mental health assessment tools are not specified. The lack of blinding details for outcome assessors and potential unmeasured confounders (e.g., baseline mental health severity) limit certainty. The clinical significance of the observed mental health improvement remains uncertain given the short follow-up and unspecified measures.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Esketamine-based OFA may be a promising alternative to opioid-based anesthesia in bariatric surgery, potentially improving immediate postoperative pain and 3-month mental health outcomes. However, larger trials with longer follow-up and validated mental health measures are needed before recommending a change in practice.

articles.title: Impact of clozapine on the proteome: A systematic review and functional analyses.
articles.authors: Yong WCS, Schubert KO, Pukala TL, et al.
articles.abstract: Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS), yet its use is limited by potentially life-threatening adverse effects including myocarditis, agranulocytosis and pneumonia. Improved mechanistic understanding may facilitate safer prescribing. We conducted the first systematic review integrating proteomic findings associated with clozapine exposure. Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Embase and Scopus were searched for clozapine-associated proteomic studies in animal, human and cell-based models. Differentially expressed proteins were mapped to Reactome pathways using the Search Tool for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes/Proteins (STRING). Using the same approach, analyses stratified all proteins by model type and replicated proteins by exposure duration and biological system. Replicated proteins were further analysed using QIAGEN Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA). Across studies, 1070 unique proteins changed following clozapine exposure (603 increased, 394 decreased, 73 discordant). Of these, 152 were identified in ≥2 studies, with 79 showing concordant directionality. Nine were replicated in ≥3 studies with consistent direction. Overall STRING analysis identified recurrent immune/inflammatory, cellular-stress and neuronal pathway enrichment, with stratified analyses providing partial support for these and related metabolic processes across model types, exposure duration and biological system. IPA highlighted necrosis-related proces
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS), but its use is limited by serious adverse effects. This systematic review and functional proteomic analysis aimed to integrate proteomic findings associated with clozapine exposure across animal, human, and cell-based models to better understand its mechanisms and potential biomarkers.

FINDINGS: Across 1070 unique proteins altered by clozapine (603 increased, 394 decreased, 73 discordant), 152 were identified in ≥2 studies, with 79 showing concordant directionality. Nine proteins were replicated in ≥3 studies. STRING pathway analysis revealed recurrent enrichment in immune/inflammatory, cellular-stress, and neuronal pathways, with stratified analyses supporting these and related metabolic processes. IPA highlighted necrosis-related processes and downstream effects in cardiovascular, hepatic, and renal systems. No direct comparison of brain and peripheral blood changes was available.

INTERPRETATION: This systematic review provides preliminary evidence that clozapine may influence immune, inflammatory, and cell-death pathways, potentially contributing to adverse effects. However, the evidence is heterogeneous, with limited replication of specific proteins and no direct clinical correlation to treatment response or adverse outcomes. The lack of longitudinal human data and time-series comparisons limits causal inference. The findings are hypothesis-generating and underscore the need for prospective proteomic studies during clozapine initiation.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current proteomic data do not yet translate to clinical practice but suggest potential biomarkers for monitoring clozapine-related adverse effects. Clinicians should remain vigilant for immune-mediated complications (e.g., myocarditis) but should not alter prescribing based on these findings alone. Further research is needed to validate these pathways as therapeutic targets or biomarkers.

articles.title: Harm reduction among refugees and displaced populations in Lebanon: a systematic review.
articles.authors: Abbas Z, Hajj A, Sacre H, et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to assess the comprehensiveness of existing policies, strategies, and research regarding harm reduction services for refugees and displaced populations in Lebanon, evaluating service availability, access barriers, and policy gaps to inform targeted and evidence-based interventions and improve health outcomes for this vulnerable group. METHOD: A systematic review was conducted to examine substance use and harm reduction among refugees in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. The study protocol was registered in PROSPERO. PubMed, EMBASE, and Google Scholar databases were searched using free-text words and MeSH terms, including substance use, drug use, harm reduction, hepatitis C virus (HCV) screening, hepatitis B virus (HBV) screening, refugees, treatment access, and displaced population. Grey literature from the Lebanese Ministry of Public Health, World Health Organization, and other global reports was reviewed separately and included in the PRISMA flowchart, alongside peer-reviewed studies. The risk for bias in included research papers was evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Tools. RESULTS: A total of 387 papers (369 peer-reviewed studies and 18 grey literature reports on harm reduction and substance use) were retrieved, and 29 were included in the review after screening and full-text evaluation (17peer reviewed articles and 12 grey literature reports). The results revealed a lack of structured harm reduction policies specif
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (PRISMA; PROSPERO-registered) examined harm reduction policies and services for substance use among refugees and displaced populations in Lebanon, a setting with high refugee density and complex legal/healthcare barriers. The review aimed to map service availability, access barriers, and policy gaps to guide interventions.

FINDINGS: Out of 387 records, 29 documents (17 peer-reviewed studies and 12 grey literature reports) were included. No structured harm reduction policies specifically for refugees were identified. Key barriers included legal restrictions, stigma, and poor integration of harm reduction into routine care. Only 4 of 12 grey literature sources mentioned harm reduction provision, and none outlined a comprehensive strategy. Many studies were broad and lacked focused substance-use data in refugee populations.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak and fragmented, with high risk of selection and reporting biases due to reliance on grey literature and heterogeneous, often non-refugee-specific studies. The Joanna Briggs Institute tool was used for risk-of-bias assessment, but the overall quality of included evidence appears low. The lack of policy specificity and integrated services is clear, but causal pathways and effect sizes remain unquantified. Further targeted research is essential to inform policy adaptation and service design.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current harm reduction services in Lebanon do not adequately address refugee needs; clinicians should anticipate gaps in access and advocate for mobile clinics and integrated HCV screening. However, evidence to guide specific clinical interventions is currently insufficient.

articles.title: Brain functional changes of suicidal ideation and behaviours: a meta-analysis of task-based fMRI studies.
articles.authors: Xu VE, Fang KK, Shao R
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Suicidal ideation and behaviour are major global mental health issues and leading causes for mortality. While existing evidence indicates brain functional deficits of suicidal thoughts and behaviours, the neural underpinnings of these deficits remain unclear, possibly due to various sources of methodological heterogeneities. METHODS: We conducted a pre-registered meta-analysis including 22 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging studies that compared suicidal individuals (N = 459, 63.83% females) with non-suicidal psychiatric controls (N = 681, 52.72% females). Separate analyses were conducted in the emotion and non-emotion (cognitive and risky decision making) domains. Subgroup and meta-regression analyses addressed methodological heterogeneities including patient diagnosis, suicidal characteristics (ideation vs. behaviours) and task type. RESULTS: In emotion tasks, general suicidality (pooling across ideation and behaviours) and suicidal behaviours were both associated with hyperactivities in the left sensorimotor cortices and hippocampus/parahippocampus, alongside hypoactivity in the bilateral visual cortices. However, only the hypoactivity among visual areas was consistently replicated in all subgroup analyses. In non-emotion tasks, general suicidality and suicidal behaviours were both associated with hyperactivity in the left precentral gyrus and the right middle temporal gyrus, which were consistently replicated in all subgroup analyses. Meta-regres
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This pre-registered meta-analysis of 22 task-based fMRI studies examined brain functional changes associated with suicidal ideation and behaviours, comparing 459 suicidal individuals with 681 non-suicidal psychiatric controls. The study aimed to clarify neural underpinnings of suicidality amid methodological heterogeneity.

FINDINGS: In emotion tasks, general suicidality and suicidal behaviours were linked to hyperactivity in the left sensorimotor cortices and hippocampus/parahippocampus, alongside hypoactivity in bilateral visual cortices. Only the visual cortex hypoactivity was consistently replicated across all subgroup analyses. In non-emotion tasks, hyperactivity in the left precentral gyrus and right middle temporal gyrus was observed for general suicidality and suicidal behaviours, consistently replicated across subgroups. Meta-regression showed larger functional changes in frontotemporal regions with higher female proportions and in hippocampal/temporal regions with older participants.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate in strength due to methodological heterogeneity across studies (e.g., varied diagnoses, task types). The consistent finding of visual cortex hypoactivity in emotion tasks and motor/temporal hyperactivity in non-emotion tasks suggests potential neural targets for intervention. However, the clinical significance of these neural changes remains uncertain, as effect sizes and direct clinical outcomes were not reported. The study’s reliance on task-based fMRI and subgroup analyses limits generalisability to routine psychiatric care.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings highlight potential neural correlates of suicidality but do not yet translate into actionable clinical tools. Further research is needed to determine if these neural patterns can guide treatment or risk assessment in psychiatric practice.

articles.title: Targeting affective cognition during pregnancy to prevent postpartum depression: a randomized controlled trial with parity-specific effects.
articles.authors: Bjertrup A, Rasmussen KH, Tørring S, et al.
articles.abstract: Postpartum depression (PPD) affects approximately 17% of women globally and is predicted by prior mental illness and socioeconomic disadvantage. Emerging evidence suggests that negative bias in the cognitive processing of infant cues and heightened reactivity to infant distress during pregnancy contribute to PPD risk and may thus represent a treatment target. This randomized controlled trial examined whether prenatal affective cognitive training (PACT) reduces PPD risk by modulating negative biases in pregnant women at heightened risk. Of 280 women assessed, 147 at heightened risk were randomized to PACT or care as usual (CAU). PACT comprised five individualized 90-minute sessions over five weeks, combining computerized and virtual-reality tasks targeting negative cognitive bias, attentional bias, emotion regulation, and working memory in response to infant stimuli. Affective cognition was assessed at baseline and post-intervention; mood was rated at baseline, post-intervention, and weekly for six weeks after birth. Diagnostic interviews (Present State Examination) were conducted six months postpartum. The primary outcome was PPD incidence within six months postpartum; secondary outcomes included depressive symptoms over the first six weeks and changes in affective cognition. Follow-up data were available for 121 (83%) participants (PACT n = 54; CAU n = 67). PACT did not significantly reduce PPD overall (p = 0.18) or depressive symptoms (p = 0.31) but increased positive inter
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This randomized controlled trial (RCT) tested whether prenatal affective cognitive training (PACT) reduces postpartum depression (PPD) risk in pregnant women at heightened risk by targeting negative cognitive biases related to infant cues. The study included 147 pregnant women identified as high-risk, randomized to PACT or care as usual (CAU), with outcomes assessed up to six months postpartum.

FINDINGS: The primary outcome, PPD incidence within six months postpartum, did not differ significantly between PACT (14%) and CAU (24%) overall (p = 0.18). Secondary outcomes, including depressive symptoms over the first six weeks postpartum, also showed no significant difference (p = 0.31). However, PACT significantly improved positive interpretation of infant emotions post-intervention (p = 0.003). Exploratory analyses revealed a markedly lower PPD incidence in multiparous women receiving PACT (5%) compared to CAU (35%), with an odds ratio of 0.10 (95% CI [0.01-0.92], p = 0.04). Follow-up data were available for 83% of participants.

INTERPRETATION: The study’s internal validity is strengthened by its RCT design and structured intervention, but the lack of overall effect on PPD incidence limits conclusions. The significant improvement in affective cognition suggests the intervention may target relevant mechanisms, though clinical significance is unclear. The exploratory parity-specific findings are intriguing but require cautious interpretation due to small subgroup sizes and lack of correction for multiple testing. The high dropout-adjusted follow-up rate (83%) is a strength, but the study’s power may have been insufficient for subgroup analyses. External validity is limited by the selective high-risk population and single-center setting.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: PACT does not currently reduce PPD risk overall, so it cannot be recommended for routine practice. However, the parity-specific effect in multiparous women warrants further investigation in larger, adequately powered trials to determine if targeted interventions could benefit specific subgroups. Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting exploratory findings.

articles.title: Structure based discovery of antipsychotic-like TAAR1 agonists.
articles.authors: Huang S, Liu H, Wu Y, et al.
articles.abstract: Schizophrenia is a severe mental illness whose current treatments primarily target dopamine and serotonin receptors. These drugs often cause side effects and vary in effectiveness across patients. The trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1), which modulates monoamine signaling, has emerged as a promising alternative target. To discover previously unexplored TAAR1 ligands, we computationally dock 65 million molecules against the active state of TAAR1 and experimentally test 55 of those highly ranked. Fourteen TAAR1 agonists emerge with potencies ranging from mid-nanomolar to micromolar. This high functional selectivity may reflect the compact conformation adopted by the activated TAAR1 orthosteric site. While this is favorable for agonist prioritization, simulations suggest that it can be over-optimized for initial hit rates at the expense of subsequent affinity maturation. Hit optimization yields nanomolar agonists whose docking-predicted poses are confirmed by cryo-EM. Three agonists have high brain exposure and potencies, with one compound showing potency comparable to the investigational drug ulotaront and two compounds exhibiting even greater potency, at levels sufficient for behavioral studies. All three potently normalize amphetamine-induced pre-pulse inhibition in mice, a model for schizophrenia, without catalepsy, a common side effect of traditional antipsychotics.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This preclinical study used computational docking and experimental screening to discover novel trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1) agonists as potential antipsychotic agents in schizophrenia, where current dopamine/serotonin-targeting treatments have limited efficacy and side effects.

FINDINGS: From 65 million computationally screened molecules, 55 were experimentally tested, yielding 14 TAAR1 agonists with mid-nanomolar to micromolar potencies. Hit optimization produced nanomolar agonists, with three compounds demonstrating high brain exposure and potency comparable to or exceeding the investigational drug ulotaront. All three normalized amphetamine-induced pre-pulse inhibition in mice (a schizophrenia model) without inducing catalepsy, a common side effect of traditional antipsychotics.

INTERPRETATION: This is a high-throughput, computational-experimental drug discovery study with strong internal validity in its methodology (docking, cryo-EM confirmation, behavioral assays). However, it is entirely preclinical, conducted in mice, and lacks human data. The functional selectivity and lack of catalepsy are promising, but clinical relevance remains uncertain until safety and efficacy are tested in humans. The risk of over-optimization for initial hit rates is noted but not quantified.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No immediate change to clinical practice is warranted. These findings justify further development and human trials but should not alter current antipsychotic prescribing.

articles.title: Effect of a Subanesthetic Dose of Esketamine on Postoperative Sleep Disturbance After Oocyte Retrieval Under Intravenous Anesthesia: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.authors: Ma Q, Li H, Wang X, et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is a common complication after oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. This study aimed to evaluate whether a subanesthetic dose of esketamine reduces the incidence of PSD. PATIENTS AND METHODS: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial included 196 women undergoing oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. Participants were randomly assigned to the esketamine or control group. During anesthesia induction, the esketamine group received an intravenous bolus of esketamine 0.2 mg/kg, whereas the control group received an equivalent volume of normal saline. The primary analysis was conducted according to the intention-to-treat principle, with missing outcome data handled using multiple imputation; 189 participants (95 in the control group and 94 in the esketamine group) were included in the per-protocol sensitivity analysis. The primary outcome was the incidence of PSD on postoperative day (POD) 3, defined using a composite criterion of an Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS) score ≥6 or a numerical rating scale (NRS) score ≥6. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of PSD on POD 1, postoperative pain scores, postoperative anxiety and depression scores, and patient satisfaction with the anesthetic technique. RESULTS: In the intention-to-treat analysis with multiple imputation, the estimated incidence of PSD on POD 3 was lower in the esketamine group than in the control group (13.06% vs 24.90%; risk difference, -11
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=196) tested whether a single subanesthetic dose of esketamine (0.2 mg/kg IV) reduces postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) on day 3 after oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia in women.

FINDINGS: In intention-to-treat analysis, PSD incidence on POD 3 was 13.06% with esketamine vs 24.90% with placebo (risk difference −11.84 pp [95% CI −22.98 to −0.69]; RR 0.52 [95% CI 0.28–0.99]; P=0.047). Per-protocol results were similar. PSD on POD 1 did not differ. Postoperative pain at 30 min was lower with esketamine (P<0.001), but dreaming was more frequent (21.4% vs 11.2%; P=0.048) and recovery metrics were modestly longer (time to alertness 12 vs 11 min; PACU stay 34 vs 31 min; both P≤0.005).

INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests a modest reduction in PSD at POD 3 with esketamine, but the effect size is small (RR ~0.5) and the confidence interval barely excludes the null. The trial is single-center, short-term, and lacks long-term sleep or functional outcomes. Recovery time and dreaming frequency are slightly increased. Overall certainty is low; confirmation in larger, multicenter studies with longer follow-up is needed.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For now, esketamine cannot be recommended routinely to prevent PSD after oocyte retrieval; any benefit appears small and may be offset by longer recovery. Monitor for transient side effects and counsel patients accordingly.

articles.title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy for depression: state-dependent mechanisms, clinical evidence, and translational challenges.
articles.authors: Deng J, Shao Y, Jiang L, et al.
articles.abstract: Depression is a highly prevalent and debilitating mental disorder. Pharmacotherapy remains the primary treatment modality; however, its efficacy is often limited by a delayed onset of action, suboptimal response in some patients, and a high risk of recurrence. Treatment-resistant depression, characterized by poor response to conventional therapies, poses a major clinical challenge and highlights the need for improved treatment strategies. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), a noninvasive neuromodulation technique, has shown promise for depression, particularly when combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy. Advances in neuroimaging, neurochemistry, and network neuroscience have clarified how high-frequency rTMS may modulate cortical excitability, monoaminergic transmission, synaptic plasticity, and distributed brain networks. Clinical evidence suggests that combined treatment may accelerate early improvement, increase response and remission, and reduce relapse risk; however, these benefits are heterogeneous across patients and symptom domains and should be interpreted in light of expectancy effects and limitations of sham blinding. Neuroimaging studies have identified treatment-associated functional and structural changes, including hippocampal volume changes, but the causal links among molecular signaling, circuit reorganization, structural findings, and symptom improvement remain unresolved. The interaction between rTMS and antidepressants should therefo
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, neuroimaging, and clinical evidence on whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy improves outcomes in major depressive disorder (MDD), and under what conditions such benefits occur.

FINDINGS: The review reports that combined rTMS plus pharmacotherapy may accelerate early symptom improvement, increase response and remission rates, and reduce relapse risk compared with either modality alone. These effects are heterogeneous across patients and symptom domains. Neuroimaging studies suggest treatment-associated changes in hippocampal volume and network connectivity, but causal links to clinical improvement remain unclear. Expectancy effects and limitations in sham blinding complicate interpretation of clinical benefits.

INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this paper synthesizes diverse evidence rather than providing pooled effect sizes or definitive conclusions. Strengths include integration across mechanistic and clinical domains; limitations include lack of quantitative meta-analysis, potential selection and publication bias, and unresolved causal pathways. The clinical significance of any observed benefits remains uncertain without standardized effect estimates and rigorous RCT data.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify routine use of combined rTMS and antidepressants outside research or highly specialized settings. Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting heterogeneous findings and await more definitive trials before changing practice.

articles.title: Health risks of alcohol consumption in Aotearoa New Zealand: modelling to inform low-risk-drinking guidelines.
articles.authors: Mizdrak A, Sherk A, Maynard K, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The present study aimed to estimate the alcohol-attributable mortality in Aotearoa New Zealand (Aotearoa) at varying levels of alcohol consumption to help inform low-risk-drinking guidelines (LRDGs) in Aotearoa. METHODS: We used the New Zealand Alcohol Intervention Model-a multi-state life-table model parameterized with Aotearoa-specific alcohol and epidemiological data-to estimate the health risks associated with a daily alcohol intake of 0-100 g/day. We modelled a cohort of 12-year-olds for their life course, with exposure and disease rates fixed to 2018 levels. We used relative risk (RR) libraries developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) and Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD). The primary output was years of life lost (YLL), with 17.5 YLL used as a proxy for alcohol-related death, at lifetime-risk thresholds of 1-in-100 and 1-in-1000. RESULTS: When the WHO RR library was used, males reached a 1-in-100 risk of alcohol-attributable death at 8.6 standard drinks (SDs, 10 g of ethanol) [95% uncertainty interval (UI) 3.1-12.0] per week, while females reach this threshold at 9.2 SDs (95% UI 3.7-12.4). The removal of health conditions receiving a one-star evidence rating from the GBD substantially reduced the number of SDs to 2.7 (95% UI 2.1-4.6) for males and 3.5 (95% UI 2.9-4.4) for females. Across all analyses, use of the GBD RR library led to more permissive results. Ethnicity-specific results showed that Māori breach the risk thresholds at lower levels o
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This modelling study estimated alcohol-attributable mortality in Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ) to inform low-risk-drinking guidelines (LRDGs), using a multi-state life-table model with NZ-specific data and WHO/GBD relative risk (RR) libraries. The cohort consisted of 12-year-olds followed over their lifetime with fixed 2018 exposure and disease rates.

FINDINGS: Males reached a 1-in-100 risk of alcohol-attributable death at 8.6 standard drinks (10 g ethanol) per week [95% UI 3.1–12.0], while females reached this threshold at 9.2 standard drinks [95% UI 3.7–12.4] using WHO RR data. Removing GBD one-star evidence conditions reduced thresholds to 2.7 (males) and 3.5 (females) standard drinks per week. Māori reached risk thresholds at lower consumption levels than non-Māori.

INTERPRETATION: The study highlights that current NZ LRDGs may underestimate alcohol-related harm, particularly when excluding low-certainty evidence. Strengths include the use of a validated life-table model and NZ-specific data; limitations include reliance on modelled RRs, fixed 2018 rates, and uncertainty intervals spanning large ranges. The clinical significance is uncertain until guideline committees formally review these thresholds and consider population-specific risks.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current NZ low-risk guidelines may need revision, especially for Māori. Clinicians should continue to advise patients on alcohol-related risks while awaiting updated national guidance.

articles.title: Clozapine, suicide prevention and risk perception in psychiatry.
articles.authors: De Las Cuevas C
articles.abstract: Clozapine remains the most effective treatment for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and one of the few psychiatric medications consistently associated with reduced suicidal behaviour. Nevertheless, its use remains markedly limited despite advances in pharmacovigilance, haematological monitoring and individualised prescribing strategies. This editorial examines whether psychiatry may continue to evaluate clozapine through historically inherited models of risk perception that emphasise treatment-attributable mortality while insufficiently incorporating the lethality of severe mental illness itself, particularly suicide. Clozapine therefore represents not only a psychopharmacological treatment, but also a revealing case study in how psychiatry conceptualises competing forms of mortality.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This editorial discusses clozapine’s role in reducing suicide risk in treatment-resistant schizophrenia, while noting its underutilization despite evidence of benefit. It explores whether historical risk perception biases in psychiatry contribute to this paradox.

FINDINGS: Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with consistent evidence for reducing suicidal behavior, including suicide attempts and completed suicides, in schizophrenia. However, its use is limited by concerns over agranulocytosis and other adverse effects, despite improved monitoring protocols.

INTERPRETATION: As an editorial, this is not a primary research study but a conceptual analysis. It highlights a potential bias in risk assessment—overemphasizing treatment-related mortality (e.g., agranulocytosis) while underweighting the mortality risk from untreated severe mental illness, particularly suicide. The argument is plausible but relies on narrative reasoning rather than empirical data. No effect sizes or statistical comparisons are provided.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The piece suggests that clinicians may be overly cautious about clozapine due to historical fears, potentially denying patients a life-saving treatment. It does not change practice directly but may encourage a re-evaluation of risk-benefit assessments in clozapine prescribing.

articles.title: Classroom-based observation and intervention of executive function for special education teachers working with preschoolers with Autism.
articles.authors: Aonsri C, Siritaratiwat W, Mongput K, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Executive function (EF) related behavioral challenges are frequently observed in preschool children with autism spectrum disorder. However, structured, classroom-based observation of these behaviors by teachers remains difficult, resulting in limited practical assessment and recommendations for classroom-based support. This study aimed to examine the feasibility of teacher-administered EF assessment in special education centers and to formulate preliminary, expert-informed recommendations for autistic children with varying communication abilities. METHODS: A mixed-methods sequential design was used. A total of 793 children with autism aged 3-6 years were assessed by trained teachers. Multidisciplinary expert consultation was conducted to formulate preliminary recommendations for classroom activities based on age and communication profiles. RESULTS: Teachers achieved at least 85% accuracy in score conversion and interpretation, supporting the feasibility of its use in a special education classroom. Patterns of EF-related behavioral challenges observed in 793 children aged 3-6 years were integrated with existing evidence and multidisciplinary expert consensus to inform preliminary recommendations for classroom activities. Working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility were most evident, especially in children with limited verbal communication and those requiring intensive classroom support. articles.summary: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Executive function (EF) related behavioral challenges are frequently observed in preschool children with autism spectrum disorder. However, structured, classroom-based observation of these behaviors by teachers remains difficult, resulting in limited practical assessment and recommendations for classroom-based support. This study aimed to examine the feasibility of teacher-administered EF assessment in special education centers and to formulate preliminary, expert-informed recommendations for autistic children with varying communication abilities.

articles.title: Preliminary Evaluation of Implementation and Effectiveness of the Relational Suicide Intervention Pilot.
articles.authors: Morgan PC, Love HA, Hardy NR
articles.abstract: Although primary interventions for suicidal ideation typically focus on individuals, couple-based clinical interventions for this population remain underdeveloped. Despite emerging evidence suggesting that relational interventions may improve suicidal ideation, currently only one couple-based intervention has preliminary evidence, and it was specifically designed for military couples. This gap highlights the need for systemic couple-based interventions in outpatient settings. We piloted the Relational Suicide Intervention (RSI), a four-session intervention grounded in Integrative Systemic Therapy and contemporary suicidology research, at a university clinic. Sixteen graduate student therapists consented to participate and received training in the intervention. Of four couples screened, three met eligibility criteria, consented, and completed the study. We used a mixed-methods approach to evaluate qualitative and quantitative data. Findings provided preliminary support for the safe and feasible implementation of RSI in this small pilot sample. Relationship satisfaction showed small average increases, particularly among partners with higher suicidal ideation, whereas suicidal ideation did not improve on average. Participants generally described the intervention as helpful, particularly regarding suicide safety planning, understanding relationship patterns, and learning mental health coping strategies. These preliminary findings suggest promise for RSI, with future research need
articles.summary: Although primary interventions for suicidal ideation typically focus on individuals, couple-based clinical interventions for this population remain underdeveloped. Despite emerging evidence suggesting that relational interventions may improve suicidal ideation, currently only one couple-based intervention has preliminary evidence, and it was specifically designed for military couples. This gap highlights the need for systemic couple-based interventions in outpatient settings.

articles.title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for the treatment of restless legs syndrome: A meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Dong Z, Zhang X, Zhang J, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The benefit of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) in patients with Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) is uncertain. This study was performed to explore the therapeutic effect of rTMS in treating RLS. METHODS: Databases including PubMed, EMbase, the Cochrane Library, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and Wanfang database were searched from their inception to May 1, 2026. Eligible studies comparing rTMS with sham stimulation were included. Data were analyzed using Review Manager Version 5.3. RESULTS: Four studies were included in the meta-analysis. The overall pooled analysis confirmed that rTMS could effectively reduce International RLS-Rating Scale (IRLS-RS) scores (mean difference [MD] = 6.46, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 4.44 -8.48, P < .00001) and Pittsburgh sleep quality index (PSQI) scores (MD = 4.80, 95% CI: 3.51-6.08, P < .00001) at different follow-up periods. Meanwhile, the overall pooled analysis confirmed that rTMS could effectively reduce IRLS-RS scores (MD = 7.79, 95% CI: 3.90-11.68, P < .0001) and PSQI scores (MD = 5.58, 95% CI: 3.81-7.35, P < .00001) in the subgroup analysis by RLS subtype. However, rTMS showed no significant effect on PSQI scores in primary RLS (MD = 1.86, 95% CI: -2.65-6.37, P = .42). In addition, the overall pooled analysis confirmed that both low-frequency and high-frequency rTMS could effectively reduce IRLS-RS scores (MD = 7.79, 95% CI: 3.90-11.68, P < .0001) and PSQI scores (MD = 5.58, 95% CI: 3.81-7.35, P
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This meta-analysis examined whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) reduces symptoms in patients with Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) compared with sham stimulation, pooling data from four small controlled studies.

FINDINGS: Across four studies, rTMS significantly lowered IRLS-RS scores (MD 6.46, 95 % CI 4.44–8.48, P < .00001) and PSQI sleep scores (MD 4.80, 95 % CI 3.51–6.08, P < .00001). Subgroup analyses suggested benefit for both low- and high-frequency rTMS, but no effect on PSQI in primary RLS (MD 1.86, 95 % CI –2.65–6.37, P = .42) and no improvement in anxiety or depression scales.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence is limited by the small number of studies (n = 4), modest sample sizes, and heterogeneity in stimulation parameters and RLS subtypes. Effect sizes on IRLS-RS and PSQI are statistically significant but may not reach clinically meaningful thresholds for many patients. The lack of benefit on mood scales and the single negative PSQI subgroup raise concerns about robustness. Larger, well-controlled RCTs with standardized protocols and longer follow-up are needed before rTMS can be recommended for routine RLS care.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current data do not justify adopting rTMS for RLS outside research settings; clinicians should await confirmatory trials before considering this intervention.

articles.title: Ketamine in psychiatry: a systematic review of clinical applications, safety considerations, and emerging challenges.
articles.authors: Kinney MM, Bowers ZL
articles.abstract: Ketamine has progressed from solely being an anesthetic agent to a drug of rising clinical and research interest due to its distinctive pharmacological properties. Its dissociative properties and rapid-acting antidepressant effects have made it a prominent area of investigation across many medical and psychiatric applications. This systematic review examines ketamine's history, mechanisms of action, clinical uses, and significant challenges. A systematic search of PubMed, SCOPUS, PsycINFO, and other sources, generated peer-reviewed publications that addressed the history of ketamine, its pharmacology, clinical applications, recreational use, safety considerations, and societal consequences. Overall, 106 articles were identified for inclusion in this study. At the receptor level, ketamine is an antagonist of NMDA receptors that triggers a number of downstream effects ranging from heightened glutamate transmission, AMPA receptor activation, increased BDNF expression, synaptogenesis, and mTOR pathway signaling. At the network level, it alters activity within large-scale brain circuits including the default mode network, affecting cognition, mood, and perception. Clinically, ketamine is used for anesthesia, treatment-resistant depression, and pain, with off-label uses for PTSD, anxiety disorders, and bipolar disorder. The review also examines current challenges related to ketamine's recreational use, associated risks, sociocultural factors, and key clinical and ethical considerat
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review synthesizes evidence on ketamine’s psychiatric applications, mechanisms, safety, and challenges, addressing its evolution from anesthesia to experimental treatments for psychiatric disorders. It aggregates findings across 106 peer-reviewed publications to evaluate clinical utility, risks, and research gaps.

FINDINGS: Ketamine acts primarily as an NMDA receptor antagonist, triggering downstream effects such as increased glutamate transmission, AMPA receptor activation, BDNF expression, synaptogenesis, and mTOR pathway signaling. Clinically, it is used for anesthesia, treatment-resistant depression (TRD), and pain, with off-label interest in PTSD, anxiety disorders, and bipolar disorder. The review highlights challenges including recreational misuse, safety monitoring needs, and ethical considerations around telehealth prescribing of oral/sublingual formulations.

INTERPRETATION: As a narrative synthesis without meta-analytic pooling, this review provides a broad overview but lacks quantitative effect sizes or direct comparisons between interventions. Strengths include integration across disciplines and identification of key gaps (e.g., long-term safety, optimal dosing, and patient selection). Limitations include heterogeneity of included studies and absence of formal risk-of-bias assessment. The clinical significance of findings remains uncertain due to the descriptive nature of the evidence.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Ketamine may offer rapid but transient relief for TRD and certain pain conditions, but routine use requires careful risk-benefit assessment due to safety concerns and recreational risks. Clinicians should monitor for dissociative effects, abuse potential, and ensure structured follow-up—especially with novel formulations. Further high-quality trials are needed to define long-term efficacy and safety.

articles.title: Excessive Yawning During Escitalopram Therapy in a Rwandan Woman with Co-Morbid Depression and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder: A Case Report.
articles.authors: Gihozo ML, Gafaranga JP
articles.abstract: Excessive yawning is an uncommon but recognized adverse effect of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). Although generally benign, it may cause distress and may be mistaken for a symptom of psychiatric or neurological illness. Case reports and pharmacovigilance data have linked escitalopram to yawning, sometimes in a dose-dependent manner. To our knowledge, this is one of the first reported cases of escitalopram-associated yawning in Rwanda. We describe a 44-year-old woman from rural Rwanda who presented with a severe depressive episode and comorbid post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Three days after starting escitalopram 10 mg daily, she reported markedly increased yawning, approximately six episodes every 15 minutes throughout the day, while her sleep and mood had begun to improve slightly. Medical and neurological causes, sleep-related causes and concurrent short-term diazepam use were considered and judged unlikely. The Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale score was 5, indicating a probable adverse drug reaction. Escitalopram was continued because of emerging antidepressant benefit, and the yawning had decreased substantially at the two-week follow-up. This case suggests that yawning occurring early in escitalopram treatment should be recognized as a probable adverse drug reaction. Awareness of this under-reported effect may prevent unnecessary investigations and premature discontinuation of an effective antidepressant.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The clinical question is whether excessive yawning can be an adverse effect of escitalopram in a patient with depression and PTSD. This case report from Rwanda describes a single patient’s experience to highlight a rare but recognized side effect of SSRIs.

FINDINGS: A 44-year-old Rwandan woman with severe depression and PTSD developed approximately six yawning episodes every 15 minutes three days after starting escitalopram 10 mg daily. The yawning was not attributed to other medical, neurological, or sleep-related causes, nor to concurrent short-term diazepam use. The Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale score was 5, indicating a probable adverse drug reaction. The yawning decreased substantially by the two-week follow-up while escitalopram was continued.

INTERPRETATION: As a case report, this study provides very low-quality evidence limited to a single patient. The Naranjo score suggests a probable but not definitive causal relationship. The lack of a control group, small sample size (n=1), and short follow-up duration (two weeks) limit generalizability. The clinical significance of yawning as an adverse effect is uncertain, but awareness may prevent unnecessary investigations and treatment changes.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should be aware that excessive yawning can occur early in escitalopram treatment and may not warrant immediate discontinuation if the antidepressant benefit is emerging. However, this single case should not change practice without further evidence.

articles.title: Amygdala neurofeedback as an adjunct to residential dialectical behavior therapy for borderline personality disorder: a pilot randomized controlled trial.
articles.authors: Hofmanová M, Santangelo PS, Kleindienst N, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is characterized by affective instability and amygdala hyperreactivity. Although dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) reduces symptoms and amygdala-related abnormalities, many patients show only partial remission. Real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) amygdala neurofeedback (amy-NF) directly targets hyperactive limbic responses and has shown promise in uncontrolled trials. We examined whether amy-NF adds benefit to inpatient DBT. METHODS: Thirty-six mid-therapy people with BPD and clinically significant residual symptoms (BSL-23 > 1.5) were randomized to DBT plus amy-NF (n = 23) or DBT alone, termed treatment as usual (TAU = 13). Post-treatment assessments were completed by 15/9 (amy-NF/TAU), with 15/8 and 12/7 completing the 3- and 6-month follow-ups. Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) of daily-life affective instability served as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included self-reports, amygdala responses during two fMRI tasks, and resting-state fMRI. Assessments occurred at pre-, post-, 3-, and 6-month follow-up. RESULTS: Participants successfully downregulated amygdala activity during neurofeedback. EMA showed improvements in negative affect, inner tension, and affective instability over time, without consistent superiority of amy-NF. Self-reports likewise showed no additional benefit of amy-NF, and BSL-23 scores increased after discharge in both groups. Amy-NF was associated with transient pre-post
articles.summary: BACKGROUND: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is characterized by affective instability and amygdala hyperreactivity. Although dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) reduces symptoms and amygdala-related abnormalities, many patients show only partial remission. Real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) amygdala neurofeedback (amy-NF) directly targets hyperactive limbic responses and has shown promise in uncontrolled trials. We examined whether amy-NF adds benefit to inpatient DBT.

articles.title: Pharmacotherapy for social anxiety disorder: An evidence-based treatment review.
articles.authors: Strawn JR, Stahl SM, Nasser A, et al.
articles.abstract: Social anxiety disorder (SAD) is a common and often chronic psychiatric illness characterized by persistent fear of social or performance situations and associated functional impairment and avoidance. Although multiple pharmacologic treatments have been studied, questions remain regarding optimal sequencing of therapies, long-term treatment strategies, and the management of partial or treatment-resistant illness. This narrative review synthesizes the evidence for pharmacologic treatments for SAD across medication classes, including antidepressants, benzodiazepines, monoamine oxidase inhibitors, GABA-related agents, second-generation antipsychotics, and emerging interventions. It also examines as-needed (PRN) interventions and steroid-based approaches, deprescribing and proposes a definition of treatment-resistant SAD. Randomized controlled trials, open-label studies, and guideline recommendations were reviewed to provide a framework for pharmacologic decision-making. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) remain the best-supported first-line pharmacotherapies for SAD. Evidence supports switching within or across antidepressant classes and integrating pharmacotherapy with behavioral interventions in patients with incomplete response. Additional treatments, including benzodiazepines, monoamine oxidase inhibitors, pregabalin, and selected augmentation strategies, may be considered for patients with persistent symp
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review addresses pharmacologic treatments for social anxiety disorder (SAD), a common and often chronic condition, by synthesizing evidence from randomized controlled trials, open-label studies, and guidelines to guide treatment decisions across medication classes and emerging interventions.

FINDINGS: SSRIs and SNRIs are supported as first-line pharmacotherapies for SAD based on available evidence. For patients with incomplete response, switching within or across antidepressant classes and combining pharmacotherapy with behavioral interventions is recommended. Additional options such as benzodiazepines, monoamine oxidase inhibitors, pregabalin, and selected augmentation strategies may be considered, though the evidence is more limited. Data on long-term outcomes and treatment-resistant populations remain sparse.

INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this study synthesizes existing evidence rather than generating new data, and its conclusions are based on a qualitative assessment of heterogeneous studies. The strength of evidence varies significantly across medication classes, with robust support for SSRIs/SNRIs but more limited data for alternatives. The review highlights important gaps, particularly regarding long-term outcomes and treatment-resistant SAD, which limit the ability to make definitive recommendations. The lack of quantitative effect sizes or direct comparisons between treatments further constrains the interpretation.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: SSRIs and SNRIs remain the cornerstone of pharmacologic treatment for SAD, with individualized sequencing and integration with behavioral interventions recommended for partial responders. Clinicians should be cautious when considering alternatives due to limited evidence, and prioritize long-term management strategies given the chronic nature of SAD. Further research is needed to clarify optimal treatment strategies for resistant cases.

articles.title: Autistic Masking and Mental Health Outcomes in Autistic Women: A Systematic Review (2015-2025).
articles.authors: Cuni E, Cantero-García M
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Autistic masking-the behavioral and cognitive strategies through which autistic individuals conceal or compensate for their autistic traits to navigate neurotypical social environments-has been consistently linked to adverse mental health outcomes, with women disproportionately affected. This systematic review examined the association between autistic masking and anxiety, depression, autistic burnout, and suicidality in autistic adult women, and identified which mental health indicators are most consistently predicted by masking. METHODS: A systematic search was conducted across five databases (PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, APA PsycINFO, and ProQuest One Psychology) covering publications from January 2015 to December 2025, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420261342682). Eligibility criteria required autistic adult women (≥ 18 years) with formal diagnosis, explicit measurement of masking, and at least one specified mental health outcome. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and CASP. RESULTS: Nine studies (2018-2025) were included, with a combined analytic sample exceeding 1,500 women across seven countries. Masking was consistently associated with anxiety (β = 0.21-0.22; d = 0.93) and depression (g = 0.56; Nagelkerke R² = 0.358 via structured lifetime diagnosis), and constituted an independent predictor of suicidality (β = 0.198; OR = 5.04 vs. general population). The CAT-Q assimilation subscale was the
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (2015–2025) asked whether autistic masking—strategies to conceal autistic traits—worsens anxiety, depression, autistic burnout, or suicidality in formally diagnosed autistic adult women, and which masking measures best predict these outcomes.

FINDINGS: Nine cross-sectional and cohort studies (>1,500 women across seven countries) showed consistent associations: masking with anxiety (β = 0.21–0.22; d = 0.93) and depression (g = 0.56; Nagelkerke R² = 0.358 for lifetime diagnosis), and an independent link to suicidality (β = 0.198; OR ≈ 5 vs. general population). The CAT-Q assimilation subscale predicted suicidal ideation via anxiety. No study measured autistic burnout with validated tools.

INTERPRETATION: Evidence is moderate in strength (mostly observational, heterogeneous measures) but points to masking as a clinically meaningful psychosocial risk factor. Effect sizes for anxiety and depression are moderate-to-large, while the suicidality association, though strong, is based on a small subset of studies and indirect comparisons. Key limitations include lack of longitudinal data, validated burnout assessment, and standardized masking instruments.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine clinical assessment should include validated masking scales (e.g., CAT-Q) and targeted suicide-risk evaluation in autistic women, especially those reporting high assimilation demands. Further longitudinal research is needed to determine whether reducing masking causally improves mental health outcomes.

articles.title: Antipsychotic-Induced Remodeling of the Gut Microbiota: Drug-Specific Patterns and Molecular Links to Metabolic Adverse Effects.
articles.authors: Papacocea RI, Adina Gabriela M, Radu-Ștefan V, et al.
articles.abstract: Antipsychotic drugs are essential for the treatment of schizophrenia-spectrum disorders and other severe psychiatric conditions, but several agents produce clinically important metabolic and gastrointestinal adverse effects. Increasing evidence suggests that these outcomes may involve bidirectional interactions between antipsychotics and the gut microbiota. This structured narrative review integrates human, animal, gnotobiotic, in vitro, pharmacokinetic, and multi-omic evidence to examine drug-specific microbiome effects and microbiota-dependent modulation of host responses. Olanzapine has the strongest mechanistic evidence, with germ-free, antibiotic-depletion, colonization, and vagotomy studies supporting a contributory role of the microbiota in weight gain, adiposity, inflammation, altered microbial metabolites, and lipid dysregulation. Risperidone also shows microbiota-dependent metabolic and neurobiological effects, whereas findings for clozapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, lurasidone, and amisulpride remain more heterogeneous or limited. Across agents, no universal taxonomic pattern has emerged. Functional pathways involving short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, epithelial barrier integrity, immune and neuroendocrine signaling, vagal pathways, and microbial drug metabolism appear more informative than individual taxa or the Firmicutes/Bacteroidota ratio. Current evidence remains limited by methodological heterogeneity, small cohorts, confounding, and predominantly preclin
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This structured narrative review examines how antipsychotic drugs (used for schizophrenia-spectrum and severe psychiatric disorders) alter the gut microbiota and whether these changes contribute to metabolic adverse effects such as weight gain and inflammation. It synthesizes human, animal, and in vitro evidence to identify drug-specific patterns and molecular pathways linking antipsychotics to microbiota-mediated metabolic effects.

FINDINGS: Olanzapine shows the strongest evidence, with germ-free, antibiotic-depletion, and colonization studies supporting microbiota-dependent contributions to weight gain, adiposity, inflammation, and lipid dysregulation. Risperidone also demonstrates microbiota-dependent metabolic and neurobiological effects, while evidence for clozapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, lurasidone, and amisulpride is more heterogeneous or limited. Functional pathways (e.g., short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, immune signaling) appear more informative than specific bacterial taxa.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence is largely preclinical with methodological heterogeneity, small human cohorts, and confounding, limiting causal inference. While olanzapine and risperidone show consistent microbiota-mediated metabolic effects in controlled studies, findings for other antipsychotics are inconsistent or preliminary. The review highlights plausible biological mechanisms but cannot yet determine clinical significance or guide treatment choices based on microbiota modulation.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support microbiome-based antipsychotic selection or adjunctive microbiome-targeted interventions in routine care. Future longitudinal multi-omic studies in treatment-naive patients are needed before considering microbiota modulation as a strategy to mitigate metabolic adverse effects.

articles.title: Autistic burnout: Early insights from a systematic review on characteristics, precipitating factors, and protective mechanisms.
articles.authors: Bory P, Fiorentino M, Bérenguier L, et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Despite sustained advocacy by autistic individuals over the years, autism research has largely overlooked autistic burnout, a critical but understudied phenomenon. Recently, scientific research has begun to address this gap. This systematic review of literature aims to consolidate scientific knowledge about autistic burnout. The objectives of this study are to provide a comprehensive overview of the known characteristics of autistic burnout, its precipitating factors and strategies for recovery and to clarify how it differs from depression. METHODS: Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines we searched PubMed, PsychINFO, and Web of Science in January 2025 to identify articles that fit our study goals. Some inclusion and exclusion criteria were determined for this review. We appraised the quality of studies with a Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) checklist. A qualitative analysis was conducted based on the final selected articles. RESULTS: Thirteen articles met inclusion criteria, revealing key characteristics of autistic burnout. Autistic burnout is characterized by a range of symptoms including mental and physical exhaustion, and impairment in cognitive capacities, particularly executive functions. Furthermore, significant impacts on mental health were reported with self-injury and suicidal ideation. Current research conceptualized autistic burnout as a chronic condition with emerging evidence distinguishing
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Autistic burnout is an understudied phenomenon with limited professional awareness despite advocacy from autistic individuals. This systematic review synthesizes early research on its characteristics, precipitating factors, recovery strategies, and distinctions from depression, using PRISMA guidelines and qualitative analysis of 13 studies.

FINDINGS: The review identified 13 studies describing autistic burnout as involving mental/physical exhaustion, cognitive impairment (especially executive dysfunction), and severe mental health impacts (e.g., self-injury, suicidal ideation). Precipitating factors included masking, social demands, and chronic stressors. Recovery often involved self-awareness, support from autistic communities, and targeted interventions, though some individuals reported incomplete recovery.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and heterogeneous, based on a small, qualitative literature with variable study quality (assessed via CASP checklists). The distinction from depression remains unclear, and representativeness is limited. The findings highlight a critical gap in clinical knowledge but cannot yet guide definitive practice changes due to methodological limitations and lack of quantitative data.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should recognize autistic burnout as a distinct, potentially severe condition with overlapping features to depression, particularly in autistic adults experiencing chronic stress or masking. Further research is needed before specific recommendations can be made; meanwhile, validating patient experiences and avoiding misdiagnosis (e.g., as solely depression) may improve care.

articles.title: Multimodal Machine Learning Approaches to Detect Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) Using Physiological and Behavioural Biomarkers: A Systematic Review.
articles.authors: Walle AD, Bargshady G
articles.abstract: Background: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by persistent symptoms of inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity that can affect individuals throughout childhood and adulthood. Accurate and timely detection is important for appropriate support and management, but current assessment relies heavily on behavioural observations, clinical assessments, and information from multiple sources, which can be time-consuming and may be influenced by subjective judgement. These challenges have increased interest in machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches that can analyse multiple physiological and behavioural data sources. Multimodal AI approaches may provide a more comprehensive and objective way to detect ADHD by combining complementary information from different data types. Objectives: This systematic review aimed to examine the use of ML and DL methods for ADHD detection using multimodal physiological and behavioural biomarkers, with particular attention to data sources, modelling approaches, multimodal fusion strategies, and reported diagnostic performance. Methods: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines to identify studies published from 2015 to 2026 that applied machine learning (ML) or deep learning (DL) methods to multimodal data for ADHD detection. We selected studies using predefined i
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (PRISMA 2020) examined whether multimodal machine learning (ML) or deep learning (DL) approaches using physiological and behavioural biomarkers can improve detection of ADHD, a common neurodevelopmental disorder. The review synthesised 25 heterogeneous studies published 2015–2026 that combined neuroimaging, EEG, HRV, EDA, behavioural assessments, and wearable/IoT data to classify ADHD.

FINDINGS: Included studies varied widely in design and sample size (n = 22 to 15,883; mostly cross-sectional). Early multimodal fusion models often reported diagnostic accuracies above 80%, with candidate biomarkers including frontal brain activity, heart rate patterns, and oculomotor behaviour. However, substantial differences in data sources, acquisition, feature extraction, modelling, and evaluation protocols precluded direct comparison and raised concerns about generalisability and reliability.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and heterogeneous, with small and often unrepresentative samples and inconsistent methodological standards. While reported accuracies are promising, the lack of standardised protocols, leakage-safe validation, and multi-site testing limits internal and external validity. Model interpretability and real-world clinical applicability remain uncertain. Stronger, standardised evidence is needed before these tools can be recommended for routine ADHD assessment.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current multimodal ML/DL approaches are not yet ready for bedside use in ADHD diagnosis. Clinicians should await larger, multi-site, standardised studies with transparent validation before considering adoption; meanwhile, standard clinical assessment remains the gold standard.

articles.title: Effects of ADHD Medications on Male Reproductive Function: A Systematic Review of In Vivo Mammalian Evidence.
articles.authors: Wojtysiak K, Ratka Z, Chłopaś-Konowałek A
articles.abstract: Long-term treatment with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) medications may begin before reproductive maturity, but their effects on male reproductive health remain uncertain. We systematically evaluated controlled in vivo mammalian evidence on male reproductive effects of medications used for ADHD, including the consistency, timing, reversibility, and certainty of reported associations. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception to 8 August 2026. Eligible studies were English-language, controlled in vivo mammalian experiments evaluating a prespecified ADHD medication and at least one male reproductive outcome. Human, in-vitro-only, uncontrolled, conference-abstract, and preprint reports were excluded. Risk of bias was independently assessed by two reviewers using the Systematic Review Centre for Laboratory Animal Experimentation (SYRCLE) tool, and certainty was evaluated using an adapted preclinical Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. Results were grouped by drug and nine prespecified outcome domains and synthesized narratively. Meta-analysis was not performed because of substantial methodological and outcome heterogeneity. Twenty-two studies were included: 19 evaluated methylphenidate (MPH), two clonidine, and one lisdexamfetamine (LDX); 17 were conducted in rats, four in mice, and one in rhesus macaques. During active MPH exposure, adverse changes predominated in spermatogenesis, sperm quant
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined controlled in vivo mammalian studies on the effects of ADHD medications (methylphenidate, clonidine, lisdexamfetamine) on male reproductive outcomes, addressing concerns about long-term use before reproductive maturity. The review synthesised evidence on consistency, timing, reversibility, and certainty of associations.

FINDINGS: Twenty-two studies were included (19 methylphenidate, 2 clonidine, 1 lisdexamfetamine), primarily in rats (n=17), with few in mice (n=4) or rhesus macaques (n=1). During active methylphenidate exposure, adverse effects were frequently reported on spermatogenesis, sperm quantity/quality, testicular microstructure, testosterone, and inflammatory markers. Post-exposure findings were often neutral or partially reversible. Clonidine studies suggested altered epididymal contractility, while the single lisdexamfetamine study reported broad adverse effects. All 18 drug-by-outcome domains were rated as very low certainty due to small samples, heterogeneity, unclear risk of bias, and indirectness to human therapeutic use.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and inconsistent, with no high or moderate certainty findings. The animal models, dosing, and exposure durations are not directly comparable to clinical ADHD treatment in humans. While signals of potential reproductive toxicity exist—particularly during active exposure—quantitative risk estimation is not possible. The review highlights critical gaps, including lack of replication, incomplete reporting, and indirectness.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify changes to clinical practice regarding ADHD medication use in males of reproductive age. Clinicians should remain aware of theoretical concerns but prioritise evidence from human studies. Further research—particularly prospective human cohorts—is needed before any risk assessment can be made.

articles.title: Predicting cognitive-behavioral therapy outcomes in obsessive-compulsive disorder from inhibitory control neural activity: A mega-analysis and machine learning study from the ENIGMA-OCD consortium.
articles.authors: Džinalija N, van den Heuvel OA, Simpson HB, et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an effective treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), yet it remains difficult to predict who will respond. This study investigates associations between neural activity during inhibitory control tasks and CBT outcomes, and its value as a predictive marker of CBT outcome. METHODS: Using fMRI data from individuals performing an inhibitory control task across five ENIGMA-OCD samples (n = 130, age range=8-57, 54% female), mass-univariate associations were analyzed between response inhibition and error processing activity and three CBT outcomes: response, remission, and change in symptom severity. Random forest classifier and support vector machine models using leave-one-sample-out and 5-fold cross-validation were used to predict CBT response and remission from fMRI activity and clinical data. RESULTS: Remission after CBT was associated with weaker activity in default mode regions during response inhibition and in the right supramarginal gyrus during error processing. Greater symptom reduction was linked to weaker pre-treatment activity across frontoparietal, dorsal attention, visual, and subcortical regions during response inhibition, and stronger default mode activity during error processing. These group-level effects were partially confirmed with machine learning, which predicted CBT response using inhibitory and error-related activity with modest AUC values of 0.66-0.67. Prediction of CBT remission or using other data
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This mega-analysis and machine learning study from the ENIGMA-OCD consortium (n=130, age 8–57, 54% female) examined whether pre-treatment fMRI activity during inhibitory control and error processing tasks could predict cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) outcomes in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

FINDINGS: Remission after CBT was associated with weaker activity in default mode regions during response inhibition and in the right supramarginal gyrus during error processing. Greater symptom reduction correlated with weaker pre-treatment activity across frontoparietal, dorsal attention, visual, and subcortical regions during response inhibition, and stronger default mode activity during error processing. Machine learning models predicted CBT response with modest AUC values of 0.66–0.67, but prediction of remission or using other data types did not exceed chance.

INTERPRETATION: The study leverages a relatively large multi-site sample and uses both mass-univariate and machine learning approaches, strengthening internal validity. However, the modest AUC values indicate limited predictive power at the individual level, and the findings are preliminary without external validation. The heterogeneity in age and imaging protocols across samples may limit generalisability to routine care settings.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current results do not support the use of inhibitory control fMRI activity as a clinically reliable biomarker for predicting CBT outcomes in OCD. Further research with larger, more homogeneous cohorts and prospective validation is needed before considering translation to bedside decision-making.

articles.title: [Deprescribing in geriatric psychiatry: overview of guideline recommendations, deprescribing algorithms, and tools].
articles.authors: Haussmann R, Borchers R
articles.abstract: Deprescribing is the process of pharmacotherapy optimization by dose reduction or discontinuation of medications. Deprescribing is of high clinical relevance in geriatric psychiatry. The reduction of psychotropic medications is possible in the majority of cases and can improve quality of life. Guidance in deprescibing is provided by lists of potentially inappropriate medications (PIM), guidelines and specific deprescribing tools, although the necessary risk-benefit analysis and individualized case assessment cannot be replaced. An essential prerequisite for a successful deprescribing process is transparent communication with patients and relatives about benefits and risks and the individualized case management. This review summarizes available deprescribing recommendations in the field of geriatric psychiatry from relevant guidelines, PIM lists and specific deprescribing tools.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This is a narrative review summarizing guideline recommendations, deprescribing algorithms, and tools for reducing or discontinuing psychotropic medications in older adults with psychiatric disorders. The clinical question is how to safely optimize pharmacotherapy in geriatric psychiatry through deprescribing.

FINDINGS: The review highlights that deprescribing is feasible in most cases and may improve quality of life. It emphasizes the use of potentially inappropriate medication (PIM) lists, guidelines, and deprescribing tools to guide practice. However, individualized risk-benefit assessment and transparent communication with patients and relatives remain essential.

INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this paper synthesizes existing guidance rather than presenting new empirical data. Its strength lies in consolidating diverse deprescribing resources, but it lacks quantitative outcomes or head-to-head comparisons. The evidence base is largely derived from guidelines and expert consensus, which may limit generalizability. The clinical recommendations are reasonable but should be applied cautiously, as deprescribing outcomes can vary widely among individuals.
