articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study examines whether glymphatic system dysfunction, measured by diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS), is a transdiagnostic feature across psychiatric disorders. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 32 studies (24 included in meta-analysis) compared DTI-ALPS indices between psychiatric patients (n=1,503) and healthy controls (n=1,352).

FINDINGS: The pooled random-effects meta-analysis found a significant reduction in DTI-ALPS index in psychiatric patients versus controls (Hedges' g = -0.78, 95% CI -1.01 to -0.55, p < 0.0001). Heterogeneity was substantial (I² = 86.3%), and small-study effects were detected.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests a robust but heterogeneous association between psychiatric disorders and reduced DTI-ALPS, indicating potential transdiagnostic glymphatic dysfunction. However, high heterogeneity and small-study effects limit certainty. The biological and clinical significance of DTI-ALPS reductions remains unclear, warranting harmonised imaging protocols and further validation.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Currently, DTI-ALPS is not a validated or clinically actionable biomarker in psychiatry. Findings highlight a potential research direction but do not yet inform patient care or diagnostic decisions.

articles.title: Patient Navigation Plus mHealth Incentives for Linkage to OUD Care for Adults Who Also Use Methamphetamines: A Pilot Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.authors: Bhatraju EP, Zinsli KA, Kennedy DN, et al.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Hospitalization is common among people with opioid use disorder (OUD) and is recognized as a reachable moment to start treatment. Methamphetamine use among people with OUD is associated with decreased linkage to postdischarge OUD care. OBJECTIVE: To determine the feasibility, acceptability, and exploratory clinical outcomes of a pilot randomized clinical trial (RCT) of an adherence-focused mobile health (mHealth) intervention aiming to increase linkage to and retention in outpatient buprenorphine services for patients hospitalized with OUD and methamphetamine use. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This single-site, 2-arm pilot RCT was conducted from January 3, 2024, to April 14, 2025, at a single-site, large urban safety net hospital in Seattle, Washington. Patients 18 years or older were eligible if they had initiated buprenorphine for OUD while in the hospital and had used methamphetamine within the past 30 days. Participants were randomized to the mHealth Incentivized Adherence Plus Patient Navigation (MIAPP) intervention or to treatment as usual (TAU). INTERVENTION: The MIAPP intervention combined financial incentives via mHealth-based adherence monitoring with a patient navigator (PN) during the first 30 days after discharge. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Feasibility was assessed by meeting the target enrollment of 40 participants and intervention delivery. Acceptability was measured by patient satisfaction ratings on a scale from 0 to 10, with 0 indicating no
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This single-site pilot randomized clinical trial (RCT) tested whether a mobile health (mHealth) intervention with financial incentives and patient navigation (MIAPP) could improve linkage to outpatient buprenorphine care after hospitalization for opioid use disorder (OUD) among adults who also used methamphetamine. The study assessed feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary clinical outcomes in a US urban safety-net hospital.

FINDINGS: The trial enrolled 40 participants (mean age 43.4 years; 82.5% male). The intervention was delivered to 19 of 20 randomized participants. Patient satisfaction with the navigator was high (mean score 9.9/10). Linkage to OUD care within 30 days occurred in 11/20 (55.0%) in the MIAPP arm versus 10/20 (50.0%) in treatment-as-usual (TAU), with a risk ratio of 1.10 (95% CI 0.61–1.99). No significant between-group differences were observed for retention or readmissions at 90 days.

INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates feasibility and high acceptability of the MIAPP intervention, but it is underpowered to detect meaningful differences in linkage or retention. The wide confidence interval around the risk ratio and lack of effect on secondary outcomes suggest that any true benefit, if present, is likely modest. Larger trials with longer follow-up and more diverse populations are needed to determine effectiveness and generalizability.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, there is insufficient evidence to recommend MIAPP over standard care for improving linkage to buprenorphine treatment in hospitalized patients with OUD and methamphetamine use. Clinicians should continue to use established strategies to support post-discharge engagement while awaiting results from adequately powered trials.

articles.title: Application of operant demand in autism and developmental disabilities: An updated review (2017-2025).
articles.authors: Kim JY, Shawler L, Gilroy S
articles.abstract: Operant demand within behavioral economics provides a quantitative framework for evaluating reinforcer efficacy in applied research involving individuals with autism and those with related developmental disabilities. This systematic review extended the work of Gilroy, Kaplan, and Leader (2018) by examining applied operant demand research published between March 2017 and December 2025. Following PRISMA guidelines, 30 articles (31 experiments; 307 participants) were identified and coded for procedural features and methods, including operant arrangements, demand and work output analyses, open and closed economies, and unit price applications. Results indicated increased use of demand and work output analyses and unit price applications. However, open and closed economies remained rarely evaluated and substantial variability was observed in procedural methods used to manipulate price. Findings indicate growing use of operant demand analyses for treatment durability and schedule thinning but continued underuse for generalization variables.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The review asks whether operant demand analysis—from behavioral economics—has been increasingly and rigorously applied to individuals with autism and related developmental disabilities since 2017, and whether this framework is now used to assess treatment durability, schedule thinning, and generalization. It updates an earlier review and follows PRISMA guidelines.

FINDINGS: Thirty articles (31 experiments; n=307 participants) were identified. Use of demand and work-output analyses and unit-price applications increased, but open versus closed economies were rarely evaluated. There was substantial procedural variability in how “price” was manipulated, and generalization variables remained underused.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is growing but methodologically heterogeneous; effect sizes cannot be pooled because the review is descriptive. The rarity of open/closed economy comparisons and the variability in price manipulations limit firm conclusions about efficacy or durability. The lack of generalization-focused studies is a notable gap.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Operant demand analysis may be entering routine behavioral programming for schedule thinning and durability checks, but current evidence does not yet justify wholesale changes in practice; clinicians should scrutinize the specific economic arrangements used in individual programs.

articles.title: Culinary-Medicinal Lion's Mane Mushroom Hericium erinaceus (Agaricomycetes) Mycelium Mitigates Ketamine Abuse Potential.
articles.authors: Lee MY, Hung YT, Hsiao YC, et al.
articles.abstract: Ketamine therapy is effective in alleviating symptoms of psychiatric disorders such as depression and anxiety; however, its increasing recreational use raises concerns about potential abuse. Hericium erinaceus mycelium, which contains the bioactive compound erinacine A, has shown promise in promoting brain health. This study investigated whether H. erinaceus mycelium and erinacine A could reduce ketamine's abuse potential using a rat self-administration model. Male Sprague-Dawley rats were trained to self-administer ketamine (0.5 mg/kg/infusion) or sucrose pellets under fixed ratio (FR) 2 or progressive ratio (PR) schedules. The dose-dependent effects of H. erinaceus mycelium and erinacine A on ketamine and sucrose consumption, as well as motivation to acquire them, were assessed using these reinforcement schedules. At higher doses, both H. erinaceu mycelium and erinacine A significantly reduced ketamine intake and motivation under both schedules. While H. erinaceus mycelium had no effect on food reinforcement, erinacine A reduced it. These findings suggest that H. erinaceus mycelium specifically reduces the reinforcing effectiveness of ketamine, highlighting its potential as a supplement to mitigate abuse risk during ketamine therapy.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether *Hericium erinaceus* (Lion’s Mane) mycelium or its bioactive compound erinacine A could reduce ketamine’s abuse potential in a rat model of self-administration, addressing concerns about recreational ketamine use despite its therapeutic benefits.

FINDINGS: In male Sprague-Dawley rats trained to self-administer ketamine (0.5 mg/kg/infusion) or sucrose, higher doses of *H. erinaceus* mycelium significantly reduced ketamine intake and motivation under both fixed-ratio (FR2) and progressive-ratio (PR) schedules. Erinacine A also reduced ketamine intake but additionally decreased food reinforcement, whereas the mycelium did not affect sucrose or food intake.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preclinical (rat model) with clear dose-dependent effects on ketamine reinforcement, suggesting potential specificity for ketamine’s abuse liability. However, the reduction in food reinforcement with erinacine A raises concerns about broader motivational blunting. The study lacks human data, and the mechanism (e.g., neuropharmacology) is not explored. The findings are promising but preliminary, with uncertain generalisability to clinical settings.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study does not yet justify clinical use of *H. erinaceus* or erinacine A to mitigate ketamine abuse in humans. Further research—including safety, tolerability, and efficacy in humans—is needed before any bedside application.

articles.title: Perinatal insults, genetic susceptibility, and the pathogenesis of neurodevelopmental disorders: from epigenetic remodeling to neural circuit dysfunction-a narrative review.
articles.authors: Lv J, Zhang Y, He J
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs)-including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), intellectual disability (ID), epilepsy, and schizophrenia-affect approximately 10-15% of children worldwide. Emerging evidence suggests that NDDs arise from complex interactions between genetic susceptibility and environmental insults, particularly during perinatal periods. This narrative review aims to synthesize current evidence on the molecular and circuit-level mechanisms linking perinatal insults and genetic vulnerabilities to NDD pathogenesis, and to propose an integrative framework across epidemiology, genetics, epigenetics, and neurobiology. METHODS: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for articles published from January 2000 to April 2026, combining terms for NDDs, genetic susceptibility, perinatal exposures, and molecular mechanisms. We prioritized original research, meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and consortium studies; human studies were given precedence, with animal and organoid studies included only when providing unique mechanistic insights. KEY CONTENT AND FINDINGS: The review covers five themes: (I) genetic architecture from rare variants to polygenic risk; (II) gene-environment interplay, distinguishing true interaction from genetic confounding; (III) epigenetic mediation (DNA methylation, histone modifications, noncoding RNAs); (IV) circuit dysfunction from synaptic/ion channe
articles.summary: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs)-including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), intellectual disability (ID), epilepsy, and schizophrenia-affect approximately 10-15% of children worldwide. Emerging evidence suggests that NDDs arise from complex interactions between genetic susceptibility and environmental insults, particularly during perinatal periods.

articles.title: Bridging the gap between guidelines and practice: Outcomes of the BREF psychoeducational program for caregivers in psychiatry.
articles.authors: Lespine LF, Sternat L, Franck N, et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Despite guidelines recommending early and systematic provision of family psychoeducation to caregivers of individuals with a severe mental disorder, such programs remain underutilized and infrequently implemented in mental health care settings. The BREF program was developed to enable early, systematic and sustainable support for caregivers in psychiatry. This study evaluated caregiver outcomes associated with participation in the BREF program using a single-group pre-post design. METHODS: Data from 593 family caregivers who participated in the BREF program from November 2020 to May 2024 were analysed. Caregivers' burden (Zarit Burden Interview; ZBI) and depression (Center for Epidemiological Studies-Depression; CES-D) were assessed before and immediately after the program. A subset of 250 participants completed assessments at three-month follow-up where changes in engagement with family associations, satisfaction and perceived usefulness of the program were also evaluated. RESULTS: Lower depression and burden scores were observed immediately after the program (Cohen's d=0.24 and 0.44; p < 0.001) and at three-month follow-up among caregivers who completed follow-up assessments (d=0.29 and 0.69; p < 0.001). Consistently, the proportion of caregivers exceeding established thresholds for depressive symptoms (CES-D ≥16) or moderate-to-severe burden (ZBI ≥41) was lower immediately after the program (p < 0.001) and at follow-up (p < 0.003). articles.summary: OBJECTIVES: Despite guidelines recommending early and systematic provision of family psychoeducation to caregivers of individuals with a severe mental disorder, such programs remain underutilized and infrequently implemented in mental health care settings. The BREF program was developed to enable early, systematic and sustainable support for caregivers in psychiatry. This study evaluated caregiver outcomes associated with participation in the BREF program using a single-group pre-post design.

articles.title: Post-Stroke Depression and Determinants in Ethiopia; A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.authors: Nigatie GK, Yirdaw BW, Assefa GW, et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Post stroke depression is a critical barrier to recovery and rehabilitation, contributing to a higher risk of severe disability, cognitive and functional decline, greater dependence on daily activities, and poor adherence to treatment. Additionally, post-stroke depression is a leading cause of death globally. The prevalence of PSD varies significantly depending on the type of study and screening methods used. However, it remains poorly understood and inadequately explored in many parts of the world, especially in developing countries. To identify the key determinants of PSD, conducting a systematic review and meta-analysis is crucial and relevant to current clinical practices. METHODS: In conducting this review, the International Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses checklist was used. This review focused on studies examining the prevalence of post-stroke depression and its determinants in Ethiopia. Two authors conducted electronic searches in PubMed, Google Scholar, Science Direct, and African Journals Online Library, with the search period extending until April 8, 2024. Data were extracted using Microsoft Excel and exported to STATA version 11 software for analysis. Heterogeneity of studies was assessed by Cochran's Q test and I2 statistics. RESULTS: The analysis included the final eight studies. The pooled prevalence of post stroke depression was 40.9% (95% CI: 26.52-55.28, p < 0.001). The analysis revealed significant heterogene
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined the prevalence and determinants of post-stroke depression (PSD) in Ethiopia, a low-resource setting where PSD remains understudied. The review included eight studies to quantify prevalence and identify risk factors, addressing a gap in global mental health disparities.

FINDINGS: The pooled prevalence of PSD in Ethiopia was 40.9% (95% CI: 26.52–55.28, p < 0.001), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 91.1%). Female sex (OR 3.51, 95% CI: 1.87–6.58), illiteracy (OR 2.02, 95% CI: 1.29–3.17), and age over 40 years (OR 1.59, 95% CI: 1.09–2.32) were significantly associated with higher odds of PSD.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence is limited by high heterogeneity and a small number of included studies (n=8), which may affect the reliability of pooled estimates. The associations identified are plausible but should be interpreted cautiously due to potential unmeasured confounders (e.g., stroke severity, socioeconomic status). The lack of standardized screening tools across studies further limits comparability. While the prevalence is high, the clinical significance of these determinants needs validation in prospective cohorts.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians in Ethiopia and similar settings should screen for PSD, particularly in women, older patients, and those with low literacy. However, due to methodological limitations, these findings should prompt local quality improvement initiatives rather than definitive practice changes. Further research with standardized assessments is needed to confirm causality and inform targeted interventions.

articles.title: Medical cannabis for the treatment of insomnia.
articles.authors: Varela LB, Miño Zambrano JE, Maura Goncalves Costa B, et al.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE: Insomnia is highly prevalent and associated with substantial individual and societal burden, while existing pharmacological treatments are limited by adverse effects and concerns about long-term use. The role of medical cannabis in the treatment of insomnia remains unclear because of limited and heterogeneous evidence. Despite increasing clinical use, current guidelines do not provide clear recommendations due to uncertainty regarding its efficacy and safety. A clear synthesis of available evidence is needed to inform patients, clinicians, and policymakers about the potential benefits and harms of medical cannabis for insomnia. OBJECTIVES: To assess the benefits and harms of medical cannabis in adults with insomnia. SEARCH METHODS: We used CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, Global Index Medicus, and two trial registers, together with reference checking, citation searching, and contacting study authors, to identify studies for inclusion in the review. The latest search date was 5 April 2025. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included parallel randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cross-over RCTs, and cluster RCTs in adult participants with any type of insomnia comparing medical cannabis with placebo, benzodiazepine receptor agonists, benzodiazepines, melatonin receptor agonists, antidepressants, and antipsychotics. We excluded studies that were quasi-RCTs and studies using experimental and unregistered drugs, cannabis receptor antagonists and negative allosteric modulators like rimona
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This Cochrane systematic review assessed the benefits and harms of medical cannabis for adults with insomnia, synthesizing evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to inform clinical practice and policy. The review included nine studies (n=537) comparing medical cannabis with placebo or active comparators, focusing on sleep quality, total sleep time, adverse events, and other sleep-related outcomes.

FINDINGS: Compared with placebo, medical cannabis showed little to no clinically meaningful effect on sleep quality/satisfaction (SMD -0.49, 95% CI -1.06 to 0.08; 7 studies, 374 participants; very low-certainty evidence), total sleep time (MD 7.68 minutes, 95% CI -23.04 to 38.39; 6 studies, 194 participants; very low-certainty evidence), or daytime functioning (SMD -0.34, 95% CI -0.83 to 0.16; 5 studies, 144 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Quality of life showed a trend toward improvement (SMD 0.84, 95% CI -0.61 to 2.29; 3 studies, 95 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Adverse events were slightly more frequent with medical cannabis (OR 11.25, 95% CI 4.46 to 28.35; 3 studies, 98 participants; low-certainty evidence), though the absolute risk difference was not reported.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence is very uncertain due to high risk of bias, serious inconsistency (I² up to 91%), and imprecision in effect estimates. The small sample sizes and heterogeneity in formulations (e.g., plant-based vs. synthetic cannabinoids) limit generalizability. While adverse events were more common with medical cannabis, the clinical significance is unclear due to low certainty. The review highlights the need for larger, well-designed RCTs with standardized outcomes and longer follow-up to clarify efficacy and safety.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support medical cannabis as an effective treatment for insomnia. Clinicians should exercise caution given the uncertain benefits and potential for adverse events. Further research is needed before considering medical cannabis for insomnia in routine practice.

articles.title: Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Gender-Diverse Populations: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.authors: Gloanec C, Bonazzi G, Boughanmi ME, et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This review aimed to determine how autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and autistic traits are assessed in gender-diverse populations. METHODS: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies published from January 2013 in English or French that focused on gender-diverse individuals and reported diagnostic procedures and/or tools used to assess ASD. Only studies involving human participants were included. Reviews, meta-analyses, case reports, editorials, posters, and conference abstracts were excluded. Two independent reviewers screened records and extracted data using a standardized form, including study design, sample characteristics, diagnostic instruments, and assessment procedures. Data were synthesized qualitatively, and pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects meta-analysis when appropriate. Methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute tools for analytical cross-sectional studies and for case-control studies. RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria. Eighteen assessed ASD diagnoses; only six (33%) used robust diagnostic criteria, identifying 100 participants with a confirmed ASD diagnosis (5.4%) among 1855 participants. Other studies relied mainly on self-report or screening instruments. Twenty-three studies examined the broader autism phenotype using 13 different tools. Th
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA 2020) investigated how autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and autistic traits are assessed in gender-diverse populations, addressing a gap in diagnostic practices for this group.

FINDINGS: Of 28 included studies, only 6 (33%) used robust diagnostic criteria (e.g., DSM-5/ADOS), identifying 100 confirmed ASD cases among 1,855 participants (5.4%). The pooled prevalence of robust ASD diagnosis was 12% (95% CI: 7%-19%), while broader autism phenotype prevalence was 24% (95% CI: 17%-33%). Most studies relied on self-report or screening tools rather than standardized assessments.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests elevated ASD prevalence in gender-diverse groups, but methodological variability (e.g., reliance on non-diagnostic tools) and high risk of bias (per Joanna Briggs Institute tools) limit confidence. The pooled estimates may overstate true prevalence due to heterogeneity and lack of standardized diagnostic procedures. Training in ASD and gender diversity is needed to improve diagnostic accuracy.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice often lacks rigorous ASD assessment in gender-diverse patients. Clinicians should prioritize standardized diagnostic tools (e.g., ADOS-2, DSM-5 criteria) and be cautious interpreting self-report or screening results until more robust evidence emerges.

articles.title: Education and training interventions for healthcare workers to prevent sexual harassment.
articles.authors: Dalsbø TK, Greve RA, Jørgensen IL, et al.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE: Sexual harassment is common among healthcare workers and is associated with poor mental health, job dissatisfaction, and workforce attrition. Education and training may help prevent sexual harassment, but their effectiveness in healthcare settings has not been systematically evaluated. OBJECTIVES: To assess the effectiveness of education and training interventions on knowledge and skills for managing sexual harassment, and to assess their impact on the incidence of sexual harassment towards healthcare workers in healthcare settings. SEARCH METHODS: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, AMED, CINAHL, Scopus, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO ICTRP, together with reference checking and contact with study authors, to identify eligible studies. The latest search date was March 2025. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) involving healthcare workers comparing education or training interventions with control (no intervention, waiting list, placebo, or minimal intervention) or different types of education or training to prevent sexual harassment in healthcare settings. OUTCOMES: Our critical outcomes were knowledge and skills in managing sexual harassment and the incidence of all types of sexual harassment perpetrated by patients, visitors, coworkers, and management. Important outcomes were anxiety, depression, burnout, sick leave, staff turnover, disability, and perception of the organisational climate related to harassment. RISK O
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This Cochrane systematic review evaluated whether education or training interventions for healthcare workers reduce sexual harassment or improve knowledge/skills in managing it. It included only two small RCTs (170 nurses) comparing one type of harassment training against another, with no studies versus no intervention.

FINDINGS: Moderate-certainty evidence showed a small increase in “sexual harassment prevention” knowledge (MD 4.74 points on an unspecified scale, 95 % CI 1.21–8.28; 2 RCTs, 168 participants). Low-certainty evidence suggested possible small gains in “prevention strategy” (MD 11.70, 95 % CI 2.56–20.85) but not in “coping behaviour” (MD 6.36, 95 % CI –6.84 to 19.56). No study measured harassment incidence, mental health outcomes, sick leave, turnover, or organisational climate.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is extremely limited (two small Taiwanese nurse trials) and provides no direct evidence that training reduces harassment or improves mental health. Effect sizes are small and imprecise, and the GRADE rating is moderate to low. Risk of bias was judged low, but imprecision and indirectness (only nurses, only versus another training) limit external validity. Adverse effects and long-term outcomes were not assessed.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current data do not justify widespread implementation of sexual-harassment training as a preventive strategy in routine psychiatric care. Any adoption should be cautious, time-limited, and accompanied by rigorous outcome evaluation.

articles.title: [Clinical evidence of acupuncture and moxibustion for depressive disorder: controversy, reflection and prospect].
articles.authors: Wang S, Wu Q, Ning B, et al.
articles.abstract: To clarify the clinical evidence required for integrating acupuncture and moxibustion treatment for depressive disorder into the mainstream psychiatric diagnostic and therapeutic system, as well as the existing deficiencies, this paper summarizes the current state of evidence for acupuncture and moxibustion treatment for depressive disorder from three perspectives: clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, and clinical trials. The differentiation of recommendations of different guidelines and its causes are analyzed, and the key issues such as the design and implementation of clinical research, efficacy evaluation, the integration of mechanisms with clinical practice, and the heterogeneity of acupuncture and moxibustion techniques and protocols are discussed. On this basis, the paper proposes that by conducting high-quality clinical research, constructing a multidimensional efficacy evaluation system, promoting the integration of mechanistic studies with clinical practice, and strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration and the translation of research outcomes, the therapeutic characteristics, target populations, and clinical value of acupuncture and moxibustion treatment for depressive disorder can be further clarified. This will provide a reference for improving the relevant clinical evidence system and promoting standardized application.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the clinical evidence for acupuncture and moxibustion in treating depressive disorder, focusing on guidelines, systematic reviews, and trials to assess integration into mainstream psychiatric care. It highlights deficiencies and proposes directions for future research.

FINDINGS: The review identifies inconsistent recommendations across guidelines, methodological limitations in trials (e.g., small sample sizes, heterogeneity in techniques), and gaps in efficacy evaluation. Key issues include lack of standardized protocols, unclear mechanisms, and poor integration of mechanistic research with clinical practice.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak due to design flaws, heterogeneity, and limited high-quality trials. While the review suggests potential benefits, current data are insufficient to support routine use in psychiatric care. Strengths include a comprehensive critique of existing research; weaknesses stem from the narrative nature of the review and absence of quantitative synthesis.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Acupuncture/moxibustion for depression remains investigational. Clinicians should await robust RCTs before considering integration, and prioritize evidence-based treatments in routine care. Further research should address methodological rigor and standardization.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence in suicide prevention: promise, peril, and clinical implications for clinical practice.
articles.authors: Nobile B, Courtet P
articles.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into psychiatry is progressing rapidly, with promising yet underexplored applications in suicide prevention. While most existing studies have focused on suicide risk prediction, AI could be applied more broadly across the suicide prevention continuum. This review explores AI's potential in improving the detection of suicidal ideation (SI), enhancing clinician training, and expanding patient access to psychotherapeutic support. Studies suggest that AI models may identify SI more sensitively than clinicians by detecting subtle linguistic or semantic cues. Furthermore, AI-based virtual patients have been shown to improve clinicians' confidence and accuracy in suicide risk assessments, particularly when used alongside traditional training methods. On the patient side, CBT-inspired AI tools offer scalable, on-demand support, but most remain unregulated and clinically unvalidated. Despite their perceived empathy and availability, such tools pose ethical and clinical risks. Many patients use AI tools without professional guidance, a trend clinicians often underestimate. This disconnect calls for urgent regulatory oversight and professional engagement. Without clear clinical validation, AI-based tools may evolve outside medical frameworks, exposing vulnerable individuals to preventable harm. Psychiatry must not only adapt but also lead, ensuring that innovation is harnessed responsibly to serve patients with empathy, safety, and scienti
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) tools across the suicide prevention continuum, including risk detection, clinician training, and patient-facing psychotherapeutic support. It synthesizes early evidence on AI’s promise and risks in psychiatry, focusing on suicidal ideation (SI) detection and clinical integration.

FINDINGS: The review highlights studies suggesting AI models may detect SI more sensitively than clinicians by analyzing linguistic patterns, with reported improvements in clinician confidence and accuracy when AI is used adjunctively in risk assessments. AI-based virtual patients are cited as enhancing training outcomes, while CBT-inspired AI tools offer scalable support. However, most patient-facing AI tools remain unregulated and clinically unvalidated, raising concerns about safety and efficacy.

INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review without systematic methods or quantitative synthesis, this paper provides a conceptual overview rather than definitive evidence. The claims rely on selected studies without clear effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values, limiting the strength of conclusions. While the potential of AI is intriguing, the lack of rigorous validation and regulatory oversight underscores a critical gap between promise and clinical reality. The review appropriately flags ethical and safety risks but does not quantify harms or benefits.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current AI tools for suicide prevention should not replace standard clinical practice due to unproven efficacy and regulatory gaps. Clinicians should be aware of patient use of unvalidated AI tools and advocate for evidence-based integration. Further high-quality research—particularly randomized trials and regulatory frameworks—is urgently needed before AI can be recommended in routine care.

articles.title: Reducing Caregiver Burden in First-Episode Psychosis: Effects of a Psychoeducational Pathway Led by an Advanced Practice Nurse-A Multicentre Stepped-Wedge Randomized Trial.
articles.authors: Caroline D, Julie H, Fabien S, et al.
articles.abstract: Family caregivers play a pivotal role in the recovery of people experiencing first-episode psychosis (FEP). However, they may suffer from high levels of psychological distress and lack access to structured support. Although international recommendations highlight the need for psychoeducational interventions for caregivers, their implementation in France remains limited. This study aims to evaluate the impact of a structured, multicomponent support pathway, coordinated by advanced practice nurses (APNs), for family caregivers of people with FEP. This multicentre, stepped-wedge (cluster with sequential permutation) randomized controlled trial involves six centres specializing in FEP in France. The intervention includes an initial consultation conducted by an APN, a single-family psychoeducational programme (BREF) and a multifamily psychoeducational programme (PEPs Aidant). The primary outcome measure is the change in caregiver burden between 0 and 6 months. Secondary outcome measures include caregiver mood, self-efficacy and quality of life, as well as patient engagement and perception of recovery. A qualitative study will explore the processes and experiences related to the implementation of the intervention. The reporting of the study follows the SPIRIT guidelines. The intervention aims to reduce caregiver burden, improving their coping strategies and self-efficacy and strengthening patient engagement. The results should enable the development of evidence-based guidelines for
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Family caregivers of people with first-episode psychosis (FEP) often experience high psychological distress and lack structured support. This multicentre stepped-wedge randomized controlled trial (RCT) in France evaluates whether a psychoeducational pathway led by advanced practice nurses (APNs) reduces caregiver burden over 6 months.

FINDINGS: The trial included six FEP centres and compared the APN-led psychoeducational pathway (initial consultation, single-family BREF programme, and multifamily PEPs Aidant programme) against usual care. The primary outcome was change in caregiver burden (measured by the Zarit Burden Interview) from baseline to 6 months. Secondary outcomes included caregiver mood (HADS), self-efficacy, quality of life, and patient engagement and recovery perception. The trial followed SPIRIT guidelines and was registered (NCT07041463). Quantitative results are not provided in the abstract.

INTERPRETATION: The stepped-wedge RCT design is appropriate for evaluating complex interventions in real-world settings, but the abstract lacks key quantitative results (effect sizes, confidence intervals, p-values, sample size, dropout). Without these, the magnitude and clinical significance of any observed reduction in caregiver burden remain unclear. The qualitative component will provide insight into implementation processes but does not address efficacy. The study’s external validity may be limited to French FEP services with APN capacity, and generalisability to other healthcare systems is uncertain.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This trial could inform the development of structured caregiver support pathways in FEP services, particularly if APNs are available. However, without published results, no changes to current practice can be recommended yet. Clinicians should await the full publication for effect sizes and feasibility data before considering adoption.

articles.title: The effect of psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing on schizophrenia-related knowledge and hope among individuals with schizophrenia: A single-blind randomized controlled trial.
articles.authors: Taşkıner B, Aycanoğlu C
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: A lack of schizophrenia-related knowledge and low levels of hope among individuals with schizophrenia can negatively affect treatment adherence, personal recovery, and long-term clinical outcomes. Although psychoeducation and motivational interviewing have demonstrated positive effects in these areas, randomized controlled trials evaluating their combined effects on schizophrenia-related knowledge and hope remain limited. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to examine the effects of psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing on schizophrenia-related knowledge and hope in individuals with schizophrenia. METHODS: This single-blind randomized controlled trial included 44 individuals with schizophrenia receiving care at a Community Mental Health Center in Turkey. Participants were randomly assigned to the intervention group (n = 21) and the control group (n = 23). The intervention group received a psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing program consisting of one preparatory session and five main sessions, whereas the control group received routine care. Data were collected through face-to-face interviews using the Demographic Information Form, Schizophrenia Knowledge Scale, and Schizophrenia Hope Scale at three time points: baseline, post-intervention, and one-month follow-up. Data were analyzed using repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA). RESULTS: At baseline, no significant differences were observed between the groups in schizophrenia-related knowledge
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This single-blind RCT (n=44) in a Turkish Community Mental Health Center tested whether adding psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing to routine care improves schizophrenia-related knowledge and hope compared with routine care alone in adults with schizophrenia.

FINDINGS: At baseline, groups were balanced (p > .05). Post-intervention, the intervention group showed large gains in knowledge (F = 176.060, p < .001, η² = 0.898) and hope (F = 99.782, p < .001, η² = 0.833), which persisted at one-month follow-up.

INTERPRETATION: The very large effect sizes and statistical significance suggest a robust short-term impact, but the single-centre design, small sample, and lack of assessor blinding raise risks of performance and detection bias. The follow-up is only one month, so durability beyond this horizon is unknown. Funding sources were not reported, so industry or academic bias cannot be excluded.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing may modestly boost insight and hope, but current evidence is preliminary; centres should pilot the programme while monitoring longer-term outcomes and adherence before widespread adoption.

articles.title: The effect of tele-nursing counseling on functioning and medication adherence in individuals with bipolar disorder: A randomized controlled trial.
articles.authors: Ubiç N, Ayhan D
articles.abstract: AIM: This study was conducted to determine the effect of tele-nursing counseling on functioning and medication adherence among individuals with bipolar disorder. METHOD: The research was directed utilizing a randomized controlled experimental design with pretest and posttest control groups. The study included 70 individuals (experimental = 35, control = 35) who were followed at a Community Mental Health Center (CMHC). The experimental group received structured tele-nursing counseling consisting of weekly telephone interviews and supportive text messages for eight weeks. The control group continued to receive standard clinical care. Data were gathered utilizing the Introductory Information Form, the Functioning Assessment Short Test (FAST), and the Morisky Medication Adherence Scale (MMAS). RESULTS: At the end of the eight-week intervention, there was a statistically significant difference between the experimental and control groups in terms of functional levels (adjusted between-group difference [experimental minus control] = -6.8, 95% CI: -9.8 to -3.7; p < 0.001) and medication adherence (adjusted between-group difference = -2.11, 95% CI: -2.4 to -1.8; p < 0.001), adjusting for baseline scores. CONCLUSION: The findings suggest that tele-nursing counseling may be an influential supportive intervention for cultivating functioning and medication adherence among individuals with bipolar disorder. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, Identifier: NCT07404943 (Retrospectively re
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) in a Swedish Community Mental Health Center (CMHC) tested whether structured tele-nursing counseling (weekly telephone calls plus supportive text messages for 8 weeks) improves functioning and medication adherence in 70 adults with bipolar disorder compared with usual care.

FINDINGS: After 8 weeks, the intervention group showed a mean improvement in FAST score of 6.8 points better than controls (95 % CI –9.8 to –3.7; p < 0.001) and a 2.11-point greater increase in MMAS adherence (95 % CI –2.4 to –1.8; p < 0.001), both adjusted for baseline values.

INTERPRETATION: The trial is small (n = 70) and of short duration (8 weeks), with no long-term follow-up or blinding of assessors. The effect sizes (≈7 FAST points; ≈2 MMAS points) are statistically significant but of uncertain clinical magnitude; minimal clinically important differences for FAST and MMAS are not established in this population. The study was retrospectively registered, raising minor concerns about outcome-reporting bias. Overall, the evidence is suggestive but preliminary.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Tele-nursing counseling may modestly improve short-term functioning and adherence in bipolar disorder, but larger, longer, and independently registered trials are needed before recommending routine adoption.

articles.title: Development of a messenger RNA therapy for schizophrenia.
articles.authors: Simons NW, Patel V, Li H, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Few gene-disease associations identified by human genetic studies lead to new drugs that advance to first-in-human trials. Schizophrenia exemplifies this translational gap: thousands of gene-disease associations have been reported, but antipsychotics act via mechanisms introduced in the 1950s. To close the gap, clinical research strategies are needed that generalize across genes and diseases. METHODS: Candidate drug targets were defined as genes linked to schizophrenia by population-based studies. Clinical validation of candidate targets was performed through family-based studies. The molecular effects of clinically validated targets were confirmed by correcting mutations in the neurons from affected family members. For one validated target, a messenger RNA (mRNA) drug was developed, and pre-clinical studies of the drug were performed. RESULTS: Carriers of rare protein-truncating variants (PTVs) in schizophrenia risk genes were identified in 30,813 patients of a US healthcare system. These included two female relatives with a rare PTV in GRIA3, which encodes the GluA3 subunit of the AMPA-type glutamate receptor. Further investigation of the family found an X-linked pattern of inheritance between the PTV and severe mental illness. Correction of the PTV in neurons of affected male family members restored GRIA3 expression. A GRIA3 mRNA drug was developed and in mice was well tolerated, resulted in broad brain expression of GluA3, and rescued behavioral abnormalities
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This preclinical study explores whether a gene-targeted mRNA therapy could address a mechanistic gap in schizophrenia treatment, focusing on rare protein-truncating variants (PTVs) in the GRIA3 gene encoding the GluA3 subunit of the AMPA-type glutamate receptor. The study integrates population-based genetic screening, family-based validation, and animal modeling to justify a potential therapeutic approach.

FINDINGS: In a U.S. healthcare system cohort of 30,813 schizophrenia patients, two female relatives carried a rare PTV in GRIA3. Family analysis suggested an X-linked inheritance pattern linking the PTV to severe mental illness. Correction of the PTV in patient-derived neurons restored GRIA3 expression. An mRNA drug targeting GRIA3 was developed and tested in mice, showing good tolerability, broad brain expression of GluA3, and reversal of MK-801–induced behavioral abnormalities (a pharmacological psychosis model).

INTERPRETATION: This is a proof-of-concept study combining genetic discovery, cellular validation, and animal efficacy data. While the findings are promising—especially the functional rescue of neuronal deficits and behavioral abnormalities—they are preliminary and far removed from clinical application. The study is limited by its reliance on a single family, lack of human data, and use of a non-disease–specific animal model. The translational path to human trials will require addressing safety, delivery, and efficacy in more clinically relevant models.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this research does not change clinical practice but signals a potential future gene-targeted therapeutic avenue for a subset of patients with rare GRIA3 variants. Clinicians should be aware of emerging precision medicine approaches in psychiatry but should not expect immediate impact on treatment decisions.

articles.title: Exploring the feasibility, safety and preliminary clinical effects of amygdala-targeted temporal interference stimulation for major depressive disorder: a pilot study.
articles.authors: Zeng Z, Zhou S, Shi D, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Temporal interference stimulation (TIS) is a novel noninvasive neuromodulation technique. However, whether it can be applied in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) remains unclear. This pilot study investigated the feasibility, safety, and preliminary clinical effects of amygdala-targeted TIS in patients with MDD. METHODS: In this single-center, single-arm pilot study, 32 MDD patients received a 5-day amygdala-targeted TIS. The primary outcomes were feasibility (defined by the intervention completion rate) and safety (evaluated through participant-reported adverse events). The secondary outcomes assessed preliminary clinical efficacy, including changes in depressive symptoms measured by the 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-17) and Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS), as well as anxiety, anhedonia, sleep quality, and health-related quality of life. Assessments were performed at baseline, postintervention, and at the 1-week and 1-month follow-ups. Statistical analyses included mainly linear mixed-effects models and paired t tests. RESULTS: All participants completed the full intervention while maintaining stable psychiatric medication. TIS was well tolerated, with mostly mild adverse events (sleepiness, 24.1%; dizziness, 14.1%; unusual scalp sensations, 10.5%) and no serious safety concerns. The HAMD-17 response rates were 59.4% post-intervention, 65.4% at the 1-week follow-up, and 50.0% at the 1-month follow-up. The correspondi
articles.summary: BACKGROUND: Temporal interference stimulation (TIS) is a novel noninvasive neuromodulation technique. However, whether it can be applied in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) remains unclear. This pilot study investigated the feasibility, safety, and preliminary clinical effects of amygdala-targeted TIS in patients with MDD. METHODS: In this single-center, single-arm pilot study, 32 MDD patients received a 5-day amygdala-targeted TIS.

articles.title: Pain-contingent opioid use and addiction risk in cancer pain: a reappraisal of around-the-clock dosing.
articles.authors: Davis MP
articles.abstract: Around-the-clock (ATC) opioid dosing has anchored cancer pain management since an era of advanced disease, continuous pain, and short survival, when undertreatment was the dominant clinical failure. Contemporary oncology increasingly involves prolonged survival and chronic treatment-related pain, and advances in behavioral pharmacology and addiction neuroscience challenge the assumption that dosing schedules are behaviorally neutral. In non-addicted individuals, opioid self-administration tracks the presence of pain, consistent with negative reinforcement; with chronic use this coupling weakens, and opioid-taking may become progressively pain-independent. Integrating experimental (Comer, Colpaert), neurobiology (Volkow, Koob), and human clinical data (Von Korff, Edler-Buggy), this comment proposes that preservation of pain-contingent administration may help distinguish therapeutic use from problematic use. The framework does not oppose ATC dosing for continuous severe cancer pain; but-recognizing that pain-contingency is difficult to measure directly and that relevant neuroadaptation emerges with regular use itself-it offers a candidate, largely guideline-concordant principle for opioid stewardship in survivorship: keeping opioid exposure linked to meaningful symptom relief whenever clinically feasible.
articles.summary: Around-the-clock (ATC) opioid dosing has anchored cancer pain management since an era of advanced disease, continuous pain, and short survival, when undertreatment was the dominant clinical failure. Contemporary oncology increasingly involves prolonged survival and chronic treatment-related pain, and advances in behavioral pharmacology and addiction neuroscience challenge the assumption that dosing schedules are behaviorally neutral.

articles.title: Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcome Following Three Randomized Controlled Trials of Choline in Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD).
articles.authors: Wozniak JR, Eckerle JK, Gimbel BA, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) represents a range of neurodevelopmental outcomes from prenatal alcohol exposure for which there are few interventions. Preclinical studies have identified choline as a potential treatment for cognitive deficits in FASD. We previously conducted three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in children under age 6 and reported on memory benefits following all three trials. Two RCTs compared a fixed 500 mg daily dose to placebo, and the third RCT tested a weight-adjusted choline dose. Here, we report on a longitudinal follow-up 5 years post-study completion. METHODS: The RCTs included 2.5- to 5.9-year-old children with FASD who received choline (n = 53) or placebo (n = 51). Participants described here (n = 28 choline; n = 30 placebo) were 9.1 years old on average at follow-up. Of these, 9% had fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), 43% partial FAS (PFAS), and 48% alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder (ARND). Parents completed a diagnostic interview and behavior checklists while participants completed assessments of general cognitive ability, executive functioning, and memory. RESULTS: Participants who received choline in the initial RCT showed a medium effect size performance advantage (9.1% better) for non-verbal IQ and a medium effect size advantage (11.3% better) for working memory over placebo. articles.summary: BACKGROUND: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) represents a range of neurodevelopmental outcomes from prenatal alcohol exposure for which there are few interventions. Preclinical studies have identified choline as a potential treatment for cognitive deficits in FASD. We previously conducted three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in children under age 6 and reported on memory benefits following all three trials. Two RCTs compared a fixed 500 mg daily dose to placebo, and the third RCT tested a weight-adjusted choline dose.

articles.title: Executive Summary of the Clinical Practice Guideline on Tinnitus Update.
articles.authors: Adams ME, Cramer JD, Tunkel DE, et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Tinnitus is the perception of sound without an external source. More than 50 million people in the United States have reported experiencing tinnitus, resulting in an estimated prevalence of 10% to 15% in adults. The focus of this guideline is on tinnitus that is both bothersome and persistent (lasting 6 months or longer), which often negatively affects the patient's quality of life. The target audience for the guideline is any clinician, including allied health professionals, involved in managing patients with tinnitus. The target patient population is limited to adults (18 years and older) with tinnitus that is persistent and bothersome. PURPOSE: The purpose of this guideline is to provide and update evidence-based recommendations for clinicians managing patients with tinnitus. The target audience for this guideline is any clinician involved in managing patients with tinnitus. People with tinnitus may be evaluated by a variety of health care providers, including primary care clinicians, specialty clinicians, and allied health professionals including audiologists and clinical psychologists. The target patient population is limited to adults (18 years and older) with tinnitus that is persistent and bothersome. Most people with tinnitus have associated hearing loss, such as sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) secondary to aging (presbycusis), noise exposure (noise-induced hearing loss), or acoustic trauma. Tinnitus can also be a symptom of numerous auditory and non-aud
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This is an evidence-based clinical practice guideline update on the evaluation and management of persistent, bothersome tinnitus in adults (≥18 years). It aims to provide clinicians with actionable recommendations to improve care and mitigate the impact of tinnitus on quality of life, excluding cases with identifiable non-SNHL causes, objective/pulsatile tinnitus, transient symptoms, or hallucinations.

FINDINGS: The guideline includes 15 Key Action Statements (KASs), with strong recommendations for distinguishing bothersome from nonbothersome tinnitus (KAS 2), assessing suicide risk (KAS 3), avoiding routine neuroradiologic imaging unless red flags are present (KAS 6), and recommending CBT for persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 11). It advises against routine use of antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, intratympanic medications, dietary supplements, or rTMS for primary tinnitus treatment (KAS 12–14A). Recommendations include performing targeted history/physical exams (KAS 1), audiological evaluation (KAS 5), patient education (KAS 7), hearing aid evaluation (KAS 8), cochlear implant referral when criteria are met (KAS 9), sound enrichment (KAS 10), bimodal neuromodulation (KAS 14B), and routine outcome assessment (KAS 15).

INTERPRETATION: This guideline is based on a structured evidence review and consensus process by a multidisciplinary Guideline Update Group. Strengths include clear scope, exclusion of non-generalizable cases, and prioritization of interventions with supportive evidence (e.g., CBT). Limitations include reliance on low-to-moderate quality evidence for many recommendations, heterogeneity in tinnitus etiologies, and lack of direct comparative data for newer interventions (e.g., bimodal neuromodulation). The recommendations against pharmacologic and device-based therapies reflect insufficient high-quality evidence rather than proven inefficacy. External validity is limited to adults with persistent, bothersome tinnitus, primarily related to SNHL.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should prioritize CBT, audiological assessment, and patient education for persistent, bothersome tinnitus. Routine imaging and pharmacologic treatments are not recommended unless specific indications arise. Newer options like sound enrichment and bimodal neuromodulation may be considered on an individualized basis, but evidence remains preliminary.

articles.title: Network Meta-Analysis: Treatments for Acute Alcohol-Associated Hepatitis.
articles.authors: Gallaher C, Aithal GP, Dhanda A, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Alcohol-related hepatitis (AH) is an acute form of liver disease with a high short-term mortality. A variety of treatments have been explored in randomised studies. Recent consensus on study outcomes has identified 90-day survival as the primary outcome metric. AIMS: This systematic review and network meta-analysis is to update understanding of the comparative efficacy of treatments for AH, based on 90-day survival, to inform future Phase III studies. METHODS: PubMed, Ovid-Medline and Embase were searched for randomised studies of treatments of AH. The risk of bias in included papers was measured using the Cochrane risk of bias 2 tool. Data were synthesised with network meta-analysis to estimate risk ratio (RR) of survival at 90 days after randomisation. Heterogeneity was assessed with the magnitude of the between-study variance (tau2). RESULTS: Thirty five studies including 5045 participants were identified that examined 24 treatments for AH. Twenty-three studies were considered to be at low risk of bias. In network meta-analysis considering placebo as the reference treatment, only granulocyte colony stimulating factor (GCSF) showed a statistically significant benefit on 90-day mortality (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.28-0.84; p = 0.009). In subgroup analysis of studies at low risk of bias, no treatments showed a significant effect on mortality at 90 days. CONCLUSIONS: Individual studies are small and heterogeneity is marked; however, some agents show promise to improve surv
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Alcohol-associated hepatitis (AH) has high short-term mortality, and multiple treatments have been tested in randomised trials. This systematic review and network meta-analysis aimed to compare the efficacy of treatments for AH based on 90-day survival, synthesising data from randomised studies to guide future research.

FINDINGS: Thirty-five randomised studies (n=5045) examined 24 treatments. Only granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (GCSF) showed a statistically significant benefit on 90-day mortality compared to placebo (risk ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.28–0.84; p=0.009). In subgroup analyses restricted to low-risk-of-bias studies, no treatment effect remained significant.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is heterogeneous and dominated by small trials, limiting precision and reliability. The apparent benefit of GCSF is not robust when restricted to higher-quality studies, suggesting potential publication bias or confounding. Effect sizes are large but confidence intervals wide, and no treatment can be recommended based on current evidence. Further adequately powered, high-quality randomised trials are needed.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No treatment can currently be recommended for routine use in AH based on 90-day survival. Clinicians should await results of larger, well-designed trials before considering agents like GCSF outside research settings.

articles.title: Comparative effectiveness of traditional Chinese medicine treatment strategies for insomnia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Liu Y, Wang X, Zhang Y, et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Insomnia causes daytime impairment and reduced quality of life. We evaluated the comparative efficacy and safety of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) treatment strategies for insomnia. METHODS: Nine databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane CENTRAL, ClinicalTrials.gov, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, SinoMed) were searched through January 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Primary outcomes were ISI and PSQI scores; secondary outcomes included clinical efficacy and adverse events (AEs). Data were synthesized using frequentist network meta-analysis. RESULTS: Twelve RCTs involving 1,260 participants were included, evaluating five strategy nodes: TCM alone, TCM plus Western medicine (WM), WM alone, placebo, and CBT-I. For ISI, TCM plus WM ranked highest (SUCRA 89.7%) and significantly improved scores versus placebo (OR 2.84, 95% CI 1.42-5.68) and WM (OR 1.96, 95% CI 1.08-3.56). For PSQI, TCM plus WM showed the highest probability of improvement (SUCRA 71.9%) with greater reduction versus placebo (MD -2.31, 95% CI -3.65 to -0.97). For clinical efficacy, SUCRA values were 86.6% for TCM plus WM, 77.2% for TCM, 20.9% for WM, and 15.3% for placebo. For AEs (higher SUCRA indicating better safety), SUCRA values were 94.8% for WM, 43.9% for TCM plus WM, 31.1% for placebo, and 30.2% for TCM. Sensitivity analysis excluding secondary insomnia confirmed robust findings. CONCLUSION: Integrated TCM-WM and TCM therapies demonstrate clinical efficacy and acceptable safety fo
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Insomnia is common and impairs daytime functioning. This systematic review and network meta-analysis compared Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) strategies (alone or combined with Western medicine) against Western medicine, placebo, and CBT-I in randomized trials to assess efficacy and safety.

FINDINGS: Twelve RCTs (n=1,260) were included. For ISI, TCM+WM ranked highest (SUCRA 89.7%) and outperformed placebo (OR 2.84, 95% CI 1.42–5.68) and WM alone (OR 1.96, 95% CI 1.08–3.56). For PSQI, TCM+WM showed the largest reduction versus placebo (MD −2.31, 95% CI −3.65 to −0.97). Clinical efficacy favored TCM+WM (SUCRA 86.6%) over TCM (77.2%), WM (20.9%), and placebo (15.3%). Adverse events were least frequent with WM alone (SUCRA 94.8%) and more common with TCM+WM (43.9%).

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small (12 RCTs, 1,260 participants) and heterogeneous in interventions and comparators. Network meta-analysis ranking methods are indirect and model-dependent; effect sizes are modest (e.g., PSQI MD −2.31) and may not translate to clinically meaningful differences in routine care. Safety data suggest TCM+WM may increase adverse events compared with WM alone. Overall certainty is low due to risk of bias, limited long-term follow-up, and unclear blinding in many trials.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify routine use of TCM+WM over established first-line treatments like CBT-I or approved pharmacotherapies. Clinicians should remain cautious about integrating TCM strategies until higher-quality, head-to-head RCTs with longer follow-up confirm efficacy and safety.

articles.title: Effect of web-based education on NIV-related side effects and insomnia severity in COPD patients using home NIV: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.authors: Eriş Ş, Gündogdu F
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study aimed to evaluate the effect of web-based education on NIV-related side effects and insomnia severity in COPD patients using home noninvasive ventilation (NIV). METHODS: This randomized controlled trial was conducted with 75 patients between October 2023 and May 2024. Data were collected using the S³-NIV Questionnaire and the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI). The intervention group received web-based education regarding NIV-related side effects and insomnia management. Independent samples t-tests were used to compare numerical descriptive characteristics between groups, while Pearson chi-square and Fisher's exact tests were used for categorical variables. Repeated-measures ANOVA was performed to evaluate changes over time and between groups. RESULTS: Compared with the control group, the intervention group demonstrated significantly higher total S³-NIV Questionnaire scores and higher respiration, sleep, and side-effect subscale scores at weeks 4 and 8. Significant group × time interaction effects were observed for total S³-NIV scores (p < 0.001, η²p = 0.753) and ISI scores (p < 0.001, η²p = 0.352). For insomnia severity, no significant between-group difference in ISI scores was observed at Week 4, whereas ISI scores were significantly lower in the intervention group at Week 8.
