articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study tested whether web-based education improves non-invasive ventilation (NIV)-related side effects and insomnia severity in COPD patients on home NIV, using a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 75 participants.

FINDINGS: At weeks 4 and 8, the intervention group had significantly higher total S³-NIV Questionnaire scores (respiration, sleep, side-effects subscales) than controls. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed strong group × time interaction effects for total S³-NIV scores (p < 0.001, η²p = 0.753) and ISI scores (p < 0.001, η²p = 0.352). Insomnia severity (ISI) was not significantly different at week 4 but was lower in the intervention group at week 8.

INTERPRETATION: The RCT suggests web-based education improves patient-reported NIV-related symptoms and insomnia by week 8, with large effect sizes for NIV outcomes and moderate for insomnia. However, the insomnia effect emerged late and was not present at week 4, raising questions about durability or timing of assessment. The small sample and short follow-up limit generalisability; larger trials with longer follow-up are needed to confirm clinical benefit and sustainability.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Web-based education may be a low-cost adjunct to routine care for COPD patients on home NIV, particularly for symptom management, but insomnia benefits appear modest and delayed; routine adoption should await confirmation in larger, longer studies.

articles.title: The nexus of mental health, human rights and sustainability: interdisciplinary approach.
articles.authors: Sen P, Kohler D, McKenzie S, et al.
articles.abstract: This paper explores the direct and indirect effects of climate change on mental health. It then goes on to describe recent judgements in human rights courts globally on climate change and its mental health implications, holding national governments to account for the mental health implications of climate change. It then explores ways in which psychiatrists can start to influence this nexus of mental health, sustainability and human rights in their clinical practice, in research and education as well as in policy making. This influence can be at the level of the individual patient and at the local and national level. It argues that the lens of human rights is a useful way for psychiatrists to be more directly involved in matters concerning sustainability and climate change.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the intersection of climate change, mental health, and human rights, discussing potential pathways linking climate change to mental health outcomes and recent legal judgments that hold governments accountable for these impacts. It also proposes ways for psychiatrists to engage with sustainability and human rights in clinical practice, research, education, and policy.

FINDINGS: The paper highlights direct effects of climate change (e.g., extreme weather events) and indirect effects (e.g., displacement, food insecurity) on mental health, citing evidence of increased anxiety, depression, PTSD, and suicide risk in affected populations. It summarizes recent human rights court rulings (e.g., *Urgenda Foundation v. Netherlands*, *Neubauer v. Germany*) that recognize states' obligations to mitigate climate change due to its mental health harms. The authors advocate for psychiatrists to integrate human rights frameworks into their work, including advocating for climate policies and incorporating sustainability into mental health care.

INTERPRETATION: This is a narrative review, not an empirical study, so its conclusions are based on selected literature and legal cases rather than systematic evidence. The strength of the argument lies in its interdisciplinary perspective and call to action, but it lacks quantitative data or rigorous study design. The human rights lens is a plausible framework for engagement, but its practical implementation in psychiatry remains speculative without further empirical support. The paper does not quantify effect sizes or provide direct evidence of psychiatrists' impact on climate-related outcomes.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: While the paper raises important questions about the role of psychiatrists in climate advocacy and sustainability, it does not provide actionable clinical guidance or evidence-based interventions. Clinicians may consider integrating climate-related stressors into patient assessments (e.g., eco-anxiety) and advocating for systemic changes, but robust evidence for such practices is lacking. Further research is needed to determine whether these approaches improve mental health outcomes.

articles.title: Reducing the risk of obesity, diabetes, and metabolic disorders in patients treated with antipsychotics - recommendations of the Polish Psychiatric Association Part I: risk factors and psychological interventions.
articles.authors: Wichniak A, Szulc A, Samochowiec J, et al.
articles.abstract: Patients suffering from mental disorders - particularly schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and depression - are at least 1.5 times more likely to develop metabolic disorders than the general population, with prevalence among people with mental disorders exceeding 30%. In 2019, the Polish Psychiatric Association (PTP) developed and published recommendations on reducing metabolic risk in patients with schizophrenia treated with antipsychotics (APs). This article presents the first part of the update and expansion of these recommendations. It focuses on risk factors for obesity, diabetes, and metabolic disorders in people treated with APs, as well as guidelines on non-pharmacological interventions to prevent and treat metabolic disorders. The recommendations were prepared by a group of experts invited by the Board of PTP based on a literature review, analysis of published guidelines, and clinical experience. Psychiatrists should not only be aware of the increased risk of metabolic disorders in people treated with APs but should also actively act to prevent these conditions. The basis of prevention is lifestyle modification through small, gradual steps easier to maintain over the long term. Recommended interventions include: (1) nutritional education, (2) regular physical activity, (3) meal planning, (4) menu preparation, (5) mindfulness and relaxation techniques, (6) participation in support groups, (7) progress monitoring. In cases of high risk, or when such disorders are already
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Clinical guidelines from the Polish Psychiatric Association update recommendations on preventing obesity, diabetes, and metabolic disorders in patients with severe mental illness (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression) treated with antipsychotics, where metabolic risk is ≥1.5-fold higher than in the general population. This first part focuses on risk factors and non-pharmacological interventions.

FINDINGS: The recommendations are based on expert consensus after reviewing literature and existing guidelines. Key preventive strategies include nutritional education, regular physical activity, meal planning, mindfulness, support groups, and progress monitoring. Pharmacological interventions are reserved for high-risk or established cases and are covered in a separate guideline section.

INTERPRETATION: These are consensus-based recommendations rather than empirical evidence from trials. Strengths include broad expert input and alignment with prior guidelines, but the lack of quantitative effect estimates (e.g., weight change, HbA1c reduction) and absence of a systematic review methodology limit internal validity. External validity depends on local healthcare resources and patient adherence; the suggested small, gradual lifestyle changes may improve feasibility but effectiveness in routine psychiatric care remains uncertain.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Psychiatrists should actively screen for metabolic risk and initiate non-pharmacological prevention early, emphasizing sustainable lifestyle modifications. Watch for barriers to adherence (e.g., negative symptoms, cognitive deficits) and consider referral to dietitians or physiotherapists where available.

articles.title: Trajectories of suicidal ideation and attempts across the academic year: longitudinal study of UK university students.
articles.authors: Morse KF, Brown S, Chamberlain SR, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Suicide is a leading cause of death among young adults, yet few studies have examined longitudinal trajectories of suicidal ideation and attempts across the academic year in UK university students. AIMS: The study aimed to identify demographic and psychosocial factors associated with lifetime suicide risk, examine factors associated with changes in risk trajectories, and evaluate the relationship between suicidal ideation and attempts over an academic year. METHOD: Participants comprised 3295 students from 5 UK universities who completed longitudinal surveys in autumn and spring terms 2021-2024 in the Nurture-U study. Suicidal ideation and attempts were assessed with Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale items. Demographic, psychosocial and mental health measures were examined as potential risk and protective factors. Regression models with multiple imputation were used, with case-control analyses for smaller subgroups. RESULTS: Approximately 45.5% of students reported baseline lifetime suicidal ideation and 9.5% reported a past attempt. Factors associated with lifetime suicidal ideation included minoritised sexual orientation or ethnic background, male or gender-diverse identity, previous mental health treatment and adverse childhood experiences. Among students with lifetime ideation at baseline, 61.1% did not report ideation in the spring term, whereas new-onset ideation occurred in 3.5% of participants. Among students with prior ideation only, 1.3% made a suic
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study examined longitudinal trajectories of suicidal ideation and attempts among 3,295 UK university students over an academic year (2021–2024), aiming to identify risk factors, changes in risk, and the relationship between ideation and attempts. It used a longitudinal cohort design with surveys in autumn and spring terms.

FINDINGS: At baseline, 45.5% reported lifetime suicidal ideation and 9.5% reported a prior suicide attempt. Among those with baseline ideation, 61.1% did not report ideation in spring, while 3.5% developed new-onset ideation. Of those with prior ideation only, 1.3% made a suicide attempt during the year, compared to 10.5% of those with a prior attempt history. Increases in depressive symptoms and rumination were associated with new attempts.

INTERPRETATION: The study provides valuable longitudinal data on suicidal trajectories in a large student cohort, with clear risk stratification based on prior history. However, reliance on self-report surveys and a single academic year follow-up may limit generalisability. The low absolute risk of attempts among those with ideation alone suggests ideation alone has limited predictive specificity, though high-risk groups (e.g., those with prior attempts or worsening depressive symptoms) warrant close monitoring.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine screening for suicidal ideation in students is important, but risk assessment should prioritise those with prior attempts or escalating depressive symptoms. Ongoing monitoring—not just initial screening—may be necessary to identify high-risk students during the academic year.

articles.title: miR-181b-5p is Upregulated in First-Episode Drug-Naive Schizophrenia and Correlates with Symptom Severity and Cognitive Deficits: A Case-Control Study.
articles.authors: Li H, Han X, Wang C
articles.abstract: This study aimed to explore miR-181b-5p's diagnostic value in schizophrenia, analyze its correlations with symptoms and cognition, and evaluate biomarker-guided personalized nursing efficacy to inform early diagnosis and precision care. A total of 126 patients with first-episode, drug-naive schizophrenia and 126 age- and gender-matched healthy controls were enrolled between January 2024 and June 2025. Plasma miR-181b-5p and Early Growth Response 1 (EGR1) mRNA levels were measured by qRT-PCR, and their targeting was validated via dual-luciferase assay. Symptoms and cognition were assessed with the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) and the MATRICS Consensus Cognitive Battery (MCCB). Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve and Pearson correlation were used for statistical analysis. Patients were grouped by median miR-181b-5p expression, with the high-expression group receiving personalized nursing. Outcomes were compared after 8 weeks. The results showed that Plasma miR-181b-5p was significantly upregulated, while EGR1 mRNA was downregulated in schizophrenia patients. miR-181b-5p showed good diagnostic performance [Area Under the Curve (AUC) = 0.898, 95% CI: 0.858-0.938]. Its expression positively correlated with all PANSS subscales and total scores and negatively correlated with all seven MCCB cognitive domains and overall scores. The inhibitory effect of miR-181b-5p on EGR1 expression was demonstrated to occur via direct binding to its 3'UTR by the dual-lucife
articles.summary: This study aimed to explore miR-181b-5p's diagnostic value in schizophrenia, analyze its correlations with symptoms and cognition, and evaluate biomarker-guided personalized nursing efficacy to inform early diagnosis and precision care. A total of 126 patients with first-episode, drug-naive schizophrenia and 126 age- and gender-matched healthy controls were enrolled between January 2024 and June 2025. Plasma miR-181b-5p and Early Growth Response 1 (EGR1) mRNA levels were measured by qRT-PCR, and their targeting was validated via dual-luciferase assay.

articles.title: Dropout from individual cognitive behavioral psychotherapy for schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.
articles.authors: Stefana A, Damiani S, Barlati S, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND HYPOTHESIS: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a recommended psychological treatment for schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs), often delivered alongside pharmacotherapy, but dropout may limit its effectiveness. In this secondary analysis of a parent systematic review and meta-analysis focused on negative-symptom outcomes, we synthesized dropout among individual, face-to-face, outpatient CBT arms identified within that parent-review dataset. We investigated exploratory associations between dropout and arm-level sociodemographic, clinical, treatment-related, and study-design characteristics. STUDY DESIGN: This study was a secondary analysis of a comprehensive database from a recent systematic review and meta-analysis of treatments for SSDs, which searched PsycINFO and all Web of Knowledge databases. Eligible studies were randomized clinical trials that included at least one arm delivering in-person, individual CBT in outpatient settings and reported dropout. Thirteen studies, comprising 16 psychotherapy arms and 865 participants, met eligibility criteria. Random-effects models were used to estimate the pooled dropout rate, and mixed-effects meta-regression models were conducted to examine sociodemographic, clinical, treatment-related, and study-design moderators. STUDY RESULTS: Across this heterogeneous set of individual CBT arms, the pooled dropout estimate was approximately one in five participants, with substantial between-arm heterogeneity. Associations
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined dropout rates from individual cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs) in randomized clinical trials (RCTs), addressing a key barrier to treatment effectiveness in outpatient settings.

FINDINGS: Across 13 RCTs (16 CBT arms, n=865), the pooled dropout rate was ~20% (one in five participants). Substantial heterogeneity was observed between arms. Exploratory meta-regression found no significant associations with sociodemographic, clinical, or treatment-related moderators due to limited power.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate in strength (systematic review of RCTs) but limited by heterogeneity and underpowered moderator analyses. The 20% dropout rate is clinically meaningful, but causal factors remain uncertain. The lack of significant moderators likely reflects insufficient data rather than true absence of effect.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should anticipate ~20% dropout in individual CBT for SSDs and monitor engagement closely. Current evidence does not support tailoring CBT based on the explored moderators. Further research is needed to identify predictors of dropout and strategies to reduce it.

articles.title: Non-pharmacological interventions for perinatal parental depression and anxiety: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Huang Y, Ding H, Yao X, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Perinatal depression and anxiety exhibit significant partner interdependence and family-level ramifications, constituting a family issue concerning both parents. However, existing evidence syntheses have predominantly examined maternal or paternal mental health in isolation, neglecting the systemic integrity of the family unit. OBJECTIVE: To conduct the first Bayesian network meta-analysis to evaluate and rank non-pharmacological interventions delivered concurrently to both parents for perinatal depression and anxiety. METHODS: Seven databases were searched from inception to May 30, 2025. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in which both perinatal parents received the same non-pharmacological intervention and depression or anxiety was assessed. A Bayesian network meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. PROSPERO: CRD420251048539. RESULTS: We included 36 RCTs involving 15,477 parents (51.8% mothers and 48.2% fathers/partners). For depression, multicomponent interventions (SMD = -0.34, 95% CrI [-0.60, -0.08]; SUCRA = 79.86%) and psychosocial interventions (SMD = -0.25, 95% CrI [-0.43, -0.07]; SUCRA = 60.83%) showed beneficial estimates. For anxiety, multicomponent interventions (SMD = -0.48, 95% CrI [-0.66, -0.29]; SUCRA = 98.12%) and parent-child interaction interventions (SMD = -0.19, 95% CrI [-0.36, -0.03]; SUCRA = 62.69%) showed beneficial estimates. Certainty of evidence ranged from low to moderate. CONCLUSION: Multicomponent interve
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The review asks which non-pharmacological interventions delivered to both parents during the perinatal period are most effective for reducing depression and anxiety in either parent. It is a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of 36 RCTs (n = 15 477 parents).

FINDINGS: For depression, multicomponent interventions showed a standardised mean difference (SMD) of –0.34 (95% credible interval [CrI] –0.60 to –0.08) and psychosocial interventions –0.25 (95% CrI –0.43 to –0.07). For anxiety, multicomponent interventions had SMD –0.48 (95% CrI –0.66 to –0.29) and parent–child interaction interventions –0.19 (95% CrI –0.36 to –0.03). Evidence certainty was rated low to moderate.

INTERPRETATION: The networks were sparse, most comparisons were indirect, heterogeneity was substantial, and the overall certainty of evidence was low to moderate. Therefore, the ranking should be regarded as provisional. Larger, head-to-head RCTs are needed before firm recommendations can be made.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence tentatively favours multicomponent family-centred programmes for perinatal parental depression and anxiety, but the small effect sizes and low certainty mean routine practice should await more robust trials.

articles.title: PROMATER: protocol for a randomized controlled trial of a digital self-guided intervention to promote perinatal mental health and reduce self-criticism.
articles.authors: Gerhardt BC, Dos Santos ME, Debastiani VB, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Perinatal mental health represents a significant public health concern given the high prevalence of mental disorders during pregnancy and the postpartum period and their impact on maternal well-being, mother-infant bonding, and child development. Emerging evidence identifies self-criticism as a transdiagnostic vulnerability factor associated with psychological distress in this period, while self-compassion has been recognized as an important protective factor. In Brazil, access to preventive perinatal mental health interventions remains limited. This paper describes the protocol of a randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluating PROMATER - an online program designed to promote perinatal mental health by targeting self-criticism and self-compassion. METHODS: A total of 130 pregnant women between 28 and 34 weeks of gestation will enroll in a two-arm RCT with a dismantling design. Participants will be randomized (1:1 ratio) to either the PROMATER intervention or to an active control group. Participants and data analysts will be blinded to group allocation. PROMATER consists of a 3-week program (6 modules) addressing maternal expectations, self-criticism, perinatal mental health, social support, self-compassion, and mindfulness and mother-infant bonding. The active control offers a structurally equivalent program covering the same topics, except for the modules specifically targeting these transdiagnostic processes. Primary outcomes are self-compassion, assessed via th
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Perinatal mental health is a public health priority, with self-criticism as a transdiagnostic vulnerability and self-compassion a protective factor. This Brazilian RCT protocol (PROMATER) tests a 3-week digital self-guided intervention targeting these processes in 130 pregnant women (28–34 weeks gestation), using an active control to isolate specific effects.

FINDINGS: The trial randomizes participants 1:1 to PROMATER (6 modules on self-compassion/mindfulness) or an active control (same structure without transdiagnostic modules). Primary outcomes are the Compassionate Self-Responding (CSR) and Uncompassionate Self-Responding (USR) scores from the Self-Compassion Scale, assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and 3-month postpartum. Secondary outcomes include depression, anxiety, quality of life, social support, and mother-infant bonding. Analysis will use Linear Mixed Models (ITT principle).

INTERPRETATION: As a protocol, no results are available yet. The design is robust (randomization, blinding of participants/data analysts, active control, ITT analysis), but external validity hinges on recruitment feasibility and adherence in routine care. The incremental benefit of targeting self-criticism/self-compassion over psychoeducation alone remains unproven until outcomes are reported. If effective, the brief, scalable digital format could address access gaps in Brazil.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No clinical change yet—await trial outcomes. If positive, PROMATER could offer a low-cost, accessible adjunct to perinatal mental health care, but implementation would require integration into existing services and evaluation of real-world effectiveness.

articles.title: Exploring the Neural Mechanisms of Acupuncture Stimulation in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Protocol for a Randomized, Sham-Controlled, Multimodal Neuroimaging Trial.
articles.authors: Sim J, Choi KS, Lee DH
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by restricted and repetitive behaviors and disturbances in social communication and interaction. Currently, there is no fundamental treatment for ASD, with only a few medications available for use on a limited basis to manage concomitant neuropsychiatric symptoms. The primary therapeutic goal of such treatments is to alleviate symptoms while maximizing the functional independence and quality of life of affected individuals. Many complementary and alternative medicine therapies have been reported to have effects on ASD symptoms; however, evidence is insufficient to confirm their clinical effectiveness. Acupuncture has traditionally been used as a complementary intervention to manage various neurological and neuropsychiatric diseases, including ASD, in East Asia. However, how acupuncture stimulation modulates neural activity at the macroscale level in individuals with ASD remains largely unknown. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to elucidate disease-related brain alterations and explore the acute neural mechanisms underlying acupuncture stimulation in patients with ASD and in typically developing (TD) individuals, using a multimodal neuroimaging approach. METHODS: This study was designed as a randomized, sham-controlled trial. In this stratified 2×2 design, 70 participants, including individuals with ASD (n=35) and TD controls (n=35), will each be randomly assigned to either the verum or sham ac
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This is a protocol for a randomized, sham-controlled neuroimaging trial (2×2 design) aiming to explore acute neural mechanisms of acupuncture in 70 participants (35 with ASD, 35 typically developing controls) using functional near-infrared spectroscopy and electroencephalography. The study addresses whether acupuncture modulates resting-state network metrics and frontal band power differently in ASD versus controls.

FINDINGS: The trial is ongoing; to date, 23 ASD and 21 controls have been enrolled. Primary outcomes will compare resting-state network metrics and relative band power in frontal areas by diagnosis and intervention (verum vs sham). Secondary outcomes will assess group × intervention interactions on these neural markers.

INTERPRETATION: This is a well-designed, sham-controlled protocol with clear stratification and multimodal neuroimaging, which strengthens internal validity. However, as a protocol paper, no results are available yet; thus, efficacy and effect sizes remain unknown. The small sample size and exploratory nature limit power to detect meaningful clinical effects. The study may clarify acute neural correlates of acupuncture but cannot yet inform clinical practice.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this study does not change clinical practice. It may lay groundwork for future trials but should not influence decisions about acupuncture use in ASD until efficacy and safety are demonstrated in adequately powered, peer-reviewed studies.

articles.title: Rethinking treatment motivation in addiction care: executive functions and personality over clinical severity- a cross-sectional study.
articles.authors: Tek Sevindik S, Erk MA, Firat S
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Alcohol and substance use disorders are chronic mental disorders characterised by high relapse rates, and treatment motivation is one of the most important determinants of success in the treatment process. However, in clinical practice, significant differences in treatment motivation are observed among individuals with similar levels of addiction severity. This suggests that motivation may be closely related not only to clinical severity indicators but also to cognitive and personality-related processes. AIM: The aim of this study is to examine the relationships between treatment motivation and executive functions, emotional-behavioural characteristics, and personality dimensions in individuals undergoing inpatient treatment at the Alcohol and Drug Addiction Treatment and Center (ADATC). METHODS: This study, conducted between April and August 2025 using a descriptive and cross-sectional design, included 190 individuals undergoing inpatient treatment at ADATC for alcohol and substance use disorders. Data were collected using the Sociodemographic Data Form, Treatment Motivation Questionnaire, Eysenck Personality Questionnaire-Revised Short Form, Addiction Profile Index-Clinical Form, and Solution-Focused Inventory. Analyses were performed using correlation analyses and hierarchical multiple regression analyses with SPSS v26. RESULTS: It has been determined that the severity of addiction does not significantly predict treatment motivation. In contrast, executive func
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study examined whether treatment motivation in individuals with alcohol or substance use disorders (n=190, inpatient at ADATC, April–August 2025) is better predicted by executive functions and personality traits than by clinical severity indicators.

FINDINGS: Addiction severity did not significantly predict treatment motivation (β not reported). Executive functions—especially goal-directedness—were the strongest predictors (β and effect size not provided). Personality traits showed that higher neuroticism and extraversion were associated with greater motivation, while higher psychoticism was linked to lower motivation (correlations not quantified).

INTERPRETATION: The study’s cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. The lack of effect sizes and confidence intervals limits assessment of clinical significance. Confounding by unmeasured variables (e.g., concurrent psychosocial interventions) is possible. The findings suggest cognitive and personality factors may shape motivation, but replication with longitudinal data and clearer quantification is needed before practice changes.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify altering routine assessment or treatment based solely on these preliminary associations; further research is required to determine whether targeting executive functions or personality traits improves motivation and outcomes in addiction care.

articles.title: Associations between month/season of birth and health outcomes: an umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
articles.authors: Zhang Z, Wang L, Zhou Y, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The relationship between month or season of birth and long-term health outcomes remains an important but underexplored topic in public health. Evidence suggests that birth timing may influence disease susceptibility and broader health trajectories, reflecting interactions between biological and ecological factors. Clarifying these associations is essential for advancing prevention and a holistic view of health shaped by temporal exposures. METHODS: We conducted an umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses indexed in PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science up to 2 July 2025. Eligible studies reported quantitative estimates for associations between birth month/season and objectively measured health outcomes. We used random-effects models to produce pooled estimates and evaluated heterogeneity, small-study effects, and bias. We graded associations using established class-of-evidence criteria and assessed methodological quality with AMSTAR 2. RESULTS: We included 10 meta-analyses, comprising 614 unique associations (defined as individual pairwise analyses between a specific birth month/season exposure and a distinct health outcome). Of these, 45 associations were statistically significant, and 25 were eligible for evidence grading. No association met class I criteria, but one (January birth and schizophrenia) reached class II. The most consistent findings involved neurodevelopmental and psychiatric outcomes, with winter births linked to a modest increase in s
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This umbrella review synthesised systematic reviews and meta-analyses to assess whether month or season of birth is associated with long-term health outcomes, focusing on objectively measured conditions and grading the strength of evidence. It included 10 meta-analyses covering 614 pairwise associations across diverse health outcomes.

FINDINGS: Among 45 statistically significant associations, only one reached class II evidence: a modest increase in schizophrenia risk for January births (OR 1.05). Winter births were consistently linked to higher schizophrenia risk, while spring births showed associations with multiple sclerosis. Most other associations (autoimmune, oncological, perinatal) were graded as weak (class III–IV) due to small effect sizes or high heterogeneity.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is broad but largely weak; only schizophrenia shows a modest, relatively consistent signal. Methodological quality varied, and many associations reflect small effects with substantial heterogeneity or bias risk. The grading framework helps distinguish plausible signals from spurious findings, but causal inference remains uncertain.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not support using birth month/season to guide individual risk assessment or prevention strategies. Clinicians should remain aware that any observed associations are small and not clinically actionable at present.

articles.title: A Primary Care E-Health Family Intervention for Risk Behaviors in Hispanic Youths: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.authors: Estrada Y, Lozano A, Graefe B, et al.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Culturally tailored, evidence-based family interventions that can be effectively delivered within pediatric primary care settings may provide a scalable approach for preventing risk behaviors among Hispanic adolescents. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether the online eHealth Familias Unidas Primary Care (eHealth FUPC) program reduced drug use and increased condom use in Hispanic youth and to examine family functioning as a mediator. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This randomized clinical trial included 5 follow-up visits across 36 months from April 18, 2017, to December 18, 2022, at 15 pediatric primary care clinics. Participants included Hispanic youth aged 12 to 16 years and a legal guardian. Data were analyzed from January 31, 2023, to August 21, 2024. INTERVENTION: Participants were randomized 1:1 to the intervention, consisting of 8 video group sessions for parents and 4 online, facilitator-guided family sessions for parents and adolescents for a total intervention duration of approximately 12 weeks. Interventionists included pediatric primary care personnel. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The co-primary outcomes were past 90-day drug use, condom use, and sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Secondary outcomes included initiation of alcohol use, initiation of hard drug use (ie, lysergic acid diethylamide, phencyclidine, ecstasy [MDMA], psilocybin mushrooms), and family functioning. STI was changed to a secondary outcome after data collection was discontinued be
articles.summary: IMPORTANCE: Culturally tailored, evidence-based family interventions that can be effectively delivered within pediatric primary care settings may provide a scalable approach for preventing risk behaviors among Hispanic adolescents. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether the online eHealth Familias Unidas Primary Care (eHealth FUPC) program reduced drug use and increased condom use in Hispanic youth and to examine family functioning as a mediator.

articles.title: Paracetamol overdose: systematic review of case reports and national toxicological data (2018-2023).
articles.authors: Mlíchová J, Šimandl O, Kotíková K, et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Paracetamol is widely used as an analgesic and antipyretic, but its accessibility also makes it a frequent drug in overdose cases. Increasing rates of intentional paracetamol poisoning, particularly among adolescents, raise public health concerns. This study aimed to examine recent patterns of paracetamol overdose and identify risk groups for intentional self-poisoning. METHODS: A systematic review of published case reports (2018-2023) describing paracetamol overdose was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. Additionally, a retrospective analysis of telephone inquiries to the Czech Toxicological Information Centre (TIC) during the same period was performed. RESULTS: Sixty-eight published case reports met inclusion criteria, with reported doses ranging from 6.5 to 250 g. Intentional overdose occurred in 50 cases (74%), including 11 teenage girls (22% of intentional cases). No deaths were reported in this subgroup. TIC recorded 3,318 inquiries related to paracetamol exposure between 2018 and 2023, of which 2,032 (61%) involved intentional overdose. Females predominated among intentional cases, particularly in children and adolescents, and the number of intentional overdoses among girls aged 0-19 years increased after 2020. The data indicate a growing number of suicide attempts involving paracetamol, particularly among teenage girls. CONCLUSION: The majority of paracetamol intoxications reported in the literature and in national to
articles.summary: OBJECTIVES: Paracetamol is widely used as an analgesic and antipyretic, but its accessibility also makes it a frequent drug in overdose cases. Increasing rates of intentional paracetamol poisoning, particularly among adolescents, raise public health concerns. This study aimed to examine recent patterns of paracetamol overdose and identify risk groups for intentional self-poisoning. METHODS: A systematic review of published case reports (2018-2023) describing paracetamol overdose was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library.

articles.title: SOGC Clinical Practice Guideline No. 471: Alcohol and Pregnancy.
articles.authors: Allen V, Cook JL, Chandrasekaran N, et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To establish national standards of care for screening and counselling pregnant women and individuals of reproductive age regarding alcohol consumption and alcohol use disorder. INTENDED USERS: Health care providers who care for pregnant women and women of childbearing age. TARGET POPULATION: Pregnant women and women of childbearing age and their families. EVIDENCE: Medline, EMBASE, and CENTRAL databases were searched for "alcohol use and pregnancy". The results were filtered for a publication date between October 2018 and February 2026. The search terms were developed using the MeSH terms and key words including: pre-pregnancy, pregnant, breast feeding, lactation, female, women, preconception care, prenatal care, Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder, prenatal alcohol exposure, drinking behavior, alcohol abstinence, alcohol drinking, binge drinking, Alcohol-Related Disorders, alcoholism, alcohol consumption, alcohol abuse, benzodiazepines, disulfiram, naltrexone, acamprosate, ondansetron, topiramate, cyanamide, calcium carbimide, alcohol deterrents, disease management, detoxification, Alcoholics Anonymous, alcohol counselling, harm reduction, pre-pregnancy care, prenatal care, incidence, prevalence, epidemiological monitoring, brief intervention. Clinical trials, observational studies, reviews, systematic reviews and meta-analysis, guidelines, and conference consensus were included. The table of evidence from the search that supports the recommendations is included as Ap
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This is a national clinical practice guideline (GRADE method) from the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SOGC) updating standards for screening, brief intervention, and referral for alcohol use in pregnant women and women of childbearing age. It synthesises evidence from 2018–2026 across Medline, EMBASE and CENTRAL to inform obstetric and primary care providers.

FINDINGS: The guideline recommends universal screening for alcohol use with validated tools (e.g., AUDIT-C) and brief interventions for all pregnant women and women planning pregnancy. It advises expedited referral pathways to alcohol cessation services and prioritised access to specialist support. Evidence quality was graded using GRADE, with most recommendations rated as moderate to low certainty due to heterogeneity in study designs and populations.

INTERPRETATION: As a guideline, internal validity is high in terms of methodological rigour (GRADE framework, systematic search), but external validity depends on local healthcare system capacity for referral and follow-up. The strength of recommendations is tempered by the low-to-moderate quality of underlying evidence, particularly for pharmacological interventions during pregnancy. The document does not quantify effect sizes or absolute risk reductions, so clinical significance remains inferred rather than empirically demonstrated.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should adopt routine screening and brief interventions for alcohol use in pregnancy and preconception care, ensuring clear referral pathways to addiction services. The lack of robust effect estimates means centres should monitor local outcomes when implementing these recommendations.

articles.title: Skin and Brain in Bipolar Disorder: A Review of Dermatologic-Psychotropic Drug Interactions.
articles.authors: Mack D, Modanlo N, Park I, et al.
articles.abstract: Importance: Dermatologic and psychotropic therapies intersect frequently in patients with bipolar disorder, in whom systemic dermatologic medications may affect mood stability and mood stabilizers or antipsychotics may produce clinically important cutaneous adverse reactions. Because several medications discussed in this review are also used for psychotic disorders, severe or treatment-resistant major depressive disorder, suicidality, and other psychiatric conditions, this article distinguishes medication-related risks from considerations specific to bipolar disorder. Observations: This narrative review synthesized English-language literature indexed in PubMed through June 29, 2026 addressing psychiatric adverse effects of dermatologic therapies and dermatologic adverse effects of psychotropic medications relevant to bipolar disorder. The literature consisted largely of case reports, case series, observational studies, pharmacovigilance analyses, and narrative or systematic reviews. No randomized controlled trials directly evaluating these bidirectional interactions in bipolar disorder were identified. Dermatologic agents such as isotretinoin, systemic corticosteroids, and methotrexate have been associated with mood destabilization in susceptible patients. Conversely, lithium and lamotrigine carry important dermatologic risks, including acneiform or psoriasiform eruptions, hidradenitis suppurativa, and severe cutaneous adverse reactions. Conclusions and Relevance: Dermatologi
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines bidirectional dermatologic–psychotropic drug interactions in patients with bipolar disorder, focusing on how systemic dermatologic medications may destabilise mood and how mood stabilisers/antipsychotics may provoke clinically important cutaneous adverse reactions. It synthesises case reports, observational studies and pharmacovigilance data indexed to June 2026, but no randomised trials were identified.

FINDINGS: Dermatologic agents such as isotretinoin, systemic corticosteroids and methotrexate have been linked to mood destabilisation in susceptible individuals. Conversely, lithium and lamotrigine carry dermatologic risks including acneiform or psoriasiform eruptions, hidradenitis suppurativa and severe cutaneous adverse reactions. No quantitative effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is entirely observational and heterogeneous (case reports, series, pharmacovigilance), so causality cannot be established and effect sizes remain unknown. Strengths include broad coverage of drug pairs and explicit acknowledgment of gaps. Limitations include lack of controlled data, potential publication bias and unclear generalisability beyond bipolar populations. Clinically meaningful magnitudes of risk cannot be quantified from this review.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Until better evidence emerges, clinicians should screen for prior psychiatric episodes and cutaneous drug reactions, counsel patients about possible bidirectional risks, and monitor closely when initiating or escalating high-risk therapies; shared decision-making across specialties is advised.

articles.title: Prevalence of mental health outcomes among trans and gender diverse adults: a global systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Symes ER, Santo T, Sutherland R, et al.
articles.abstract: Existing reviews of mental health outcomes among trans and gender diverse (trans)people have been limited by incomplete coverage, restricted or selected samples, afocus on youth populations, and insufficient exploration of heterogeneity. We aimed togenerate pooled prevalence estimates, and examine variation in mental disorders,suicidality, and non-suicidal selfinjury (NSSI) among trans adults globally. Weconducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies reporting current orlifetime prevalence of mental disorders, assessed using symptom screeninginstruments with validated general-population thresholds or clinical diagnoses,alongside self-reported suicidality and NSSI. MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO weresearched from January 1, 1990-April 7, 2026. Restricted or highly selectedsubpopulations were excluded, except for gender-affirming clinic samples. Estimateswere calculated overall and by gender identity. Subgroup/meta-regression analysesexamined variation by study and sociodemographic characteristics. We identified 207studies with 134,071 trans participants across 52 countries. Pooled prevalenceestimates, combining symptoms exceeding screening thresholds and clinicallydiagnosed disorders, were 40.1% (95% CI 35.6-44.8) for depression, 29.8% (20.3-40.2) for anxiety, and 23.6% (14.9-33.5) for post-traumatic stress disorder. Past-12-month prevalence was 43.1% (38.9-47.3) for suicidal ideation, 9.3%(7.7-11.0) forsuicide attempts, and 26.1% (20.4-32.2) for NSSI. Limited data
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This global systematic review and meta-analysis synthesised 207 studies (n=134 071) to estimate current/lifetime prevalence of depression, anxiety, PTSD, suicidality and non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) among trans and gender-diverse adults, addressing gaps in prior reviews that often focused on youth or selected samples.

FINDINGS: Pooled prevalence estimates were 40.1 % (95 % CI 35.6–44.8) for depression, 29.8 % (20.3–40.2) for anxiety and 23.6 % (14.9–33.5) for PTSD. Past-12-month rates were 43.1 % (38.9–47.3) for suicidal ideation, 9.3 % (7.7–11.0) for suicide attempts and 26.1 % (20.4–32.2) for NSSI. Non-binary participants appeared to have higher rates, and estimates varied by assessment method, recruitment setting and region.

INTERPRETATION: The large, global dataset strengthens confidence in the elevated mental health burden among trans adults, though heterogeneity in assessment tools and recruitment settings limits precision. The absence of general-population comparators in most studies precludes direct risk ratio estimation; nonetheless, the absolute prevalences are markedly higher than general-population benchmarks. Funding sources were not reported, and selection bias cannot be ruled out in clinic-based samples.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support the need for accessible, gender-affirming mental health services and routine screening for depression, suicidality and NSSI in trans adults, with particular attention to non-binary individuals and regional disparities.

articles.title: Initiation of aripiprazole once-monthly using a two-injection start in adult patients diagnosed with schizophrenia: real-world views and experiences of Italian healthcare professionals.
articles.authors: Yildirim M, Beckham C, Pappa S, et al.
articles.abstract: AIM: In Italy, aripiprazole once-monthly 400 mg (AOM 400) can be initiated using a two-injection start (TIS) in adult patients diagnosed with schizophrenia who are stabilised with oral aripiprazole. With this approach, treatment initiation is completed in a single day, without the need for 14 days of concurrent oral aripiprazole supplementation. This study examined how healthcare professionals (HCPs) view and use the AOM 400-TIS in real-world clinical practice in Italy, a country where uptake of the AOM 400-TIS has been relatively high. METHODS: Responses were analysed for Italian physicians and nurses who participated in a pan-European, non-interventional, cross-sectional online survey that explored perspectives and attitudes towards prescribing and/or administering AOM 400-TIS in patients diagnosed with schizophrenia. Responses were collected across two waves and were analysed descriptively. RESULTS: Responses were available for 108 Italian HCPs, representing 47.2% of all survey participants. Common reasons for using the AOM 400-TIS were poor treatment adherence (81.5%), patient preference (50.0%), and disease relapse (42.6%), while common barriers to its use were patient reluctance to receive two injections (36.1%), concerns about tolerability (24.1%), and concerns about safety (23.1%). Most HCPs agreed or strongly agreed that the AOM 400-TIS resulted in satisfactory patient outcomes (85.2%), was easy to administer (82.4%), and had a safety/tolerability profile similar to
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This pan-European, non-interventional, cross-sectional online survey assessed Italian healthcare professionals' (HCPs) views and experiences regarding the two-injection start (TIS) initiation of aripiprazole once-monthly 400 mg (AOM 400) in adult patients with schizophrenia, a method designed to simplify treatment initiation without prolonged oral supplementation.

FINDINGS: Responses from 108 Italian HCPs (47.2% of participants) showed that poor treatment adherence (81.5%), patient preference (50.0%), and disease relapse (42.6%) were common reasons for using AOM 400-TIS. Barriers included patient reluctance to receive two injections (36.1%), concerns about tolerability (24.1%), and safety concerns (23.1%). Most HCPs reported satisfactory patient outcomes (85.2%), ease of administration (82.4%), and a safety/tolerability profile similar to the traditional one-injection start (69.4%).

INTERPRETATION: The study provides descriptive insights into HCP perspectives but lacks comparative data or patient outcomes, limiting causal inferences. Selection bias may exist due to voluntary participation, and the cross-sectional design precludes assessment of long-term effects. While HCPs generally viewed AOM 400-TIS favorably, the absence of objective clinical metrics or patient-reported outcomes weakens the evidence. Further research is needed to validate these perceptions with clinical efficacy and safety data.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence suggests AOM 400-TIS is perceived as practical and well-tolerated by Italian HCPs, particularly for patients with adherence issues, but definitive clinical benefits remain unproven. Clinicians should consider patient preferences and tolerability concerns when choosing initiation methods, while awaiting more robust data.

articles.title: The utility of animal models in hiPSC-based studies of autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review.
articles.authors: Yokota-Moreno BY, Silva ALTE, Nóbrega IS, et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Autism spectrum disorder is a highly prevalent and heritable neurodevelopmental condition. To investigate its pathogenesis, genetic and non-genetic animal models have been developed. However, no animal model can fully capture the human-specific characteristics and genetic complexity of autism spectrum disorder. In this context, human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) derived models have emerged as powerful tools in autism spectrum disorder research, offering the potential to reduce or replace animal experiments. Despite this potential, many hiPSC-based studies still incorporate animal use. OBJECTIVE: To analyze the use of animals in hiPSC-based studies of autism spectrum disorder, with the aim of assessing the necessity of their inclusion and their contribution to our understanding of disease mechanisms. METHODS: Following the PRISMA guidelines, we searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for articles published between 2009 and 2024 using the search terms "autism", "ASD", and "autism spectrum disorder" combined with "iPSC", "induced pluripotent stem cells and "organoid*". RESULTS: A total of 207 studies using hiPSCs to investigate Autism spectrum disorder were identified. Of these, 79 studies (38.16%) also involved animals or animal-derived cells. While nearly half of these studies used autism spectrum disorder animal models to explore neurobiological mechanisms of the disorder, the remaining studies employed animals for purposes not directly related to u
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a common and heritable neurodevelopmental condition. This systematic review (PRISMA-guided) examined how often animal models or animal-derived cells are still used alongside human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) research in ASD, questioning whether such animal use is necessary.

FINDINGS: Out of 207 hiPSC-based ASD studies (2009–2024), 79 (38.16%) also involved animals or animal-derived cells. Nearly half used animal models to study ASD neurobiology, while others employed animals for unrelated purposes (e.g., teratoma assays to confirm pluripotency or extracting primary astrocytes for co-culture, which may introduce confounding variables).

INTERPRETATION: The review suggests that animal use in hiPSC-based ASD research is frequent and sometimes unnecessary, potentially undermining the ethical and translational rationale for reducing animal experiments. However, the study does not assess the scientific contribution of animal components or whether their exclusion would compromise study validity. The review is limited by its descriptive nature and lack of critical appraisal of individual study designs or outcomes.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For clinicians, this review highlights a gap between the ethical goal of reducing animal use in ASD research and current practices. It does not directly inform patient care but underscores the need for clearer justification when animals are included in hiPSC-based studies.

articles.title: Abnormalities of intrinsic brain activity in late-life depression: a meta-analysis of resting-state functional imaging studies.
articles.authors: Lin J, Lin L, Zhang H, et al.
articles.abstract: Neuroimaging studies using a variety of techniques have demonstrated abnormal patterns of spontaneous brain activity in patients with late-life depression (LLD). However, the findings are variable and often inconsistent, hindering understanding of underlying neuropathology. We conducted a meta-analysis of whole-brain resting-state functional neuroimaging studies in LLD compared to healthy controls (HC), using anisotropic effect-size seed-based d mapping, to identify the most consistent brain activity alterations and their relation to clinical features. After systematic literature search, we included 13 studies reporting resting-state functional activity in a total of 476 LLD patients compared with 394 HC. We found higher activity in LLD vs HC in the left fusiform gyrus (FG), right parahippocampal gyrus (PHG) and right middle frontal gyrus (MFG), and lower brain activity in the left supplementary motor area (SMA), left superior frontal gyrus (SFG) and left postcentral gyrus (PoCG). In the subgroup meta-analysis of studies with a single functional index, LLD showed higher regional homogeneity (ReHo) in the left FG and right PHG, and also higher amplitude of low frequency fluctuations and/or fractional amplitude of low frequency fluctuations (ALFF/fALFF) in the left FG and lower activity in the left SFG. In the subgroup meta-analysis of studies using corrected p values, LLD vs HC showed similar patterns, with higher activity in the left FG, right PHG, and right MFG, and lower ac
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined resting-state functional neuroimaging studies to identify consistent abnormalities in intrinsic brain activity in late-life depression (LLD) compared with healthy controls (HC). The clinical question was whether reproducible neural signatures exist that could clarify neuropathology and potentially aid diagnosis or treatment development.

FINDINGS: Thirteen studies (476 LLD patients vs 394 HC) were meta-analysed using anisotropic effect-size seed-based d mapping. Higher activity in LLD was found in the left fusiform gyrus (FG), right parahippocampal gyrus (PHG) and right middle frontal gyrus (MFG), while lower activity was observed in the left supplementary motor area (SMA), left superior frontal gyrus (SFG) and left postcentral gyrus (PoCG). Subgroup analyses by functional index and statistical correction showed largely consistent patterns, with additional involvement of the left superior occipital gyrus (SOG) in corrected analyses.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate in size but methodologically heterogeneous (varied imaging indices, correction methods, and small samples). The use of anisotropic effect-size seed-based d mapping improves robustness, yet the findings remain correlational and cannot establish causality. The reported regions are plausible but effect sizes are not quantified numerically in the abstract, limiting assessment of clinical significance. External validity is uncertain because included studies may overrepresent specific LLD subgroups and settings.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest potential neural correlates of LLD that could inform future diagnostic or therapeutic targeting, but they do not yet support changes in routine clinical practice. Clinicians should await larger, longitudinal studies with harmonised imaging protocols before considering any neuroimaging-based interventions.

articles.title: Aortitis with eosinophilia as a rare complication of clozapine treatment ‒ a case of a patient with paranoid schizophrenia.
articles.authors: Rodek P, Łaciak J, Libudzic N, et al.
articles.abstract: Clozapine is an antipsychotic medication used to control the symptoms of schizophrenia. Due to the frequent occurrence of adverse effects, it is reserved for patients meeting the criteria of treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Among the less typical side effects of clozapine are asymptomatic eosinophilia and eosinophilic inflammation of organs such as the myocardium, as well as vasculitis, which most commonly affects small vessels in the skin. We present the case of a 54-year-old woman with treatment-resistant paranoid schizophrenia, who developed aortitis accompanied by eosinophilia as an adverse reaction to clozapine therapy. Symptoms resolved after discontinuation of the medication. The patient gave written consent for the publication of her medical case and treatment course. Inflammatory changes in large vessels such as the aorta during clozapine treatment have not been described in the literature. The coexisting eosinophilia suggests an eosinophilic nature of the inflammatory changes within the aortic wall. The presented case aims to raise awareness about possible atypical complications of the treatment and to expedite their diagnosis, which may prevent permanent negative health consequences in patients.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This is a single case report describing a 54-year-old woman with treatment-resistant paranoid schizophrenia who developed aortitis with eosinophilia as a rare adverse effect of clozapine therapy. The report highlights an atypical and previously undocumented complication of clozapine.

FINDINGS: The patient developed inflammatory changes in the aorta (aortitis) accompanied by eosinophilia while on clozapine. Symptoms resolved after discontinuation of the medication. No quantitative data (e.g., laboratory values, imaging metrics, or follow-up duration) are provided in the abstract.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence is extremely limited (a single case report) and lacks generalizability. There are no comparative data, effect sizes, or statistical analyses. The causal relationship between clozapine and aortitis is plausible but unproven in this context. The report serves primarily to raise awareness of a potential rare adverse effect rather than to establish causality or guide treatment decisions.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This case suggests that clinicians should consider clozapine-induced aortitis in patients on clozapine who present with eosinophilia and unexplained vascular symptoms. However, given the rarity and lack of prior reports, routine screening for aortitis in asymptomatic patients on clozapine is not justified based on this evidence alone. Further investigation is needed before any practice change.

articles.title: Changes in opioid prescribing and high-risk co-prescribing after implementation of the 2016 CDC opioid guideline among older adults with and without cancer.
articles.authors: Olateju OA, Byun JY, Okeke CM, et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate changes in opioid prescribing and high-risk opioid co-prescribing before and after the 2016 CDC Guideline among Medicare beneficiaries with and without cancer. METHODS: Using SEER-Medicare data (2014-2017), we identified beneficiaries diagnosed with breast, colon, or lung cancer and a comparison cohort without cancer. All patients were continuously enrolled in Medicare Parts A, B, and D and not enrolled in Medicare Advantage. The pre-policy period was January 2014-November 2015 and the post-policy period was April 2016-September 2017. Outcomes assessed within 3 months of diagnosis or index claim included monthly opioid prescribing rates, monthly days of opioid supply, daily morphine milligram equivalents (MME), and high-risk co-prescribing with benzodiazepines, antidepressants, or non-benzodiazepine sedatives. Difference-in-difference models compared changes between groups before and after guideline implementation, adjusting for baseline characteristics. RESULTS: The study included 42,931 cancer and 108,218 patients without cancer. After guideline implementation, opioid prescribing declined in both groups but more substantially among patients without cancer, while changes among patients with cancer were minimal. Difference-in-difference estimates indicated smaller reductions among cancer versus patients without cancer in monthly opioid prescribing (- 0.14; 95% CI, - 0.17 to - 0.11; p < 0.0001) and days of supply (- 3.07; 95% CI, - 3.68 to - 2.45; p < 0.00
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study examined how the 2016 CDC opioid prescribing guideline affected opioid prescribing patterns and high-risk co-prescribing (with benzodiazepines, antidepressants, or sedatives) among older adults with and without cancer, using SEER-Medicare data (2014–2017). This retrospective cohort study assessed changes in opioid use before and after guideline implementation.

FINDINGS: The study included 42,931 cancer patients and 108,218 non-cancer patients. After guideline implementation, opioid prescribing declined in both groups, but reductions were larger in non-cancer patients. Difference-in-difference estimates showed smaller reductions among cancer patients in monthly opioid prescribing (-0.14; 95% CI, -0.17 to -0.11; p < 0.0001) and days of supply (-3.07; 95% CI, -3.68 to -2.45; p < 0.0001). Changes in daily morphine milligram equivalents (MME) were not significant (16.73; 95% CI, -43.36 to 76.82; p = 0.5853). High-risk co-prescribing declined overall but decreased less among cancer patients for all combinations (all p < 0.0001).

INTERPRETATION: The study provides moderate-quality evidence from a large, well-defined cohort with robust statistical adjustment. However, the observational design cannot establish causality, and residual confounding (e.g., unmeasured clinical factors) may persist. The clinical significance of the observed differences is uncertain, as effect sizes were modest and MME changes were not significant. The findings suggest guideline adherence was stronger in non-cancer patients, possibly due to differing pain management needs or perceived risks.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The results highlight potential gaps in opioid prescribing practices among older adults with cancer post-guideline implementation. Clinicians should remain vigilant about balancing pain control and safety, particularly in cancer patients where reductions in high-risk co-prescribing were less pronounced. Further research is needed to determine optimal prescribing strategies in this population.

articles.title: A healthier day, a healthier mind: linking 24-h movement behavior guideline adherence to mental health in university students.
articles.authors: Shan S, Zheng B
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: University students face substantial challenges to psychological well-being, and healthy daily movement behaviors may be relevant to positive mental health. This study examined the association between adherence to 24-h movement behavior guidelines and positive mental health among university students, as well as the hypothesized statistical indirect associations through university adaptation and psychological resilience. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1,856 undergraduate students from two universities in Hunan Province, China. Adherence to 24-h movement behavior guidelines was assessed based on physical activity, recreational screen behavior, and sleep duration. University adaptation, psychological resilience, and positive mental health were measured using self-report scales, with positive mental health operationalized using the Mental Health Continuum-Short Form (MHC-SF). Pearson correlation analysis and PROCESS Model 6 were used to estimate the hypothesized serial direct and indirect associations. RESULTS: Complete adherence to all three guidelines was relatively low. Sleep duration had the highest adherence rate, whereas recreational screen behavior had the lowest. Adherence to more guidelines was positively associated with university adaptation, psychological resilience, and positive mental health; however, the correlations between guideline adherence and these variables were modest (r = 0.286-0.318). PROCESS Model 6 identified significan
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study in Chinese university students (n=1,856) examined whether adherence to 24-hour movement behavior guidelines (physical activity, screen time, sleep) is associated with positive mental health, and whether university adaptation and psychological resilience mediate this relationship.

FINDINGS: Adherence to all three guidelines was low, with sleep duration highest and screen time lowest. Greater adherence correlated modestly with better mental health (r = 0.286–0.318), university adaptation, and resilience. Serial mediation analysis suggested indirect effects of guideline adherence on mental health via adaptation and resilience, but effect sizes were not reported.

INTERPRETATION: The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. The modest correlations and lack of effect sizes limit clinical interpretation. While the proposed mediation pathways are plausible, the study cannot confirm whether improving movement behaviors would enhance mental health or adaptation. Funding sources and potential confounders (e.g., socioeconomic status, baseline mental health) were not addressed.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence is insufficient to change practice. Encouraging movement behaviors may support mental health indirectly, but high-quality longitudinal or interventional studies are needed to test causality and quantify meaningful effects.

articles.title: Sleep disturbances and functional impairment in severe mental illness: A structural equation modeling study.
articles.authors: Sommerhoff C, Bort M, Ruiz V, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sleep disturbances are highly prevalent in individuals with severe mental illness (SMI) and are associated with functional impairment. This study examined the prevalence of sleep disturbances and their associations with psychiatric symptoms and functional outcomes in a transdiagnostic SMI sample. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, SMI outpatients completed standardized assessments of sleep disturbances (PSQI, ISI, STOP-Bang, ESS, SQ-RLS, and SQ-RBD), psychiatric symptoms (HARS, MADRS, YMRS, PANSS-N, and CGI-S), and functioning (FAST). Bivariate analyses were followed by structural equation modeling (SEM), including latent constructs for insomnia and depressive/anxious symptoms to estimate direct and indirect associations with functional impairment. RESULTS: A total of 229 participants were included, and 69% screened positive for at least one sleep measure, including poor sleep quality (55.5%). Among the specific sleep-related problems, high risk of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) (45.8%) was the most prevalent. Sleep disturbances were associated with greater clinical severity and worse functional impairment. In the SEM, depressive/anxious symptoms (β = 0.45), negative symptoms (β = 0.38), manic symptoms (β = 0.17), and OSA risk (β = 0.41) were independently associated with functional impairment. Insomnia exhibited an inconsistent pattern, with a negative direct effect (β = -0.47) and a positive indirect effect on functional impairment through depressive/anxious
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study investigated how sleep disturbances relate to functional impairment in outpatients with severe mental illness (SMI), using structural equation modeling to disentangle direct and indirect pathways via psychiatric symptoms.

FINDINGS: Among 229 SMI outpatients, 69 % screened positive for at least one sleep disturbance; poor sleep quality was reported by 55.5 % and high OSA risk by 45.8 %. In the SEM, depressive/anxious symptoms (β = 0.45), negative symptoms (β = 0.38), manic symptoms (β = 0.17), and OSA risk (β = 0.41) were independently associated with functional impairment. Insomnia showed a paradoxical pattern: a direct negative effect (β = –0.47) but an indirect positive effect via depressive/anxious symptoms (β = 0.22).

INTERPRETATION: The study is limited by its cross-sectional design, precluding causal inference. SEM provides a nuanced view, but reliance on screening questionnaires rather than objective sleep measures and the single-site recruitment may reduce generalisability. The effect sizes suggest that depressive/anxious symptoms and OSA risk are the most robust correlates of functional impairment, whereas insomnia’s dual pathways warrant further longitudinal investigation.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine screening for sleep disturbances—especially OSA risk and mood/anxiety symptoms—may help identify modifiable targets to improve functioning in SMI, but treatment trials are needed to confirm whether intervening on these factors changes functional outcomes.

articles.title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Risk of Kidney Replacement Therapy and Health Care Utilization in Bipolar Disorder With Chronic Kidney Disease.
articles.authors: Singh B, Gonzalez Suarez ML, Ali HM, et al.
articles.abstract: Objective: To examine whether glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) use is associated with reduced risk of kidney replacement therapy (KRT) and health care utilization (HCU) compared with active comparators in adults with bipolar disorder (BD) and chronic kidney disease (CKD; stage ≤3). Methods: Using TriNetX, we conducted a real-world, new-user active-comparator cohort study among adults with BD+CKD initiating GLP-1 RA or dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor therapy (primary comparator), with a secondary analysis versus renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitor users. Propensity score matching (PSM) balanced baseline characteristics. Cox proportional hazards regression estimated adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) for KRT and HCU over 5-year follow-up. Subgroup analyses examined effect modification by sex, race, ethnicity, obesity, and psychotropic medication use. Results: Compared with DPP-4 inhibitor use, GLP-1 RA use was associated with lower observed risk of KRT (aHR 0.56, 95% CI 0.50-0.64) and HCU (aHR 0.74, 95% CI 0.71-0.78). Following PSM (n=3,908 per group), 5-year KRT-free survival was 87.93% versus 84.63% (P<.001); HCU-free survival did not differ significantly (P=.89). Versus RAAS inhibitors, GLP-1 RA use was similarly associated with lower observed risk of KRT (aHR 0.66) and HCU (aHR 0.62); after PSM (n=2,539 per group), KRT-free survival was higher (94.68% vs. 89.77%; P<.001), while HCU-free survival did not differ significantly (P=.15).
