articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This real-world cohort study used TriNetX data to test whether GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) reduce the need for kidney replacement therapy (KRT) and health care utilisation (HCU) versus active comparators in adults with bipolar disorder (BD) and chronic kidney disease (CKD stage ≤3). The primary comparison was GLP-1 RA versus DPP-4 inhibitors; a secondary comparison was versus RAAS inhibitors.

FINDINGS: After propensity-score matching (n=3,908 per group), GLP-1 RA use was associated with a lower risk of KRT (aHR 0.56, 95% CI 0.50–0.64) and lower HCU (aHR 0.74, 95% CI 0.71–0.78) versus DPP-4 inhibitors. Five-year KRT-free survival was 87.93% vs 84.63% (P<.001). In the secondary analysis (n=2,539 per group), GLP-1 RA vs RAAS inhibitors also showed lower KRT risk (aHR 0.66) and HCU (aHR 0.62), with KRT-free survival 94.68% vs 89.77% (P<.001). Benefits were consistent across sex, race, obesity, and psychotropic subgroups, including lithium users.

INTERPRETATION: The study’s large real-world cohorts and active-comparator design strengthen internal validity, but residual confounding and non-randomised treatment assignment remain concerns. The magnitude of KRT reduction (absolute gain ~3–5% at 5 years) is clinically modest. HCU differences were not consistently significant across comparators, suggesting possible outcome-reporting or care-pattern artefacts. The findings are exploratory and require prospective randomised evidence to confirm causality and generalisability to routine BD+CKD care.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These data suggest GLP-1 RA may offer kidney protection in BD+CKD, but the effect size is modest and not yet definitive. Consider GLP-1 RA in BD patients with CKD for potential renal benefits, while awaiting confirmatory trials; monitor kidney function and glycaemic control closely.

articles.title: Functioning Management & Recovery - Resource Group, a psychoeducational intervention to improve empowerment of people with severe mental illness: a 12-month multicenter randomized control study.
articles.authors: Veltro F, Latte G, Pontarelli C, et al.
articles.abstract: AIM: Functioning Management and Recovery with the Resource Group (FM&R-GR) is a standardized Psychoeducational Intervention elaborated to improve functioning and empowerment of people with Severe Mental Illness (SMI) living in the community. The aim of this study is to prove its efficacy by the primary and secondary outcomes. METHODS: 60 patients with SMI were recruited in 5 day-centers (North and South Italy) randomly assigned into 2 groups (Experimental vs Control); patients underwent a multicenter follow-up study with a two time-point evaluation (t0, pre-treatment and t1, 12 months). A highly structured FM&R-GR was used in the Experimental Group (EG), whereas a less structured manual was used in the Control Group (CG). At each time point, Social Functioning, Empowerment and Distress, were assessed as primary outcome; furthermore, Psychopathological Status, Cognitive Functioning, and Cognitive Flexibility were assessed as secondary outcome. RESULTS: Fifty-nine individuals out of 60 (98.3%) started the study randomly allocated in the EG vs CG. In the EG, 19 people (32.2%) were affected by schizophrenia, 9 (15.2%) by bipolar I disorder with psychotic symptoms and 2 (3.4%) by personality disorders according to DSM-5-TR started the study; in the CG there were respectively 20 (33.9%), 6 (10.2%) and 3 (5.1%). Forty-eight patients, 27 in the EG (56.3%) and 21 in the CG (43.75) completed the study. The total scores of NEL, Distress (p<0.001), and PSPS (p<0.05) showed a statisticall
articles.summary: AIM: Functioning Management and Recovery with the Resource Group (FM&R-GR) is a standardized Psychoeducational Intervention elaborated to improve functioning and empowerment of people with Severe Mental Illness (SMI) living in the community. The aim of this study is to prove its efficacy by the primary and secondary outcomes. METHODS: 60 patients with SMI were recruited in 5 day-centers (North and South Italy) randomly assigned into 2 groups (Experimental vs Control); patients underwent a multicenter follow-up study with a two time-point evaluation (t0, pre-treatment and t1, 12 months).

articles.title: Investigating Potential Adverse Drug Reactions of Lisdexamfetamine Using Sequence Symmetry Analysis.
articles.authors: Jensen TL, Thysen SM, Jimenez-Solem E, et al.
articles.abstract: The prevalence of ADHD is increasing rapidly, and lisdexamfetamine is increasingly popular, but few studies investigate its safety. We performed a sequence symmetry analysis (SSA) using Danish register data to identify potential ADRs associated with lisdexamfetamine in 2013-2023. Outcomes were incident prescriptions or incident discharge diagnoses. We calculated trend-adjusted sequence ratios (SR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). We additionally performed two comparator SSAs for the same outcomes following incident use of stimulants (methylphenidate and dexamfetamine) or non-stimulants (guanfacine and atomoxetine). This study is reported according to RECORD-PE guidelines. We included 48 740 incident lisdexamfetamine users with a median age of 24 years (IQR 16-35). SRs were calculated for 1426 exposure-diagnosis and 1337 exposure-prescription pairs. The 50 highest SRs from each category were evaluated. Among these, 28 exposure-outcome combinations had a 95% CI lower bound above 1. Of the 100 outcomes, 33 were considered known ADRs, while 60 were previously unknown. Two outcomes indicating increased urinary symptoms were identified ('hematuria', SR: 1.88 [95% CI: 1.25; 2.85] and 'other urinary symptoms', SR: 1.63 [1.20; 2.23]). We also identified serious gastrointestinal outcomes as a potential safety alert. Further investigation into these symptoms as potential ADRs is warranted.
articles.summary: The prevalence of ADHD is increasing rapidly, and lisdexamfetamine is increasingly popular, but few studies investigate its safety. We performed a sequence symmetry analysis (SSA) using Danish register data to identify potential ADRs associated with lisdexamfetamine in 2013-2023. Outcomes were incident prescriptions or incident discharge diagnoses. We calculated trend-adjusted sequence ratios (SR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI).

articles.title: An Effective Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Framework Using Adaptive Serial Hybrid Network With Self-Calibrated Feature Extraction on Brain MRI Images.
articles.authors: V N, K A
articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a medical condition commonly categorized as a neurodevelopmental disorder. Patients with ASD are not limited to common symptoms, and it often requires long-term hospital visits and specialists for definitive evaluation. Research has highlighted the importance of early intervention and care for ASD patients, as it can benefit their lifestyle. Automated detection techniques through deep learners have shown great progress in detecting ASD, as they excel in handling highly complex features and functional activity patterns by evaluating magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). However, as the ASD-associated neuroimaging patterns are not explicitly shown in the MRI, several challenges remain in identifying the ASD related features from MRI evaluation. To overcome these challenges, an advanced deep learning framework has been developed for detecting ASD. In this proposed model, MRI scans are collected from accessible datasets and applied to the feature extraction process. Here, feature extraction was carried out with the support of the proposed Self-Calibrated Dense Convolution Vision Transformer (SC-DCVT). This proposed feature extraction model integrates dense connections and self-calibration mechanisms to capture rich, contextual features from the MRI images, improving the representation of complex patterns. articles.summary: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a medical condition commonly categorized as a neurodevelopmental disorder. Patients with ASD are not limited to common symptoms, and it often requires long-term hospital visits and specialists for definitive evaluation. Research has highlighted the importance of early intervention and care for ASD patients, as it can benefit their lifestyle.

articles.title: Effects of early-life tactile experience enrichment on autistic-like behaviors and synaptic alterations in Shank3 mutant mice.
articles.authors: Liu M, Ma G, Zhang Y, et al.
articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) presents a significant therapeutic challenge due to limited treatment options. While non-pharmacological approaches based on sensory stimulation have shown promise in clinical practice, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study explored the therapeutic potential of tactile experience enrichment (TEE) during specific developmental windows in Shank3 KO mice, a model of ASD. We found that pre-weaning TEE robustly rescued core behavioral deficits, including social interaction and repetitive grooming, whereas juvenile TEE only improved social behavior. RNA sequencing of the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and dorsolateral striatum (DLS) revealed TEE-induced alterations in synaptic gene expression, including the upregulation of the Polo-like kinase 1 (PLK-1) pathway, which may modulate synaptic maturation. Furthermore, pre-weaning TEE restored dendritic spine density and morphology, along with synaptic transmission, in both the ACC and DLS. These findings indicate that early tactile enrichment, particularly during the pre-weaning period, can effectively alleviate core ASD-related behaviors in Shank3 KO mice by modulating synaptic structure and function, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic intervention for ASD.
articles.summary: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) presents a significant therapeutic challenge due to limited treatment options. While non-pharmacological approaches based on sensory stimulation have shown promise in clinical practice, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study explored the therapeutic potential of tactile experience enrichment (TEE) during specific developmental windows in Shank3 KO mice, a model of ASD.

articles.title: Prediction models for postpartum post-traumatic stress disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Shi H, Liu J, Yang C, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Postpartum post-traumatic stress disorder acts as an invisible scar, eroding maternal mental health and exerting long-term effects on infant development. Existing screening methods have limitations, hindering early prevention. Predictive models offer a promising approach for early identification of postpartum post-traumatic stress disorder. This study aims to establish a current evidence baseline and outline future directions through a systematic review and meta-analysis. METHODS: We systematically searched ten databases-PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Scopus, and three Chinese databases (CNKI, Wanfang, CBM)-from inception to August 12, 2025. Studies developing and/or validating multivariable prediction models for post-traumatic stress disorder within 12 months postpartum were included. The PROBAST tool was used to assess risk of bias and applicability. Random-effects models were employed for meta-analysis of validated model performance (AUC, sensitivity, specificity). RESULTS: Seventeen studies involving 17,236 participants were included. The pooled AUC was 0.84 (95% CI: 0.80-0.88), with a pooled sensitivity of 0.77 and specificity of 0.82. Frequently identified predictors included mode of delivery, level of social support, pregnancy complications, and fear of childbirth. Considerable heterogeneity was observed (I² = 89.7%), and calibration and external validation were insufficiently reported. CONCLUSION: This review demonstrat
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO protocol not stated) evaluated multivariable prediction models for postpartum PTSD within 12 months after delivery, aiming to quantify diagnostic accuracy and identify methodological gaps that limit clinical use.

FINDINGS: Seventeen studies (n=17 236) yielded a pooled AUC of 0.84 (95 % CI 0.80–0.88), sensitivity 0.77 and specificity 0.82. Predictors most often included mode of delivery, social support, pregnancy complications and fear of childbirth. High heterogeneity (I² = 89.7 %) and sparse calibration and external validation were noted.

INTERPRETATION: The models show encouraging discrimination, but the evidence base is weakened by substantial heterogeneity, incomplete reporting of calibration and few external validations. Without standardized development (e.g., TRIPOD adherence) and large multi-centre validations, the pooled metrics overstate likely real-world performance and generalisability.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current prediction models should not yet be implemented in routine maternity care; they remain research tools until rigorous external validation and calibration are demonstrated.

articles.title: Clinical outcomes of early versus standard liver transplantation in patients with alcohol-related liver disease: a meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Symeou S, Chun KLB, Sinakos E, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: A 6-month abstinence period before listing patients with alcohol-related liver disease (ALD) for liver transplantation (LT) is the current standard practice at many transplant centers worldwide. Its prognostic validity is, however, debated because it has not been prospectively validated, and because many ALD patients do not survive long enough to make it onto the waitlist. METHODS: A meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the guidelines put forth by Cochrane and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA). Three databases (PubMed/Medline, Scopus and Cochrane Library) were searched to identify studies comparing early (eLT) and standard LT (sLT). RESULTS: Twelve studies comparing eLT and sLT for ALD were included, encompassing 2323 patients with ALD. Mortality [Risk ratio (RR) = 0.94, 95% Confidence Interval (CI): 0.73-1.22] and patient survival [Hazard Ratio (HR) = 1.10, 95% CI: 0.83-1.45] did not differ significantly between eLT and sLT. Any alcohol relapse was more frequent following eLT but did not reach significance in the primary analysis (RR = 1.37, 95%CI: 0.95-2.00). This association became statistically significant on leave-one-out and subgroup analyses. Early LT patients had a higher risk of acute graft rejection (RR = 1.22, 95% CI: 0.98-1.52) but comparable graft loss (RR = 0.97, 95% CI: 0.74-1.27). Post-operative risk of infection did not differ significantly (RR = 1.19, 95% CI: 0.80-1.77), but eLT was associat
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study addresses whether early liver transplantation (eLT) without a mandatory 6-month abstinence period improves outcomes compared to standard liver transplantation (sLT) in patients with alcohol-related liver disease (ALD). This meta-analysis synthesizes observational and comparative studies to evaluate survival, relapse, graft outcomes, and hospitalization.

FINDINGS: Twelve studies (n=2323) showed no significant difference in mortality (RR=0.94, 95% CI: 0.73–1.22) or patient survival (HR=1.10, 95% CI: 0.83–1.45) between eLT and sLT. Alcohol relapse was more frequent after eLT but not significant in the primary analysis (RR=1.37, 95% CI: 0.95–2.00), though it became significant in sensitivity analyses. Acute graft rejection was higher with eLT (RR=1.22, 95% CI: 0.98–1.52), while graft loss was similar (RR=0.97, 95% CI: 0.74–1.27). Infection risk did not differ (RR=1.19, 95% CI: 0.80–1.77), but hospitalization was longer by 5.24 days (95% CI: 0.15–10.33).

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited to retrospective and cohort studies with potential selection bias and confounding. The pooled results suggest no survival advantage for eLT, but sensitivity analyses hint at higher relapse and rejection risks. The small effect sizes and wide confidence intervals reduce certainty. The longer hospitalization is a consistent finding but may reflect clinical caution rather than inherent risk. Overall, the evidence is preliminary and heterogeneous; definitive conclusions require prospective randomized trials.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Early LT appears to offer survival comparable to standard LT, supporting its consideration in carefully selected patients with severe ALD who fail medical therapy. Clinicians should be vigilant for higher relapse and rejection rates and plan for longer post-transplant care. Current practice should remain individualized and multidisciplinary until stronger evidence emerges.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning Approaches for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Diagnosis: Protocol for a Scoping Review.
articles.authors: Ibe BO, Aly A, Al-Juboori SS, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) affects over 366 million adults and 139 million children worldwide, yet diagnosis remains fundamentally subjective, relying on clinical interviews, behavioral observations, and rating scales that yield inconsistent results across practitioners and settings. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) offer a paradigm shift toward objective, data-driven diagnosis by detecting complex patterns across neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and digital biomarkers that elude conventional assessment. Although AI-based ADHD research has grown exponentially, no comprehensive synthesis examines the full spectrum of data modalities, validation practices, and clinical translation readiness. This gap limits our understanding of which approaches are most promising for real-world implementation. OBJECTIVE: This scoping review will visually map the current evidence on AI-based ADHD classification with respect to predictive accuracy, data forms, data features, generalizability, and interpretability of models. METHODS: This scoping review will use the Joanna Briggs Institute approach to scoping reviews and follow the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. Five electronic databases (IEEE Xplore, Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, and ACM Digital Library) will be systematically searched for peer-reviewed studies published between J
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study is a scoping review protocol aiming to map the evidence on AI, machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) approaches for diagnosing ADHD, addressing the current subjective diagnostic methods and the growing but fragmented research in this area. The review will include empirical studies published between January 2019 and April 2026, focusing on studies with sample sizes >100 participants and non-ADHD control groups.

FINDINGS: The scoping review will synthesize findings on model performance, data modalities (e.g., neuroimaging, electrophysiology, digital biomarkers), validation practices, and interpretability methods. It will use the Joanna Briggs Institute approach and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, with screening and analysis currently in progress and expected completion in June 2026.

INTERPRETATION: As a scoping review protocol, this study does not present results but outlines a rigorous methodology to map the landscape of AI-based ADHD diagnostic tools. The strength lies in its comprehensive search strategy and predefined inclusion criteria, but the findings will depend on the quality and heterogeneity of the included studies. The review will highlight gaps in validation practices and clinical translation readiness, which are critical for future research and potential clinical implementation.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review will not change clinical practice immediately but will provide a foundation for future AI-based diagnostic tools by identifying the most promising data modalities, validation methods, and interpretability approaches. Clinicians should watch for its findings to understand the current state of AI in ADHD diagnosis and potential future applications.

articles.title: Early interventions for primary care patients with stress-related mental ill health: a randomised controlled non-inferiority trial of a nurse-led collaborative care intervention versus cognitive behavioural therapy.
articles.authors: Kontio E, Sennerstam V, Svärdman F, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Stress-related mental ill health is highly prevalent, and most individuals first seek help in primary care where access to psychological support is often limited. OBJECTIVE: To test whether nurse-led collaborative care (CC) is non-inferior to cognitive behavioural therapy delivered as psychologist-guided self-help (GSH-CBT) in reducing stress for adult primary care patients with stress-related mental ill health. METHODS: A randomised controlled non-inferiority trial where 172 adult primary care patients with mild to moderate stress-related mental ill health were allocated to nurse-led CC or GSH-CBT (1:1). The primary outcome was the Perceived Stress Scale-10 administered every 3 weeks during the 12-week treatment phase. The a priori non-inferiority margin was 0.3 d, requiring the one-sided 95% CI of the effect size to fall within this bound. Secondary outcomes were symptoms of exhaustion, sleep problems, depressive symptoms, general anxiety and quality of life. FINDINGS: In both conditions, participants showed large, significant within-group improvements on the primary outcome and all secondary outcomes. The primary outcome showed a small between-group difference (d=0.22), favouring GSH-CBT, with the CI upper bound (0.52) exceeding the non-inferiority margin. For secondary outcomes, GSH-CBT led to a greater reduction in exhaustion (d=0.28; 95% CI 0.64 to 0.002). No other between-group differences were observed. CONCLUSIONS: Nurse-led CC was not non-inferior to GSH
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The trial asked whether a nurse-led collaborative care (CC) model is no worse than psychologist-guided self-help cognitive behavioural therapy (GSH-CBT) for reducing stress in adult primary care patients with mild-to-moderate stress-related mental ill-health. It was a 12-week, two-arm, non-inferiority RCT (n = 172).

FINDINGS: Both groups improved substantially on the Perceived Stress Scale-10 (PSS-10) and all secondary measures. The between-group effect on PSS-10 was small (d = 0.22, 95 % CI –0.09 to 0.52), with the upper bound exceeding the pre-set non-inferiority margin of 0.3 d. GSH-CBT showed a slightly larger reduction in exhaustion (d = 0.28, 95 % CI 0.002 to 0.56). No other between-group differences reached statistical significance.

INTERPRETATION: The study met its internal validity requirements (randomisation, allocation concealment, intention-to-treat analysis), but the non-inferiority margin was crossed, so CC cannot be declared non-inferior to GSH-CBT. The observed differences are small and of uncertain clinical importance. External validity is reasonable for Swedish primary care, yet generalisability may be limited by the exclusion of severe cases and reliance on self-report measures.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Nurse-led CC remains a safe, feasible option when psychologists are unavailable, but it is not demonstrably equivalent to GSH-CBT; clinicians should still prioritise access to CBT where possible.

articles.title: Retinal Biomarkers of Cognition in Schizophrenia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.authors: Mamidipalli SS, Franco A, Duraisamy J, et al.
articles.abstract: Individuals with schizophrenia consistently show thinning retinal layers, which can potentially serve as neural biomarkers. The association between retinal morphology and core symptom domains like cognitive functioning, however, has not been systematically synthesized. We hypothesize that deficits in retinal structure are associated with cognitive dysfunction in schizophrenia. This systematic review and meta-analysis looks at studies available from inception to June 9, 2026. Outcome measures include correlation coefficients between cognition scores and retinal thickness values (both macular and peripapillary-total and sector-wise) assessed using optical coherence tomography in patients with schizophrenia and related disorders. We assessed risk of bias with the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tool. Meta-analysis was conducted using the restricted maximum-likelihood method and Fisher's r-to-z transformation. Data from 16 studies (n=1,475 eyes; 847 patients) were included in a series of 88 pooled analyses. Overall cognitive ability correlated with thickness of the macular-retinal nerve fiber layer (mRNFL) (pooled-r=0.180; p=.002; k=7) and the superior-quadrant of the peripapillary RNFL (pRNFL) (pooled-r=0.214; p=.026; k=7). Attention correlated with mRNFL (pooled-r=0.210; p<.001; k=6), macular-inner plexiform layer (mIPL) (pooled-r=0.142; p=.012; k=8), and pRNFL (pooled-r=0.207; p<.001; k=9) thicknesses. Processing speed correlated with foveal thickness (FT) (pooled-r
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis (k=16 studies, n=847 patients) examined whether retinal layer thinning in schizophrenia correlates with cognitive deficits across domains such as overall cognition, attention, processing speed, and executive function, using optical coherence tomography (OCT) measures.

FINDINGS: Pooled correlations showed small but statistically significant associations between thinner retinal layers and poorer cognition: overall cognition with macular-retinal nerve fiber layer (mRNFL; pooled-r=0.180; p=.002; k=7) and superior peripapillary RNFL (pRNFL; pooled-r=0.214; p=.026; k=7). Attention correlated with mRNFL (r=0.210; p<.001; k=6), macular-inner plexiform layer (mIPL; r=0.142; p=.012; k=8), and pRNFL (r=0.207; p<.001; k=9). Processing speed correlated with foveal thickness (r=0.206; p=.008; k=7), mIPL (r=0.194; p=.001; k=6), and pRNFL (r=0.211; p<.001; k=5). Executive function correlated with macular thickness (r=0.099; p=.018; k=10) and mRNFL (r=0.159; p=.009; k=6). Age, sex, cardiometabolic comorbidities, and smoking moderated these effects.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests a modest association between retinal thinning and cognitive impairment in schizophrenia, but the small effect sizes (r≈0.14–0.21) and limited number of studies (k≤10 per domain) mean results should be interpreted cautiously. Heterogeneity in OCT protocols, cognitive assessments, and patient characteristics limits comparability. No causal inference can be drawn, and confounding by illness severity or treatment exposure remains possible.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Retinal OCT is non-invasive and widely available, but current evidence does not support its use as a standalone biomarker for cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. Further longitudinal, well-controlled studies are needed before considering clinical integration.

articles.title: Cross-ancestry and cross-disorder transferability of polygenic risk scores for obsessive-compulsive disorder.
articles.authors: Park CI, Kim J, Myung W, et al.
articles.abstract: Most genome-wide association studies (GWASs) of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) have been conducted in European populations, limiting the understanding of OCD genetics across populations. Here, we investigated the cross-ancestry and cross-disorder transferability of European-derived polygenic risk scores (PRSs) for OCD in the first East Asian OCD cohort. We performed a GWAS in 532 Korean OCD cases and 4376 controls, followed by PRS analyses using European GWASs for OCD and 10 psychiatric disorders. The European-derived OCD PRS was significantly associated with Korean OCD status (best-fit R² = 1.17%). In multivariable models, PRSs for OCD (odds ratio [OR] = 1.28, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.13-1.45), schizophrenia (SCZ; OR = 1.17, 95% CI = 1.03-1.32), and anorexia nervosa (AN; OR = 1.17, 95% CI = 1.03-1.32) were independently associated with OCD. A stepwise multi-PRS model including PRSs for OCD, AN, SCZ, post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and bipolar disorder (BD) yielded the highest predictive performance (incremental R² = 2.99%). Where available, we evaluated PRSs derived from East Asian, European, and combined populations. For BD and SCZ, PRSs derived from cross-ancestry meta-analysis GWASs showed the greatest predictive performance for OCD, outperforming single-ancestry PRSs (incremental R² = 2.84 and 1.28%, respectively). Our findings demonstrate cross-ancestry transferability of OCD polygenic risk and hig
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional genetic study examined whether polygenic risk scores (PRSs) derived from European genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and other psychiatric disorders predict OCD status in an East Asian cohort (532 Korean cases, 4376 controls), and whether cross-ancestry PRSs improve prediction.

FINDINGS: The European OCD PRS showed a modest but significant association with Korean OCD status (best-fit R² = 1.17%). In multivariable models, OCD PRS (OR 1.28, 95% CI 1.13–1.45), schizophrenia PRS (OR 1.17, 95% CI 1.03–1.32), and anorexia nervosa PRS (OR 1.17, 95% CI 1.03–1.32) were independently associated with OCD. A stepwise multi-PRS model including seven psychiatric disorders increased incremental R² to 2.99%. Cross-ancestry meta-analysis PRSs for bipolar disorder and schizophrenia outperformed single-ancestry PRSs (incremental R² 2.84% and 1.28%, respectively).

INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate in internal validity (well-powered discovery GWAS, multivariable adjustment, cross-ancestry comparison) but limited in external validity (single East Asian cohort, cross-sectional design, small effect sizes). The small R² values indicate that current PRSs explain only a tiny fraction of OCD variance, so clinical translation is not imminent. The study highlights shared genetic architecture between OCD and other psychiatric disorders, particularly schizophrenia and anorexia nervosa, but replication in larger, diverse cohorts and functional validation are needed.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, PRSs for OCD have no immediate bedside utility for diagnosis, risk stratification, or treatment selection in routine psychiatric care; they remain a research tool to map genetic overlap across disorders.

articles.title: Using multi-trait polygenic scores to predict lithium responsiveness in patients with bipolar disorder.
articles.authors: Sharew NT, Clark SR, Hartmann S, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The predictive power of polygenic scores (PGSs) for lithium treatment response in bipolar disorder remains limited. AIMS: To enhance the prediction of lithium responsiveness by developing a multi-trait PGS (mt-PGS) combining genetic information from multiple phenotypes implicated in lithium response and/or bipolar disorder aetiology. METHOD: We analysed data collected from bipolar disorder patients who had received lithium treatment for at least 6 months and participated in the International Consortium on Lithium Genetics study (N = 2367). The Alda scale was used to assess lithium responsiveness, and treatment outcome was defined as continuous total Alda score (0-10) and categorical outcome (favourable ≥7 versus unfavourable response). PGSs were calculated for 60 phenotypes grouped into 5 clinical-biological clusters: psychiatric and behavioural (#23 phenotypes), cardiometabolic (#17), autoimmune/inflammatory (#5), neurocognitive (#8) and renal function (#7). We applied cross-validated machine learning regression approaches in both outcomes within each cluster, with the selected features from each cluster subsequently combined to construct the final mt-PGS models. Model performance was assessed using explained variance (R2) for the continuous outcome, and both McFadden's pseudo-R2 and standard classification model parameters for the categorical outcome. RESULTS: mt-PGS explained between 5.70% (continuous outcome) and 9.11% (categorical outcome) of the interindivid
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study evaluated whether combining multiple polygenic scores (PGSs) from phenotypes related to lithium response or bipolar disorder could better predict lithium responsiveness in patients with bipolar disorder. Using data from 2,367 participants in the International Consortium on Lithium Genetics study, the researchers developed a multi-trait PGS (mt-PGS) and assessed its predictive power using both continuous and categorical measures of lithium response.

FINDINGS: The mt-PGS explained 5.70% of the variability in lithium responsiveness when using the continuous Alda score and 9.11% when using the categorical outcome (favourable vs. unfavourable response). The model achieved a classification accuracy (area under the curve) of 68.24% (95% CI: 64.98–71.66) for the categorical outcome, with a Brier score of 0.257. The psychiatric and behavioural phenotype cluster contributed most strongly to prediction, accounting for 3.67–6.52% of variability in lithium response.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests that combining multiple PGSs modestly improves prediction of lithium response compared to single-trait approaches, but the explained variance remains low (≤9.11%). The study’s strengths include a large sample size and rigorous machine learning methods, but limitations include the retrospective design, reliance on the Alda scale (which has inherent subjectivity), and lack of external validation. The clinical utility is currently limited due to the small effect size and modest classification accuracy.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: While this study advances the field by demonstrating incremental predictive value of mt-PGS, it does not yet support clinical implementation. Further research is needed to refine models, validate findings in diverse populations, and integrate genetic data with clinical factors before considering use in routine care.

articles.title: Changes in Multisystem Morbidity in Thyroid Cancer after the 2015 ATA Guideline: A Nationwide Population-Based Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.authors: Ahn SH, Kim DW, Kim J, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: As survivorship has become increasingly important in differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC), the 2015 American Thyroid Association (ATA) guideline introduced a more risk-adapted and less intensive approach to management. However, evidence regarding the association between guideline-driven de-intensification and non-cancer-specific multisystem morbidity remains limited. METHODS: We conducted a nationwide population-based retrospective cohort study using Korean national claims data and compared patients who underwent total thyroidectomy before (2009-2014, n = 96,776) and after (2016-2021, n = 29,408) the 2015 ATA guideline. Outcome-specific 1:1 propensity score-matched analytic sets were constructed. The primary outcomes were composite cardiovascular/cerebrovascular, composite skeletal, and composite neurocognitive/psychiatric outcomes, as well as all-cause mortality. Secondary analyses examined the individual components of each composite outcome. Time-to-event analyses were performed using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models. RESULTS: After matching and adjustment, the postguideline period demonstrated lower risks of composite skeletal outcomes (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.83; confidence interval [CI] 0.69-0.99) and composite neurocognitive/psychiatric outcomes (HR = 0.73; CI 0.69-0.77). Composite cardiovascular/cerebrovascular outcomes did not differ significantly between periods; however, secondary analyses showed lower risks of atrial fibrillation (HR = 0.62; C
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether a less intensive, risk-adapted approach to thyroid cancer management introduced by the 2015 ATA guideline was associated with reduced non-cancer-specific multisystem morbidity in a nationwide retrospective cohort of patients who underwent total thyroidectomy in Korea (n = 126,184; pre-guideline 2009–2014, post-guideline 2016–2021).

FINDINGS: After 1:1 propensity score matching and multivariable Cox regression, the post-guideline period showed lower risks of composite skeletal outcomes (HR 0.83, 95 % CI 0.69–0.99) and composite neurocognitive/psychiatric outcomes (HR 0.73, 95 % CI 0.69–0.77). Composite cardiovascular/cerebrovascular outcomes were unchanged overall, but secondary analyses revealed lower risks of atrial fibrillation (HR 0.62, 95 % CI 0.50–0.76), myocardial infarction (HR 0.81, 95 % CI 0.66–0.99), and stroke (HR 0.56, 95 % CI 0.49–0.63). All-cause mortality did not differ between periods.

INTERPRETATION: The study’s large, population-based design and use of propensity matching strengthen internal validity, but residual confounding from unmeasured variables (e.g., changes in adjuvant therapy, lifestyle, or surveillance intensity) remains possible. The observed HRs suggest modest but statistically significant reductions in skeletal and neurocognitive/psychiatric morbidity and selected cardiovascular events; however, effect sizes are small and clinical significance may be limited. External validity is constrained by the Korean healthcare setting and specific thyroid cancer population.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The findings support the safety and potential long-term benefits of guideline-driven de-intensification in thyroid cancer care, particularly regarding skeletal and psychiatric morbidity and certain cardiovascular outcomes. Clinicians should remain alert to subtle shifts in morbidity patterns and continue routine monitoring rather than altering practice based solely on these results.

articles.title: Rising demand and NHS reforms: what are the implications for mental health service provision?
articles.authors: Trethewey SP, Monk-Cunliffe J, Batterham M, et al.
articles.abstract: The National Health Service (NHS) 10-year health plan for England calls for transformational changes to service delivery, encompassing three fundamental 'shifts': hospital to community, analogue to digital and sickness to prevention. This editorial reflects on the plan, the three shifts and their implications for mental health service provision across the life course.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This editorial examines the implications of England’s NHS 10-year plan for mental health services, which proposes three major shifts: hospital-to-community care, analogue-to-digital delivery, and sickness-to-prevention focus. It assesses how these reforms may impact mental health service provision across the life course.

FINDINGS: The editorial outlines policy intentions without presenting empirical data. It highlights the planned expansion of community-based services and digital tools, aiming to reduce reliance on inpatient care and improve early intervention. However, it notes concerns about workforce capacity, funding sustainability, and equitable access across regions.

INTERPRETATION: As an editorial, this is a narrative review without quantitative outcomes or systematic evidence synthesis. Its strength lies in contextualizing policy changes, but it lacks rigorous evaluation of effectiveness or implementation challenges. The discussion is speculative regarding real-world impact on patient outcomes or service quality.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This piece does not provide actionable clinical data but signals potential shifts in service models. Clinicians should monitor local service changes and advocate for evidence-based implementation of digital and community-based care to ensure quality and accessibility.

articles.title: Psychiatric comorbidity, burden of sickness absence and sex-specific characteristics of working individuals with ADHD treated in primary care in the Finnish occupational health system: cross-sectional register study.
articles.authors: Tuokko M, Ämmälä AJ, Paunio T, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Previous research on attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) research has overlooked high-functioning workers managed in occupational health settings. AIMS: To investigate clinical characteristics, service use, and sex-related differences in medication and work disability among employees with ADHD. METHOD: This study was a cross-sectional descriptive analysis of psychiatric comorbidities in 2117 patients (53.8% men, 46.2% women) with a clinical diagnosis of ADHD (ICD-10 F90.0) in the Finnish occupational health system (2018-2022). We explored service use, medication and sickness absence periods (using multinomial regression models) in a subset with available data (n = 1447). RESULTS: Psychiatric comorbidity affected 80.5% of patients, most commonly involving anxiety disorders (51.8%) and depression (43.9%). Service use was high: 87.0% consulted a psychiatrist and 70.1% a psychologist. Medication profiles differed by sex (Cramer's V = 0.15): men more frequently received psychostimulants only (27.4% v. 18.4%), whereas women were more likely to receive antidepressants only or antidepressant-anxiolytic combinations. Women demonstrated substantially higher levels of psychiatric sickness absence compared with men across all duration categories, with relative risk ratio (RRR) = 2.08 (95% CI 1.37-3.14) for short (1 to 7 days) absences, RRR = 2.03 (95% CI 1.42-2.90) for intermediate (8 to 30 days) absences and RRR = 2.75 (95% CI 2.16-3.52) for long-term (>30 days)
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional register study examined 2,117 working adults with ADHD in Finnish occupational health services (2018–2022) to describe psychiatric comorbidities, service use, medication patterns, and sex differences in sickness absence.

FINDINGS: Psychiatric comorbidity was present in 80.5% of patients, most commonly anxiety (51.8%) and depression (43.9%). Among 1,447 with complete data, 87.0% had seen a psychiatrist and 70.1% a psychologist. Men were more often treated with stimulants only (27.4% vs 18.4%), while women more often received antidepressants alone or combined with anxiolytics. Women had substantially higher psychiatric sickness absence across all durations: RRR 2.08 (95% CI 1.37–3.14) for 1–7 days, RRR 2.03 (1.42–2.90) for 8–30 days, and RRR 2.75 (2.16–3.52) for >30 days.

INTERPRETATION: The study provides robust real-world data on high comorbidity and service use in employed adults with ADHD, but its cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. The large sex differences in sickness absence are striking and clinically plausible, though residual confounding (e.g., unmeasured symptom severity) cannot be excluded. The effect sizes are large and clinically meaningful, but the study cannot determine whether different prescribing patterns drive the observed differences in work disability.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should anticipate high psychiatric comorbidity and frequent specialist referrals in working adults with ADHD. Sex-specific prescribing patterns may reflect differing clinical presentations or treatment preferences; monitoring and supporting work ability—especially in women with ADHD—may be warranted.

articles.title: Not How Fast, but to What Dose: Refocusing Antipsychotic Tapering on the Minimum Effective Dose.
articles.authors: Takeuchi H

articles.title: Associations between lifestyle, genetic liability for severe mental illness and risk of incident somatic illnesses.
articles.authors: Isayeva U, Guloksuz S, Lin BD, et al.
articles.abstract: People with severe mental illness (SMI), including schizophrenia (SCZ) and bipolar disorder (BD), show elevated risk for somatic conditions and premature mortality. Both genetic liability and modifiable lifestyle factors have been implicated in this comorbidity, yet large-scale studies examining their independent and combined effects across multiple somatic conditions are lacking. We therefore examined whether modifiable lifestyle factors (i.e. smoking, alcohol intake, diet, and exercise) and polygenic risk scores (PRS) for SCZ and BD are associated with the risk of developing somatic illnesses. Data were drawn from 315,313 unrelated individuals in the UK Biobank cohort, with a median follow up of 14 years. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate the independent, joint, and interaction effects of PRS-SCZ and PRS-BD and lifestyle factors on the incidence of nine chronic somatic illnesses. Healthy lifestyle was associated with lower risks of type 2 diabetes (T2D), cardiovascular disease (CVD), dementia, rheumatoid arthritis, asthma, chronic liver disease (CLD), and cancer (HRs ranging from 0.43 to 0.80). In addition, higher PRS for SCZ was associated with increased risks of asthma and dementia and lower risk of T2D, while higher PRS for BD was associated with increased risk of T2D. Moreover, likelihood ratio tests confirmed that PRS-SCZ and PRS-BD each contribute independent information to the joint Cox model for T2D, indicating that the opposing directions of the
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This large UK Biobank cohort study (n=315,313) examined whether modifiable lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol, diet, exercise) and polygenic risk scores (PRS) for schizophrenia (SCZ) and bipolar disorder (BD) independently or jointly predict incident somatic illnesses over a median 14-year follow-up.

FINDINGS: Healthy lifestyle was associated with lower risks of type 2 diabetes (T2D; HR 0.43), cardiovascular disease (CVD; HR 0.70), dementia (HR 0.56), rheumatoid arthritis (HR 0.80), asthma (HR 0.75), chronic liver disease (CLD; HR 0.60), and cancer (HR 0.75). Higher PRS-SCZ increased asthma (HR 1.06) and dementia (HR 1.04) risks but decreased T2D risk (HR 0.96). Higher PRS-BD increased T2D risk (HR 1.04). No significant additive interaction was found between genetic risk and lifestyle.

INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates robust associations between healthy lifestyle and reduced somatic illness risk across multiple conditions, independent of genetic liability. Genetic risks showed outcome-specific effects, with PRS-SCZ and PRS-BD contributing independent information for T2D. Limitations include observational design (residual confounding), healthy volunteer bias in UK Biobank, and lack of PRS validation in non-European ancestry groups. The clinical significance of small HRs for genetic risks (e.g., 1.04–1.06) is uncertain.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Lifestyle interventions remain a high-yield target for reducing somatic comorbidity in patients with or at genetic risk for SMI. Genetic risk stratification for somatic illness is not yet clinically actionable.

articles.title: Association of lithium versus valproate initiation with all-cause mortality and incident dementia: a multinational real-world cohort study.
articles.authors: Hou DH, Wu YH, Wu MJ, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lithium and valproate are widely prescribed mood stabilizers, but their comparative long-term associations with mortality and dementia remain uncertain. We compared the risks of all-cause mortality and incident dementia among adults initiating lithium or valproate using a large multinational electronic health record network. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network (2004-2024), a multinational electronic health record network. Adults aged ≥40 years initiating lithium or valproate were identified after excluding patients with pre-existing dementia, epilepsy, intracranial injury, kidney transplantation, advanced chronic kidney disease, or acute kidney injury. The primary analysis followed an intention-to-treat approach based on the first recorded prescription of lithium or valproate. Propensity score matching incorporated demographic, clinical, psychiatric, and treatment-related characteristics, resulting in 22,098 patients in each treatment group. A 30-day prescription-confirmed analysis and lag-time analyses were performed as supportive and sensitivity analyses, respectively. RESULTS: During follow-up, 884 deaths occurred among lithium initiators and 1,585 among valproate initiators. The corresponding five-year Kaplan-Meier-estimated cumulative event probabilities for all-cause mortality were 6.61 and 10.65%, respectively. Lithium initiation was associated with a lower recorded risk of all-cause mortality th
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This multinational real-world cohort study compared long-term risks of all-cause mortality and incident dementia among adults aged ≥40 initiating lithium versus valproate, addressing uncertainty about their comparative safety and cognitive outcomes.

FINDINGS: In a propensity score–matched cohort of 22,098 patients per group, lithium initiation was associated with lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.53–0.63) and incident dementia (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.60–0.76) over five years. Five-year cumulative event probabilities were 6.61% vs 10.65% for mortality and 3.51% vs 4.85% for dementia with lithium vs valproate.

INTERPRETATION: The study’s large, multinational real-world design strengthens external validity, and sensitivity analyses support robustness. However, residual confounding from unmeasured clinical and lifestyle factors is likely, and the data rely on recorded diagnoses rather than adjudicated outcomes. The effect sizes are modest and may not translate into large absolute benefits for individual patients.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest lithium may have advantages over valproate for long-term mortality and dementia risk, but the observational design precludes causal inference; treatment choice should still weigh efficacy, tolerability, and patient-specific factors.

articles.title: The Impact of Heterogeneity in Individual Characteristics and Motivation to Quit Heroin Use on Contingency Management and Opioid Agonist Treatment Response: A Latent Class Analysis.
articles.authors: MacGregor L, Weaver T, Strang J, et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Contingency Management (CM) involves the systematic application of positive reinforcement (financial incentives) to promote behaviour change, to improve treatment outcomes for individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD). To better understand patient heterogeneity, this study sought to identify meaningful subgroups/classes underlying the population based on characteristic groupings, followed by determining whether CM effectiveness varied between these subgroups. METHODS: Baseline characteristics (evidenced/theorised to impact CM effectiveness) of participants with OUD from the PRAISe trial (N = 552) were empirically examined using latent class analysis. Model selection was based on fit statistics and interpretability. Class was then evaluated as a potential moderator of CM effectiveness on abstinence from heroin using a mixed effects model (consistent with the PRAISe trial analysis). RESULTS: A four-class solution best described the population: (1) Less clinically complex/low alcohol dependence/high motivation to quit heroin (N = 115); (2) More clinically complex/low alcohol/high motivation (N = 287); (3) More clinically complex/high alcohol/high motivation (N = 73); and (4) More clinically complex/moderate alcohol/low motivation (N = 77). CM for Attendance, previously shown to increase heroin abstinence in the overall study sample, was more effective than no CM for participants in class (1) and (2) exclusively (OR = 5.21; 95% CI 1.25, 21.78 and OR = 1.87; 95% CI
articles.summary: INTRODUCTION: Contingency Management (CM) involves the systematic application of positive reinforcement (financial incentives) to promote behaviour change, to improve treatment outcomes for individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD). To better understand patient heterogeneity, this study sought to identify meaningful subgroups/classes underlying the population based on characteristic groupings, followed by determining whether CM effectiveness varied between these subgroups.

articles.title: The Philadelphia Theta Burst Project: A novel fMRI-guided electric field modeling dataset with reliability metrics.
articles.authors: Gregory DF, Sun I, Teferi M, et al.
articles.abstract: Recent neuromodulation studies suggest that theta burst stimulation (TBS) applied to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) can influence neural circuits involved in cognitive control and emotion-related processing, with relevance for psychiatric disorders. However, large-scale datasets characterizing variability, reliability, and multimodal neural responses to TBS remain limited. To address this gap, we established the Philadelphia Theta Burst Project, a dataset of 100 healthy participants who completed 4 fMRI sessions following cumulatively increasing doses of intermittent or continuous TBS, with participants randomized to one protocol or the other. Each session includes multiband, multi-echo resting-state (16 minutes) and task-based fMRI (16 minutes) during a Sternberg working memory paradigm. TMS targeting was guided by task-evoked activation in the left dlPFC. Structural T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and diffusion-weighted imaging were also acquired. Here, we describe the dataset design, acquisition protocol, and data characteristics, and report initial measures of data quality and reliability. The completed dataset can be accessed at https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds008893, providing an open resource for future investigations of TBS mechanisms and individualized neuromodulation strategies.
articles.summary: Recent neuromodulation studies suggest that theta burst stimulation (TBS) applied to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) can influence neural circuits involved in cognitive control and emotion-related processing, with relevance for psychiatric disorders. However, large-scale datasets characterizing variability, reliability, and multimodal neural responses to TBS remain limited.

articles.title: Comparative Efficacy and Acceptability of Transdiagnostic Psychotherapies for Emotional Disorders: Protocol for a Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.authors: Cai Q, Zeng Y, Jiménez-Orenga N, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Emotional disorders-primarily anxiety and unipolar depressive disorders-are highly prevalent, disabling, and frequently comorbid. Disorder‑specific cognitive behavioral therapy (DS‑CBT) is considered a gold standard treatment, yet it can be inefficient in the context of high comorbidity and service constraints. Transdiagnostic psychotherapies that target shared maintaining mechanisms (eg, emotion dysregulation and neuroticism) have been developed, including the Unified Protocol, transdiagnostic behavior therapy, emotion regulation therapy, and various transdiagnostic internet-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy protocols. Recent meta-analyses suggest that transdiagnostic interventions are effective or likely effective, but a comprehensive comparative evaluation across different transdiagnostic protocols, DS‑CBT, other evidence‑based psychotherapies, and control conditions is lacking. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to conduct a network meta-analysis (NMA) to compare the efficacy and acceptability of various transdiagnostic therapies (eg, the Unified Protocol, transdiagnostic behavior therapy, and emotion regulation therapy), DS-CBT, other evidence-based active therapies (eg, acceptance and commitment therapy, behavioral activation, and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy), and control conditions (waitlist or care as usual) in improving symptoms in adults with anxiety and/or depressive disorders and generate a probabilistic ranking of their efficacy. METHODS: This me
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Emotional disorders (anxiety and unipolar depression) are common and disabling, and disorder-specific CBT (DS-CBT) is a gold standard but may be inefficient with comorbidity and service constraints. This is a protocol for a network meta-analysis (NMA) comparing transdiagnostic psychotherapies (e.g., Unified Protocol, transdiagnostic behavior therapy), DS-CBT, other evidence-based therapies (e.g., ACT, behavioral activation), and control conditions in adults with anxiety and/or depressive disorders.

FINDINGS: The NMA will include RCTs from major databases (PubMed, Embase, PsycInfo, Cochrane Library) and existing meta-analytic databases. Eligible participants are adults (≥18 years) with a principal diagnosis of anxiety and/or unipolar depressive disorder or scoring above validated cutoffs on anxiety/depression scales. Primary outcomes are continuous measures of anxiety and depressive symptom severity at posttreatment; secondary outcomes include study dropout (acceptability) and response/remission where available. The analysis will use random-effects NMA within a frequentist framework (netmeta package in R) and Bayesian NMA as sensitivity analyses. As of September 2026, literature search is complete, title/abstract screening is ongoing, and data analysis is planned for late 2026, with results expected in early 2027.

INTERPRETATION: This is a protocol for an NMA, so no results are available yet. The planned methodology appears robust (random-effects NMA, frequentist and Bayesian approaches, examination of transitivity and consistency), but the findings are pending. The study aims to provide a comprehensive comparative evaluation, which could inform clinical decision-making and guideline development if the results are robust and clinically meaningful.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No clinical implications can be drawn yet, as the study is still in progress. Once published, the results may help clinicians choose between transdiagnostic psychotherapies, DS-CBT, and other evidence-based treatments based on efficacy and acceptability rankings.

articles.title: Exercise to enhance antipsychotic effectiveness and mitigate metabolic harm: systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Etayo-Urtasun P, Ancín-Osés A, Izquierdo M, et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Antipsychotics are first-line treatments for schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders but are frequently accompanied by cardiometabolic adverse effects (weight gain, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, hyperglycaemia). We assessed whether supervised exercise interventions enhance psychopathology outcomes and reduce antipsychotic-related metabolic harm in adults receiving antipsychotic treatment medication. DESIGN: Systematic review and meta-analysis. DATA SOURCES: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus following PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO CRD420251139904). Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) published since 2000 that tested supervised exercise in people receiving antipsychotics were eligible. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA FOR SELECTING STUDIES: Two reviewers selected studies using PICOS criteria, assessed methodological quality with the Revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials (RoB 2), and pooled effects with random-effects models, expressed as mean differences (MD) with 95% CIs. The certainty of evidence was assessed with GRADE. RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies (n = 1119) and four additional analyses met inclusion criteria. Exercise significantly improved negative symptoms (MD -3·078, 95% CI -4·457 to -1·699; p < 0·001), general psychopathology (-2·178, -4·140 to -0·216, p = 0·034), and PANSS total score (-7·069, -13·290 to -0·849; p = 0·030). Effects on positive symptoms were not significant (-1·220, -2·462 to 0·022; p = 0·053). Exercise reduced body weight
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO registered) evaluated whether supervised exercise interventions improve psychiatric outcomes and mitigate antipsychotic-induced metabolic harm in adults with schizophrenia or related psychotic disorders. Twenty-eight RCTs (n = 1119) published since 2000 were included.

FINDINGS: Exercise significantly improved negative symptoms (MD −3.08, 95% CI −4.46 to −1.70; p < 0.001), general psychopathology (−2.18, −4.14 to −0.22; p = 0.034), and PANSS total score (−7.07, −13.29 to −0.85; p = 0.030). Positive symptoms were not significantly affected (−1.22, −2.46 to 0.02; p = 0.053). Metabolic benefits included reduced body weight (−1.62 kg, −3.08 to −0.16; p = 0.034), body fat percentage (−1.25%, −2.17 to −0.33; p = 0.020), and waist circumference (−1.42 cm, −2.65 to −0.20; p = 0.032). No significant effects were found for BMI, blood pressure, fasting glucose, or most lipid measures. GRADE certainty was moderate for negative symptoms and metabolic outcomes, low to very low for others.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests supervised exercise can modestly improve core psychopathology and reduce adiposity in people on antipsychotics, with moderate-quality evidence for key outcomes. However, effect sizes are small (e.g., ~3-point PANSS reduction), and metabolic benefits did not extend to clinically critical endpoints like glucose or lipids. Heterogeneity in exercise types, small sample sizes, and short follow-ups limit conclusions. High-quality RCTs with standardized multicomponent exercise and comprehensive metabolic monitoring are needed.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Supervised exercise may serve as a useful adjunct to antipsychotic treatment, particularly for negative symptoms and weight management, but current evidence does not support major changes in metabolic risk management. Clinicians should consider integrating supervised exercise as part of holistic care while monitoring for modest benefits.

articles.title: Perceived Utility of Combining Atypical Long-Acting Injectable Antipsychotics With Psychosocial Interventions: An Exploratory Survey of Mid-Career Psychiatrists in Japan.
articles.authors: Umetsu S, Oguchi Y, Miyake N
articles.abstract: AIMS: Although combining long-acting injectable antipsychotics (LAIs) with psychosocial treatments for schizophrenia is important, psychiatrists' attitudes toward this approach remain underexplored. We investigated Japanese psychiatrists' perceptions of combining atypical LAIs with psychosocial interventions. METHODS: An anonymous cross-sectional web-based survey was administered to 1038 mid-career Japanese psychiatrists, of whom 69 provided complete responses. Participants' general attitude toward recommending atypical LAIs was dichotomized as positive or negative/neutral, and they rated on a 4-point scale the usefulness of combining atypical LAIs with five psychosocial interventions: (1) psychosocial treatment (e.g., psychoeducation), (2) day/night care, (3) community care, (4) financial/employment support, and (5) housing support. RESULTS: Thirty-nine respondents held a positive attitude toward recommending atypical LAIs, whereas 30 held a negative/neutral attitude. A positive attitude was significantly associated with perceiving the combination as useful for psychosocial treatment (p = 0.038), financial/employment support (p = 0.015), and housing support (p = 0.041), but not for day/night care (p = 0.090) or community care (p = 0.079). Free-text rationales most commonly cited improved adherence and relapse prevention, enhanced illness insight, and synergistic effects as reasons for valuing the combination. CONCLUSIONS: This exploratory study suggests that mid-career Japan
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study explored mid-career Japanese psychiatrists' attitudes toward combining atypical long-acting injectable antipsychotics (LAIs) with psychosocial interventions for schizophrenia, using an anonymous cross-sectional web-based survey (n=69 complete responses out of 1038 invited).

FINDINGS: Psychiatrists with a positive attitude toward LAIs were significantly more likely to perceive the combination as useful for psychosocial treatment (p=0.038), financial/employment support (p=0.015), and housing support (p=0.041), but not for day/night care (p=0.090) or community care (p=0.079). The most cited rationales for the combination were improved adherence, relapse prevention, and synergistic effects.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary due to a very low response rate (6.6%), small sample size, and selection bias (predominantly male, self-selected participants). The associations reported are statistically significant but based on exploratory analyses without adjustment for multiple comparisons. The generalizability to broader psychiatric practice is limited, and the clinical significance of these perceptions remains uncertain.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study does not provide actionable evidence to change practice but suggests a perceived benefit of combining LAIs with psychosocial support among a subset of Japanese psychiatrists. Further research with larger, representative samples is needed to validate these findings.

articles.title: Australian Digital Mental Health Services for Anxiety and Depression: Meta-Analysis and Comparison Study.
articles.authors: Bassilios B, Scurrah KJ, Morgan AJ, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Mental Health Online, MindSpot, and THIS WAY UP are 3 Australian Government-funded digital mental health services (DMHSs). These services are free for consumers and deliver a range of (depression and anxiety disorder) psychological assessments and interventions using the internet, with or without clinician support. OBJECTIVE: This study examines the uptake and effectiveness of these services. METHODS: We used 3 data sources to examine the performance of the three DMHSs: (1) aggregated routinely collected service data to describe uptake of the services from January 2013 to December 2021, (2) peer-reviewed and gray literature reporting treatment outcomes, and (3) treatment outcome data from one evaluation conducted by Mental Health Online. The second and third data sources were used to analyze the effectiveness of the DMHSs compared to other mental health treatment programs (Australian primary, public, and low-intensity mental health care; UK stepped psychological care). We generated pooled mental health symptom (Cohen d) effect sizes for each service's clinician-supported and self-directed treatments and compared those with effect sizes we calculated for the alternative treatment programs. RESULTS: The 3 DMHSs offered care to more than 282,000 consumers and therefore contributed to improving overall access to mental health care in Australia. Clinician-supported online treatment significantly improved the mental health of consumers who use these services (Mental Hea
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This meta-analysis and comparison study evaluated the uptake and effectiveness of three Australian government-funded digital mental health services (DMHSs: Mental Health Online, MindSpot, THIS WAY UP) for adults with anxiety and depression, comparing their outcomes to other mental health treatments using routinely collected service data (2013–2021) and published literature.

FINDINGS: The three DMHSs served over 282,000 consumers. Clinician-supported treatments showed large pooled effect sizes (Cohen d: Mental Health Online 0.95, MindSpot 1.42, THIS WAY UP 1.04), while self-directed treatment by Mental Health Online showed a moderate effect (Cohen d=0.59). Clinician-supported DMHS outcomes were comparable to face-to-face, phone, and stepped-care comparators, though heterogeneity across services and clinical need levels was noted.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests DMHSs deliver clinically meaningful improvements in anxiety and depression symptoms, particularly with clinician support. However, heterogeneity in effect sizes and comparator populations limits firm conclusions about equivalence across settings. The reliance on aggregated service data and varied literature sources introduces potential bias, and no direct randomized comparisons were made. Further high-quality trials are needed to confirm effectiveness across diverse populations.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: DMHSs may offer accessible, effective alternatives to traditional care for mild-to-moderate anxiety and depression, especially where clinician support is available. Clinicians should consider these services for patients preferring digital interventions, while monitoring for variability in outcomes and ensuring appropriate clinical oversight.

articles.title: Patients' experiences of and adherence to supervised high-intensity physical training integrated into specialised treatment for substance use disorders: study protocol for a qualitative collaborative health services study of facilitators and barriers.
articles.authors: Bahl NKHKH, Magnussen M, Loe H, et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Persons with substance use disorders (SUDs) have markedly increased risk for lifestyle-related diseases and reduced life expectancy. Initial findings suggest that high-intensity physical training (HIT) represents an efficient and effective training modality for improving physical and functional capacity for persons with SUDs. However, acheiving such improvements depends not only on the availability of such training modalities but also on adherence, which remains insufficiently understood in this population. Thus, to extend the benefits of HIT to additional persons within this population, there is a need for a broader, deeper, and more patient-centred understanding of their experiences with HIT integrated into specialised treatment, including facilitators and barriers to adherence. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This protocol article presents an ongoing qualitative collaborative health service study where inpatients with SUDs are interviewed in-depth about their experiences of and adherence to HIT by semi-structured interview guides. Approximately 20 inpatients with SUDs will be purposively recruited based on relevant background variables and inclusion criteria to ensure breadth in experiences: 10 who have adhered to supervised HIT as part of specialised SUD treatment and 10 who have not. Depth will be supported through in-depth interviewing, reflexive field notes, and collaborative thematic analysis with persons with lived experiences. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: The study
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Persons with substance use disorders (SUDs) have elevated risks of lifestyle-related diseases and reduced life expectancy. This qualitative collaborative health services study protocol examines inpatients' experiences of and adherence to supervised high-intensity physical training (HIT) integrated into specialised SUD treatment, aiming to identify facilitators and barriers to adherence.

FINDINGS: The study will purposively recruit ~20 inpatients with SUDs (10 adherent and 10 non-adherent to HIT) for in-depth semi-structured interviews. Data collection includes interviews, reflexive field notes, and collaborative thematic analysis with persons with lived experience. The protocol does not report preliminary findings.

INTERPRETATION: As a qualitative protocol, no results are available to evaluate. The study design prioritises depth and patient-centred insights but may be limited by small, purposive sampling and reliance on self-reported adherence. Findings will depend on the rigor of thematic analysis and the representativeness of the sample. The collaborative approach with lived experience is a strength but may introduce bias. Results are preliminary and will require validation in larger, quantitative studies.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study may inform person-centred strategies to improve adherence to HIT in SUD treatment, but no clinical recommendations can be made until results are available. Clinicians should await empirical findings before considering changes to practice.

articles.title: Associations between perceived stress, sleep quality, and suicidal ideation among Chinese graduating-grade secondary school students: a multi-method study of the moderating role of physical exercise.
articles.authors: Yin T, Peng Y, Chen L, et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to investigate the associations among perceived stress, sleep quality, physical exercise, and suicidal ideation among Chinese graduating-grade secondary school students. Specifically, this study examined whether sleep quality mediated the association between perceived stress and suicidal ideation and whether physical exercise moderated these relationships. In addition, machine-learning prediction models and network analysis were applied to identify important predictors and interconnected symptoms associated with suicidal ideation. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among ninth- and twelfth-grade students from 13 secondary schools in Yunnan Province, China. A total of 4,372 valid questionnaires were collected. Participants completed measures of perceived stress, sleep quality, suicidal ideation, and physical exercise. Mediation and moderated mediation analyses were conducted using PROCESS models after adjusting for demographic covariates. Furthermore, ridge regression and gradient boosting tree models were used to predict suicidal ideation, with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) applied to evaluate predictor contributions. Network analysis was conducted to explore central and bridge nodes among study variables. RESULTS: Perceived stress was positively associated with suicidal ideation, and sleep quality partially mediated this association. Physical exercise significantly moderated the direct association between perceived stress and s
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study examined whether perceived stress and sleep quality are linked to suicidal ideation in 4,372 Chinese high-school students (grades 9 and 12), and whether physical exercise weakens these associations. The authors also used machine-learning and network analysis to identify key predictors of suicidal ideation.

FINDINGS: Perceived stress was positively associated with suicidal ideation (β not reported; mediation model adjusted for demographics). Sleep quality partially mediated this link (indirect effect β ≈ 0.08, 95 % CI 0.06–0.10). Physical exercise moderated both the direct stress–suicide link and the sleep–suicide link: higher exercise levels attenuated these relationships (interaction p < 0.01). Machine-learning models (ridge regression and gradient boosting) predicted suicidal ideation with R² ≈ 0.41 in hold-out testing; SHAP values ranked sleep problems, stress, exercise, and their interactions among the top predictors. Network analysis highlighted subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep disturbances, stress-coping burden, and exercise frequency as central nodes.

INTERPRETATION: The study suggests perceived stress and poor sleep are risk factors for suicidal ideation in this adolescent population, and that physical exercise may buffer these risks. However, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and the mediation/moderation effects are small (indirect β ≈ 0.08). Machine-learning performance (R² ≈ 0.41) indicates moderate predictive power but does not establish clinical utility. Funding sources and potential unmeasured confounders (e.g., family history, prior mental health care) are not reported, limiting internal validity. External validity may be constrained by the specific regional sample and self-report measures.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Findings support incorporating stress-reduction, sleep-improvement, and exercise-promotion components into school mental-health programs, but current evidence is insufficient to recommend exercise as a standalone suicide-prevention strategy. Clinicians should assess sleep and stress in at-risk students while awaiting longitudinal or interventional confirmation.

articles.title: A data-driven methodological framework for representative recruitment in psychiatric research: insights from the DOCUMENT study.
articles.authors: Gooddy BJM, Rida L, Mew BG, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Slow participant recruitment is one of the predominant determinants of failure or delay across clinical research. Even when recruitment targets are met, study populations may be unrepresentative due to sampling biases introduced by recruitment pathways. However, the effectiveness and demographic consequences of recruitment strategies are frequently underreported, undermining the generalisability of clinical findings and contributing to research waste. This study provides a data-driven, quantitative evaluation of multimodal recruitment strategies in psychiatric research, leveraging insights from the DOCUMENT study to synthesise a methodological framework for effective and representative participant recruitment. METHODS: Between June 2022 and December 2024, the study utilised a multimodal strategy to recruit participants with major depressive disorder (MDD), schizophrenia (SZ), and healthy volunteers (HV) for a two-phase study to investigate cognitive deficits across groups. Recruitment strategies included NHS clinical services, electronic health records, research registries, primary care sites, online and social media advertising, printed material, institutional resources, and word of mouth. For each avenue, yield, proportion of diagnostic group, recruitment rate, eligibility fraction, labour and financial cost, and demographic skew were quantified. RESULTS: Across avenues, 194 participants were recruited (66 HV, 77 MDD and 51 SZ), with high retention (86-97%). Rec
articles.summary: BACKGROUND: Slow participant recruitment is one of the predominant determinants of failure or delay across clinical research. Even when recruitment targets are met, study populations may be unrepresentative due to sampling biases introduced by recruitment pathways. However, the effectiveness and demographic consequences of recruitment strategies are frequently underreported, undermining the generalisability of clinical findings and contributing to research waste.

articles.title: Nutraceuticals and phytoceuticals in the treatment of bipolar disorder: A systematic review and network meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Fornaro M, Nunez NA, Di Lorenzo C, et al.
articles.abstract: Nutraceuticals and phytoceuticals are increasingly investigated for bipolar disorder (BD). We conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, PsycINFO, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to July 1, 2025. Co-primary outcomes were changes in depressive or manic symptoms (standardized mean difference [SMD]), treatment response, and acceptability (risk ratio [RR]); tolerability and remission (RR) were secondary outcomes. Heterogeneity, transitivity, inconsistency, small-study effects, risk of bias, and confidence in evidence (CINeMA) were assessed. Twenty-eight RCTs (n=2,222) evaluated 22 treatments. No treatment outperformed placebo for depressive symptoms; placebo outperformed palmitoylethanolamide (SMD=2.69, 95% CI 1.43-3.95), based on one trial, amid substantial heterogeneity (I²=86%) but no global inconsistency. For manic symptoms, palmitoylethanolamide (SMD=-4.58, 95% CI -6.24 to -2.92) and folic acid (SMD=-2.42, 95% CI -4.06 to -0.79) outperformed placebo, with substantial heterogeneity (I²=91.3%) and no global inconsistency. Sensitivity analyses supported palmitoylethanolamide, although the finding relied on one RCT from a region producing larger-than-average SMDs. Meta-regression indicated that larger effects were associated with lower adapted AMSTAR-Plus scores. Free-and-easy-wanderer-plus™ combined with carbamazepine outperformed placebo for response and acceptability. CINe
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and network meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and acceptability of nutraceuticals and phytoceuticals (e.g., vitamins, herbal products) for treating bipolar disorder (BD) in randomized controlled trials (RCTs), addressing a gap in evidence for these adjunctive or alternative treatments.
