FINDINGS: Twenty-eight RCTs (n=2,222) assessed 22 treatments. No nutraceutical outperformed placebo for depressive symptoms; placebo outperformed palmitoylethanolamide (SMD=2.69, 95% CI 1.43–3.95) in one trial with high heterogeneity (I²=86%). For manic symptoms, palmitoylethanolamide (SMD=-4.58, 95% CI -6.24 to -2.92) and folic acid (SMD=-2.42, 95% CI -4.06 to -0.79) outperformed placebo, but with substantial heterogeneity (I²=91.3%). Only one RCT supported palmitoylethanolamide’s effect, and meta-regression linked larger effects to lower methodological quality (AMSTAR-Plus scores). Confidence in evidence (CINeMA) was predominantly low or very low.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak, with high heterogeneity, reliance on single small trials, and low methodological quality ratings. The statistically significant findings for manic symptoms are not robust due to inconsistency, small sample sizes, and potential bias. No treatment can be recommended based on current data; further high-quality RCTs are urgently needed.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should not use nutraceuticals or phytoceuticals as evidence-based treatments for acute bipolar depression or mania. Patients using these products should be monitored closely, and clinicians should discuss the lack of robust evidence supporting their efficacy.

articles.title: Pharmacological interventions for alcohol use disorder on quality of life: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.authors: Fluyau D, Revadigar N, Kim P
articles.abstract: AIMS: Quality of life (QoL), a critical factor for sustaining recovery from alcohol use disorder (AUD), has been examined as an AUD-related outcome in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated pharmacotherapy for AUD. This review evaluates the efficacy of this therapy in improving mental and physical health-related QoL. METHODS: RCTs were identified across seven databases. Study quality was evaluated using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials version 2. A systematic review with meta-analysis was conducted. The review adhered to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis guidelines and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261277890). RESULTS: Eighteen RCTs with 4376 participants were evaluated. Naltrexone was linked to improvements in both mental QoL (d = 0.30, 95% CI: 0.08-0.52) and physical QoL (d = 0.16, 95% CI: 0.01-0.31). Nalmefene improved physical QoL (d = 0.13, 95% CI: 0.02-0.25) but not mental QoL (d = 0.18, 95% CI: -0.004 to 0.354). Topiramate showed no improvement in either domain. However, further analysis indicated that topiramate was associated with a small improvement in physical QoL, which could correlate with a reduced percentage of heavy drinking days. Interpret these findings with caution. Acamprosate, sertraline, and psilocybin were associated with improved mental or physical QoL, whereas ketamine, varenicline, levetiracetam XR, and quetiapine were not. Interpretation is limited to single trials-no eligible RC
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 randomized controlled trials (n=4376) examined whether pharmacotherapies for alcohol use disorder (AUD) improve mental and physical quality of life (QoL), a key outcome for sustaining recovery.

FINDINGS: Naltrexone improved both mental QoL (d=0.30, 95% CI 0.08–0.52) and physical QoL (d=0.16, 95% CI 0.01–0.31). Nalmefene improved physical QoL (d=0.13, 95% CI 0.02–0.25) but not mental QoL (d=0.18, 95% CI –0.004 to 0.354). Topiramate showed no clear benefit, though a post-hoc analysis suggested a small physical QoL gain linked to reduced heavy drinking. Evidence for other agents (acamprosate, sertraline, psilocybin) was based on single trials.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate in size but heterogeneous, with small effect sizes and limited data for many drugs. Risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane RoB 2, but selective reporting and heterogeneity limit certainty. Statistically significant effects do not necessarily translate into clinically meaningful improvements in daily functioning or well-being.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current pharmacotherapies may offer modest QoL benefits for some patients with AUD, but routine QoL monitoring is not yet supported by robust evidence. Clinicians should individualize treatment and consider QoL outcomes alongside traditional measures like abstinence or relapse rates.

articles.title: Psychosocial interventions for military personnel with PTSD: protocol of a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Angelakis I, Donegan S, Hughes K, et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a serious mental health condition. It may develop following exposure to an extremely threatening event. Military personnel face an increased likelihood of developing PTSD because they sometimes bring experiences of difficult events from before they joined the military and because they have higher odds of being exposed to potentially traumatic events during service. To support the mental health of military personnel, several psychological interventions have been developed to help them manage PTSD symptoms. Although there is a lot of research demonstrating how well these interventions work, we do not know how the different interventions (eg, trauma-informed therapy, cognitive-behavioural therapy) compare. Because many of these interventions include more than one type of treatment (eg, behavioural activation), we do not know which specific component works best. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: To explore these questions, we will identify previous studies that have examined interventions for PTSD in military personnel. We will then use network meta-analysis methods to make comparisons between all interventions, including some that have never been compared against each other in previous studies, to identify the best treatments. We also aim to identify which individual components are effective, even when delivered in combination. We will work with people with lived experiences, researchers, and mental health professionals to guide the pro
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The review asks which psychosocial interventions are most effective for military personnel with PTSD and how their components compare, using a planned network meta-analysis of existing trials. This matters because PTSD is common in this population and multiple therapies exist but head-to-head evidence is sparse.

FINDINGS: The protocol describes a systematic review followed by network meta-analysis to compare all psychological interventions for PTSD in current and former military personnel. It will also examine which specific treatment components drive benefit when delivered in combination. The team will involve lived-experience advisors, clinicians and researchers throughout.

INTERPRETATION: Because this is a protocol rather than completed analyses, no effect sizes, confidence intervals or p-values are yet available. The planned methods (network meta-analysis) can rank treatments even when they have never been directly compared, but the eventual certainty of the evidence will depend on the number and quality of included studies, their comparators and risk of bias. Involvement of stakeholders is a strength that may improve relevance to practice.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this protocol signals that updated comparative evidence is coming; clinicians should await the final results before changing practice.

articles.title: Effects of Benzodiazepines on Heart Failure Outcomes and Adverse Events: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.authors: Huang YS, Prawesti GN, Chiang YC, et al.
articles.abstract: The effects of benzodiazepines (BZDs) for insomnia on heart failure (HF) remain unclear, particularly among high-risk populations. Relevant studies were retrieved by searching seven databases from inception to August 7, 2025. Hazard ratios (HRs) or risk ratios estimated for related HF outcomes were extracted. Meta-analyses were conducted using a random-effects model, and study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Eleven studies met the inclusion criteria, with follow-up durations ranging from 180 days to 15 years. The meta-analysis demonstrated that BZD use was associated with increased risks of HF incidence (HR = 1.41, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.16-1.72) and HF hospitalization (HR = 1.29, 95% CI 1.01-1.65) compared to non-use. BZD use also suggested an increased risk of HF hospitalization and rehospitalization compared to antipsychotics, z-drugs, and suvorexant. Benzodiazepine use was associated with an increased risk of HF-related outcomes. Since most of the included studies were observational, these findings indicate associations rather than causal relationships. BZDs should be used with caution among populations at risk of HF when treating insomnia.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether benzodiazepine (BZD) use for insomnia is associated with adverse heart failure (HF) outcomes in high-risk populations. Eleven observational studies were included, with follow-up ranging from 180 days to 15 years.

FINDINGS: Benzodiazepine use was associated with increased risks of HF incidence (HR = 1.41, 95% CI 1.16–1.72) and HF hospitalization (HR = 1.29, 95% CI 1.01–1.65) compared to non-use. It also showed higher HF hospitalization risk than antipsychotics, z-drugs, and suvorexant. All included studies were observational, limiting causal inference.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests an association between BZD use and worse HF outcomes, but causality cannot be established due to the observational design. Confounding by indication (e.g., insomnia itself may worsen HF outcomes) and lack of randomized data weaken conclusions. The effect sizes are modest and may not translate to clinically meaningful differences in all patients.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Caution is warranted when prescribing BZDs to patients with or at risk of HF, but insomnia management should not be withheld without considering alternatives. Further research—particularly randomized or well-controlled studies—is needed to clarify causality and guide safer prescribing.

articles.title: Efficacy of a Prescription-Based Mobile Digital Therapeutic as an Adjunct to Pharmacotherapy for the Acute Phase of Panic Disorder: Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.authors: Ko Y, Kim J, Park S, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Although pharmacotherapy is the primary treatment for patients with acute-phase panic disorder, its incomplete efficacy causes them to experience frequent panic attacks and severe anticipatory anxiety for a considerable period. A prescription-based mobile digital therapeutic (DTx) that integrates self-guided cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), real-time symptom management, and lifestyle tracking can be used as an adjunct to pharmacotherapy for these patients, helping them achieve rapid symptom recovery. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of this adjunctive DTx in alleviating symptoms in patients with acute-phase panic disorder. METHODS: In total, 66 acute-phase patients experiencing frequent panic attacks were recruited from 6 institutions and randomly divided into a group receiving pharmacotherapy combined with DTx or pharmacotherapy alone, participating in an 8-week multicenter single-blind trial. The DTx app included 3 major services: training service consisting of structured CBT modules, companion service of just-in-time modules for coping with panic attacks, and care service providing daily self-management tracking tools. The self-report scales used as efficacy indicators were administered via paper questionnaires during a total of 4 visits at baseline, week 2, week 4, and week 8. The primary end point, the change in the Panic Disorder Severity Scale-Self Report (PDSS-SR) score, and the secondary end points, such as changes in overall anxiet
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This multicenter, single-blind RCT (n=61 completers) tested whether adding a prescription-based mobile digital therapeutic (DTx) to pharmacotherapy improves acute-phase panic disorder symptoms (frequent panic attacks) over 8 weeks. The DTx combined structured CBT modules, just-in-time panic coping, and daily tracking.

FINDINGS: The DTx group achieved a 40.29% (SD 26.68%) reduction in PDSS-SR scores versus 17.61% (SD 30.37%) in controls at week 8 (P=.007). Benefits emerged early (week 2: 26.66% vs 11.05%; P=.02). Responder rate (≥40% PDSS-SR reduction) was higher with DTx (53.12% vs 17.24%; P=.007). Adherence averaged 78.12%; no difference between responders/nonresponders.

INTERPRETATION: The trial suggests adjunctive DTx yields statistically significant and clinically detectable improvements in panic severity and related cognitions, with early onset and sustained effects. Strengths include RCT design, objective adherence metrics, and clinically meaningful responder thresholds. Limitations include small sample, single-blind design (assessors unblinded), short 8-week horizon, and lack of long-term follow-up. Funding sources and adverse events were not reported in the abstract.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: DTx could be considered as a practical adjunct to pharmacotherapy for acute-phase panic disorder, particularly where access to CBT is limited. Clinicians should monitor adherence and integrate app-generated data into routine care, while awaiting replication and longer-term outcomes.

articles.title: Association between cortisol levels and psychosis in at-risk and diagnosed individuals: protocol for a systematic review.
articles.authors: Mnyaka-Dawethe P, Musarurwa HT, Mahamba A, et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Psychosis poses a significant global health challenge, with growing evidence linking dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and altered cortisol levels to its onset and progression. This systematic review protocol aims to synthesise case-control and cohort studies to achieve two main objectives: to evaluate the association between cortisol levels and psychosis, and to examine cortisol levels in individuals at risk of developing psychosis. The review will consolidate existing empirical evidence on the relationship between cortisol levels and psychosis in both at-risk populations and diagnosed patients. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: Electronic searches will be conducted in academic databases, including Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus, Embase and PsycINFO, using a PECO (Population, Exposure, Comparator, Outcome) framework. A search strategy will be developed in Web of Science and adapted for other databases. Additionally, a search will be performed on Google Scholar, reviewing the first 1000 publications to crosscheck findings. The initial PECO-derived search will use Medical Subject Headings terms: ('Cortisol' OR 'Hydrocortisone') AND ('Psychosis' OR 'Psychotic disorders' OR 'Schizophrenia') AND ('HPA axis' OR 'Stress response') AND ('Clinical high risk' OR 'Prodromal' OR 'Ultra-high risk'), along with phrases identified from related literature. The review will focus on case-control and cohort studies reporting original research on individuals at ri
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This is a protocol for a systematic review examining whether cortisol levels (a marker of HPA-axis dysregulation) are associated with psychosis in at-risk populations and in patients with diagnosed psychotic disorders. The review will include case-control and cohort studies to clarify the temporal and cross-sectional links between cortisol and psychosis.

FINDINGS: The protocol specifies comprehensive searches across five databases plus Google Scholar, inclusion of case-control and cohort designs, and dual risk-of-bias assessment with the Joanna Briggs Institute tool and GRADE. No results are reported yet; the review is ongoing and registered in PROSPERO.

INTERPRETATION: Because this is a protocol, no empirical findings are available. The planned methodology appears rigorous, but the ultimate strength of the evidence will depend on the quality and heterogeneity of the included studies. Until results are published, clinical implications remain uncertain.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this protocol does not change practice. Clinicians should await the completed review to see whether cortisol measurement could aid risk stratification or monitoring in psychosis.

articles.title: Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR) for ICU-related psychological distress among adult intensive care survivors: a scoping review.
articles.authors: Satkunam S, Dimitriou I, Shaikh M
articles.abstract: Background: Psychological morbidity is common following admission to adult intensive care units (ICUs), with many patients experiencing post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety, and depression as part of post-intensive care syndrome. Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR) is an established trauma-focused psychological therapy; however, its evidence base within critical care populations remains emerging.Objectives: This scoping review aimed to map the extent, characteristics, and findings of the available literature on the use of EMDR for ICU-related psychological distress.Methods: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The review aimed to systematically identify and synthesise evidence relating to the application and reported outcomes of EMDR in ICU survivors.Results: Seven publications representing six independent study populations were included. Participants included adult ICU patients experiencing PTSD symptoms, delirium-related psychological disturbances, and COVID-19-related distress. EMDR was delivered using either standard protocols or the Recent Traumatic Episode Protocol (R-TEP). Across the evidence base, EMDR was associated with reductions in trauma-related distress, although evidence for improvements in anxiety and depression was less consistent. Where qualitative data were available, participants additionally reported improved integration and proces
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Post-intensive care syndrome includes PTSD, anxiety, and depression after adult ICU admission. EMDR is a trauma-focused therapy, but its evidence in ICU survivors is emerging. This scoping review mapped the literature on EMDR for ICU-related psychological distress.

FINDINGS: Seven publications (six independent samples) were included; participants were adults with ICU-related PTSD symptoms, delirium-related disturbances, or COVID-19 distress. EMDR (standard or R-TEP) was associated with reductions in trauma-related distress; improvements in anxiety/depression were less consistent. Qualitative reports noted better integration of ICU experiences. Methodological heterogeneity, small samples, overlapping cohorts, and limited controlled data constrain conclusions.

INTERPRETATION: Confidence in the evidence is low due to design limitations and small, heterogeneous samples. No controlled trials were identified, so effectiveness remains unproven. The signal of benefit is plausible but preliminary; larger RCTs with standardised outcomes and longer follow-up are needed before EMDR can be recommended routinely in ICU survivors.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: EMDR cannot yet be considered an evidence-based treatment for ICU-related psychological distress. Clinicians may consider it cautiously in selected cases, but should prioritise established trauma-focused therapies with stronger evidence bases and monitor outcomes closely.

articles.title: Communication strategies in medical imaging departments for autistic patients. A systematic review exploring person-centred care practices.
articles.authors: Ukaji N, Malamateniou C, Potts B, et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Communication barriers are one of the major contributors to inaccessible healthcare for autistic people. Literature highlights the need for autism-informed care in medical imaging settings, but evidence on communication interventions in imaging is limited. This review aimed to synthesise communication interventions used in imaging departments to support autistic service users' accessibility to imaging. METHODS: The protocol was registered on PROSPERO and followed PRISMA guidelines. Literature searches were performed across six databases using keywords such as "medical imag∗", "communication strateg∗", "Autis∗", and "improv∗ access∗". In total, 5531 articles were screened by title and abstract, with 26 full-text articles reviewed against pre-determined eligibility criteria. Six studies were included in the review. Risk of bias was assessed using relevant CASP tools. Studies were synthesised using the Pillar Integration Process. RESULTS: Most interventions were explored in an MRI setting (n = 3) and paediatric population (n = 5). Common interventions included picture schedules, at-home procedural videos, and iPad app social scripts. Three central themes were developed: 1) employing flexible approaches to communication can foster acceptance; 2) optimising communication can improve patients/caregivers' imaging experience, and 3) defining positive outcomes requires a balance of patients' perspectives and quantitative results. CONCLUSION: The findings suggest that fle
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (PROSPERO-registered, PRISMA-guided) synthesised six studies on communication interventions in medical imaging departments to improve accessibility for autistic patients, primarily in MRI and paediatric settings.

FINDINGS: Five of six studies were paediatric; three focused on MRI. Interventions included picture schedules, at-home procedural videos, and iPad social scripts. Qualitative synthesis identified three themes: flexible communication fosters acceptance, optimised communication improves experience and scan completion, and outcomes should balance patient perspectives with quantitative metrics.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small (n=6), heterogeneous, and at high risk of bias; most studies are paediatric and MRI-focused, limiting generalisability to adults or other imaging modalities. The reported improvements in experience and completion rates are plausible but not quantified with effect sizes or confidence intervals, so clinical significance remains uncertain. The review’s strength lies in its structured synthesis and identification of research gaps rather than definitive effect estimates.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings support trialling flexible, multimodal communication strategies in imaging departments for autistic patients, especially children undergoing MRI, while awaiting higher-quality trials that measure both patient-reported and objective outcomes.

articles.title: A Problem-Solving Therapy With Apple Watch Support for College Students With Alcohol Use Disorder Symptoms: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.authors: Hallihan H, Lee S, Adomah R, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) involves an impaired ability to stop or control alcohol use despite adverse consequences and represents a major public health problem. While AUD is most prevalent among college students, integrated evidence-based treatments for this population are lacking. OBJECTIVE: The objectives of our study were to test the feasibility and acceptability of a newly developed behavioral intervention, problem-solving therapy and Apple Watch (PST-APPLE), and to preliminarily investigate the effectiveness of PST-APPLE among college students with symptoms of AUD. METHODS: Participants were recruited through online advertising and on campus at universities in the Chicago area between May and September 2024. They were randomized in a 1:1 ratio using block randomization to the intervention group (PST-APPLE: n=12 individuals) or the control group (education-only: n=14 individuals), with the data analyst blinded to treatment assignment. Participants in the intervention group completed 12 weeks of the PST-APPLE intervention, delivered remotely via Zoom videoconferencing and interactions with the Apple Watch. Participants in the control group were asked to watch a 20-minute abstinence-motivation video and then participate in a 30-minute group discussion via Zoom. All participants completed follow-up assessments at 3 months. Outcomes included alcohol-related problems (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test [AUDIT] and Rutgers Alcohol Problem Index [RAPI]) and d
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study tested a novel, remote problem-solving therapy augmented by an Apple Watch (PST-APPLE) versus education-only control in college students with alcohol use disorder (AUD) symptoms. It aimed to assess feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary effectiveness on alcohol-related outcomes and drinking motives.

FINDINGS: Twenty-six students (mean age 22.5 years) were randomized 1:1. At 3 months, the intervention group showed reductions in AUDIT (mean difference −4.70, 95% CI −8.69 to −0.70) and in DMQR social (−0.85, 95% CI −1.51 to −0.18) and enhancement (−0.75, 95% CI −1.47 to −0.04) drinking motives versus control. Within-group paired t-tests also indicated reductions in AUDIT and RAPI scores post-intervention.

INTERPRETATION: This pilot RCT suggests PST-APPLE is feasible and acceptable, with small-to-moderate baseline-adjusted effects on alcohol misuse and drinking motives. However, the sample is tiny, not powered for efficacy, and lacks blinding of participants and therapists; effect sizes may be overestimated. Long-term outcomes and generalizability to broader student populations remain unknown.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence is insufficient to change practice; PST-APPLE may be promising for digitally literate college students, but larger, adequately powered trials with longer follow-up are needed before recommending adoption.

articles.title: Antidepressant maintenance versus active monitoring after depression remission: a decision analysis and framework linking recurrence probability and patient preferences.
articles.authors: Meyerson WU, Cai T, Smoller JW
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: When deciding on antidepressant maintenance with clinicians, remitted patients must weigh the burdens of continued use against the benefit of less time depressed. This benefit is often inferred qualitatively from relapse-frequency data, even though expected time depressed also depends on episode duration, antidepressant re-initiation, and how evidence from highly recurrent populations applies to patients with fewer prior episodes. METHODS: We developed a health-state transition model to combine evidence on recurrence, episode duration, re-initiation, and treatment effects into expected time depressed and time taking antidepressants under maintenance versus active monitoring. Adults in remission were simulated for 5 years across groups based on depression history. We summarized the trade-off as additional antidepressant use required to avert 1 month of depression. The decision framework links this estimate to patient preferences by comparing required with acceptable use, allowing patients who expect greater consequences of relapse or experience fewer treatment burdens to consider more antidepressant use acceptable. RESULTS: Maintenance efficiency varied substantially with recurrence history. Each month of depression averted required 1.5 additional years of antidepressant use among patients with 4-5 prior episodes; 2.8 years with 2-3 prior episodes, 5.1 years after one moderate-to-severe episode, and 11.8 years after one mild episode. When these trade-offs are accep
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This decision-analysis model compared long-term outcomes of antidepressant maintenance therapy versus active monitoring after remission from major depressive disorder (MDD), quantifying the trade-off between reduced depression recurrence and increased antidepressant exposure across patients with varying prior episode histories.

FINDINGS: Over a 5-year horizon, the model estimated that averting one month of depression required 1.5 additional years of antidepressant use in patients with 4–5 prior episodes, 2.8 years with 2–3 episodes, 5.1 years after one moderate-to-severe episode, and 11.8 years after one mild episode. The trade-off ratio increased steeply with fewer prior episodes, reflecting lower baseline recurrence risk.

INTERPRETATION: The study provides a transparent framework linking recurrence probability, treatment burden, and patient preferences, but relies on modeling assumptions rather than empirical data. The wide variation in trade-off ratios highlights the need for individualized risk–benefit assessment. The model’s validity depends on the accuracy of input parameters (e.g., recurrence rates, episode duration) and may not generalize to settings with different treatment practices or patient populations.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This model can guide shared decision-making by translating abstract relapse data into concrete trade-offs, helping clinicians and patients weigh maintenance therapy against active monitoring based on episode history and personal values. However, it should be used cautiously until validated in real-world cohorts.

articles.title: Addiction management and rehabilitation programs in Saudi Arabia: a scoping review of current practices and opportunities for healthcare technology integration.
articles.authors: Baklola M, Terra M, Al-Azab M, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Substance use disorders (SUDs) represent a growing public health challenge in Saudi Arabia despite strict legal and social controls. Addiction management is primarily delivered through centralized inpatient and residential rehabilitation programs; however, the available evidence remains fragmented, and opportunities for healthcare technology integration have not been comprehensively synthesized. METHODS: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines to map addiction management and rehabilitation programs in Saudi Arabia and identify opportunities for healthcare technology integration. Comprehensive searches were performed across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and supplementary sources from database inception to October 2025. Original empirical studies evaluating addiction treatment, rehabilitation, or aftercare services in Saudi Arabia were included. Data were systematically charted and synthesized using a descriptive thematic narrative approach. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). RESULTS: Nine studies published between 1995 and 2024 met the inclusion criteria. The evidence demonstrated a progressive evolution from predominantly detoxification-focused services toward multidisciplinary rehabilitation models incorporating therapeutic communities and structured aftercare. Despite these advances, long-term retention remained limited, relapse and hospital readmission were co
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review maps current addiction management and rehabilitation programs in Saudi Arabia and explores opportunities for healthcare technology integration, addressing fragmented evidence and evolving service models in a context with strict legal and social controls.

FINDINGS: Nine studies (1995–2024) showed a shift from detoxification-focused care to multidisciplinary rehabilitation with therapeutic communities and aftercare, but long-term retention was poor, relapse and readmission were common, and community-based services were underused. Social factors like unemployment and family conflict consistently impacted outcomes. Healthcare technology use was minimal, with no studies on telehealth, mobile apps, remote monitoring, or AI-supported care. Methodological quality was moderate overall, with only three high-quality studies.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited and heterogeneous, with moderate methodological quality and no high-quality evaluations of digital interventions. While service evolution is evident, persistent gaps in long-term support and community integration undermine effectiveness. The absence of technology-based studies highlights a major research and implementation gap rather than proven ineffectiveness.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice remains largely traditional, with limited integration of digital tools despite potential benefits. Clinicians should be cautious about extrapolating benefits from other settings; more robust, locally relevant research is needed before advocating widespread adoption of healthcare technologies in Saudi addiction care.

articles.title: Ketamine Use Disorder and Entrenchment of Delusional Beliefs: A Case Report.
articles.authors: Yang SS, Goud R, Weleff J
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ketamine has gained increasing attention for its therapeutic potential, yet concerns remain regarding its misuse and the associated complications of its use. Ketamine use and ketamine use disorder can induce psychotic symptoms, but the persistence of such symptoms with chronic use and effective treatment of these symptoms is poorly characterized. Although case reports of ketamine use and medical and psychiatric consequences exist in the literature, there is limited evidence regarding the treatment of ketamine use disorder (KUD). CASE SUMMARY: We present the case of a 36-year-old man who developed persistent delusional beliefs and medical complications over 2 years of heavy, chronic ketamine use. In the absence of any prior psychiatric diagnoses other than alcohol use disorder, he met DSM-5-TR criteria for KUD. His beliefs were primarily grandiose and hyper-religious in content, incorporating fringe online content. Although there was a limited impact on his functioning, his beliefs were maintained in delusional intensity. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient. CONCLUSIONS: This case report illustrates a manifestation of enduring delusional beliefs in the setting of chronic ketamine use and other important medical sequelae of its use. Limited literature exists concerning the treatment of ketamine use disorder or related psychotic symptoms, and there is a need for standardized treatment guidelines so interventions may be provided promptly to prevent
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The case report examines a 36-year-old man with ketamine use disorder (KUD) who developed persistent delusional beliefs over 2 years of heavy ketamine use, highlighting the limited evidence on treating KUD and associated psychotic symptoms.

FINDINGS: The patient met DSM-5-TR criteria for KUD with no prior psychiatric diagnoses (other than alcohol use disorder). His delusions were grandiose and hyper-religious, maintained at delusional intensity despite limited functional impact. No quantitative outcomes (e.g., symptom scales) were reported.

INTERPRETATION: This is a single case report with no comparator, making it impossible to infer causality or generalizability. The lack of standardized treatment data underscores the preliminary nature of the evidence. The clinical significance of the delusions remains unclear due to the absence of functional impairment metrics.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The case underscores the need for vigilance regarding psychotic symptoms in chronic ketamine users but does not inform treatment decisions due to its anecdotal nature. Further research is required to guide management of KUD and its psychiatric sequelae.

articles.title: Towards risk-stratified clozapine haematological monitoring: lessons from Hong Kong and Japan.
articles.authors: Nagamine T

articles.title: From discovery to proof: a Translation Evidence Map for precision psychiatry.
articles.authors: Baune BT
articles.abstract: Precision psychiatry aims to improve individual-patient decisions by measuring clinically meaningful heterogeneity, not by privileging any one data type, biomarker, or analytical method. This Personal View proposes a Translation Evidence Map that stages claims, from Level 0 (defined use case or discovery-positioning statement) to Level 6 (post-deployment monitoring), linked to measurement reliability, generalisable inference, decision value, safe delivery, and proportionality to risk, clinical need, and inaction. The Map does not replace Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE), biomarker qualification, prediction-model, regulatory, or roadmap frameworks; it identifies the highest defensible claim across components of unequal maturity and the next evidence step for compound precision claims. The Personal View discusses examples spanning inflammatory and circuit-based depression stratification, psychosis relapse monitoring, and suicidality monitoring, illustrating how the Map makes claim maturity, stopping points, stakeholder roles, and trade-offs important to patients explicit.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This Personal View proposes a Translation Evidence Map (TEM) to stage claims in precision psychiatry from discovery (Level 0) to post-deployment monitoring (Level 6), aiming to improve individual-patient decisions by quantifying clinically meaningful heterogeneity across biomarkers, data types, and analytical methods.

FINDINGS: The TEM framework evaluates claims based on measurement reliability, generalisable inference, decision value, safe delivery, and proportionality to risk/clinical need/inaction. Examples include inflammatory and circuit-based depression stratification, psychosis relapse monitoring, and suicidality monitoring. The Map does not replace existing frameworks (e.g., GRADE, biomarker qualification) but identifies the highest defensible claim and next evidence steps for compound precision claims.

INTERPRETATION: The TEM provides a structured approach to assess the maturity of precision psychiatry claims, emphasizing transparency in evidence progression and stakeholder roles. However, as a conceptual framework, it lacks empirical validation or quantitative outcomes. Its utility depends on integration with existing regulatory and clinical pathways, and its external validity remains untested in routine care.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This framework may guide clinicians in evaluating emerging precision psychiatry tools but does not yet offer actionable clinical recommendations. Clinicians should await validation studies and regulatory approvals before adopting such methods.

articles.title: Subacute effects of ketamine on neural correlates of reward processing.
articles.authors: Briem E, Stöhrmann P, Dörl G, et al.
articles.abstract: Ketamine induces a sequence of temporally distinct effects on brain function, yet its impact on reward processing beyond the acute post-administration phase remains unclear. In this single-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study, 28 healthy participants received 0.5 mg/kg racemic ketamine or placebo via a 40 min intravenous infusion. Functional magnetic resonance imaging was acquired approximately 5 h post-infusion during the Monetary Incentive Delay (MID) task, targeting the subacute phase after resolution of acute dissociative effects. Plasma concentrations of ketamine and norketamine were obtained for pharmacokinetic modeling and area under the curve estimation. At 5 h post-administration, ketamine did not significantly modulate brain activation during the MID task in either ROI-based or whole-brain analyses, despite measurable subjective drug effects. Pharmacokinetic modeling yielded ketamine and norketamine concentration-time profiles consistent with expected pharmacokinetic patterns, however, neither individual drug exposure nor psychometric measures showed robust associations with MID task-related neural activation. These findings suggest an absence of detectable task-evoked effects under the present methodological conditions. When considered alongside prior work, they are consistent with the possibility that ketamine's effects on reward circuitry are time-sensitive and may be more prominent during the acute post-administration phase or in clinical populations with
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether ketamine, given to healthy volunteers, alters brain reward processing five hours after infusion (subacute phase) using fMRI during a reward task. The question matters because ketamine’s antidepressant effects may involve reward circuitry, but prior work focused mainly on acute effects. This was a single-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study in 28 healthy adults.

FINDINGS: At 5 hours post-infusion, ketamine did not significantly change brain activation during the Monetary Incentive Delay task in either region-of-interest or whole-brain analyses. Plasma ketamine and norketamine levels confirmed expected pharmacokinetics, but neither drug exposure nor subjective effects correlated robustly with neural activation. No effect sizes or p-values are reported in the abstract.

INTERPRETATION: The single-blind, crossover design and healthy volunteer sample limit internal validity; blinding may have been compromised by ketamine’s subjective effects. The absence of detectable changes could reflect true lack of subacute reward-circuit modulation or insufficient power to detect small effects. The study cannot address whether effects would appear in patients with depression or anhedonia, where reward circuitry may be more sensitive. Overall, the evidence is preliminary and does not support subacute modulation of reward processing in healthy individuals under these methods.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify changing practice regarding ketamine’s use for reward-related symptoms. Clinicians should note that any antidepressant benefits likely involve mechanisms beyond subacute normalization of reward-task activation in healthy brains.

articles.title: Unlocking School Nurses' Capacity for Suicide Risk Screening: Implications for Multitiered System of Supports.
articles.authors: Pestaner MC, Reich JC, Mechling BM, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: School nurses play an important role in identifying students at risk for suicide, yet their screening methods remain understudied. The purpose of this study was to examine the methods of suicide risk screening used by school nurses, evaluate how district-level integration of school nurses into suicide prevention policies is associated with screening methods, and assess associations between screening methods, self-efficacy, and referral-making. METHODS: Data were derived from a national cross-sectional, correlational study examining school nurses' roles in youth suicide prevention (N = 578). RESULTS: School nurses whose responsibilities were explicitly defined in district suicide prevention policies were more likely to use standardized screening questions. In a separate analysis, use of standardized screening questions was indirectly associated with a greater number of referrals to community-based services through higher screening self-efficacy. IMPLICATIONS FOR SCHOOL HEALTH POLICY, PRACTICE, AND EQUITY: District-level integration of school nurses into suicide prevention policies may strengthen school nurses' capacity to identify and refer students at risk. CONCLUSIONS: Within a multitiered system of supports (MTSS) framework, integrating school nurses into suicide prevention efforts may strengthen coordinated, equitable approaches to identifying and responding to students at risk for suicide.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study investigated how school nurses screen students for suicide risk and whether district-level suicide prevention policies influence their screening methods, self-efficacy, and referral rates. It was a national cross-sectional survey (N = 578) examining school nurses' roles in youth suicide prevention.

FINDINGS: School nurses whose roles were explicitly defined in district suicide prevention policies were more likely to use standardized screening questions. Use of standardized screening was indirectly associated with a higher number of referrals to community services, mediated by increased screening self-efficacy.

INTERPRETATION: The cross-sectional design limits causal inference; associations do not prove that policy integration improves screening or referrals. The mediation by self-efficacy suggests a plausible mechanism, but unmeasured confounders (e.g., school resources, nurse training) could influence results. The study highlights a potential policy lever but requires longitudinal or experimental validation to confirm impact.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: If confirmed, integrating school nurses into formal suicide prevention policies could enhance standardized screening and referral practices, but current evidence is preliminary and does not yet mandate practice changes.

articles.title: Law Enforcement Officers and Autism Stigma: Changes Associated With Autism Training.
articles.authors: Gardner L, Powell L, Montoya K, et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Law enforcement officers (LEOs) frequently interact with autistic individuals, often without autism-specific training. Limited training may contribute to stigmatizing attitudes that influence these encounters. This study evaluated changes in LEOs' autism stigma toward autistic individuals following autism training. METHODS: A nonrandomized pre-post intervention design examined changes in autism stigma among 438 LEOs who attended autism training in California or Florida. Officers completed either a 2-h or 4-h training, with the California program including additional virtual reality training. Autism stigma was assessed before and after training using a validated measure. RESULTS: Overall autism stigma decreased significantly following training. For both samples, female officers reported higher neurodiversity affirming attitudes than male officers before either training. Male officers showed significant increases in neurodiversity affirming attitudes in the California sample. For the Florida sample, officers with a relationship to an autistic person reported higher neurodiversity affirming attitudes; officers without a relationship reported greater increases in neurodiversity affirming attitudes. Item-level analyses showed both positive and unexpected changes with increased neurodiversity-affirming attitudes alongside greater endorsement of normative behavioral expectations and reduced trust in information provided by autistic individuals. CONCLUSIONS: Autism-specific
articles.summary: PURPOSE: Law enforcement officers (LEOs) frequently interact with autistic individuals, often without autism-specific training. Limited training may contribute to stigmatizing attitudes that influence these encounters. This study evaluated changes in LEOs' autism stigma toward autistic individuals following autism training. METHODS: A nonrandomized pre-post intervention design examined changes in autism stigma among 438 LEOs who attended autism training in California or Florida.

articles.title: EVIDENCE-BASED PHARMACOTHERAPY FOR ANXIETY DISORDERS COMORBID WITH PTSD: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW.
articles.authors: Bashkirova L, Romanova I, Yatsynovych V, et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of pharmacological interventions for anxiety outcomes in adults with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), including confirmed comorbid anxiety disorders and clinically significant anxiety symptoms. MATERIAL AND METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched for randomized controlled trials and prospective cohort studies published from 2000 to 2025. Risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane tools, and certainty of evidence with GRADE. RESULTS: Twenty-two studies involving 2,708 participants were included. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) reduced anxiety symptoms (standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.46; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.62 to -0.30; moderate certainty) and PTSD symptoms (SMD -0.43; 95% CI -0.58 to -0.28; moderate certainty). However, applicability to formally diagnosed comorbid anxiety disorders was limited by inconsistent diagnostic reporting. Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduced anxiety symptoms (SMD -0.38; 95% CI -0.55 to -0.21; low certainty), whereas evidence for PTSD outcomes was less certain. Atypical antipsychotics showed possible benefit but increased discontinuation due to adverse events (RR 2.14; 95% CI 1.43 to 3.21). CONCLUSIONS: SSRIs provide moderate-certainty evidence for reducing anxiety outcomes in PTSD populations. Evidence for confirmed comorbid anxiety disorders remains limited. SNRIs and atypica
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review with GRADE assessment evaluated pharmacological treatments for anxiety symptoms in adults with PTSD, including those with comorbid anxiety disorders or clinically significant anxiety, synthesizing RCTs and prospective cohorts from 2000–2025.

FINDINGS: Across 22 studies (n=2,708), SSRIs reduced anxiety symptoms (SMD −0.46, 95% CI −0.62 to −0.30; moderate certainty) and PTSD symptoms (SMD −0.43, 95% CI −0.58 to −0.28; moderate certainty). SNRIs reduced anxiety symptoms (SMD −0.38, 95% CI −0.55 to −0.21; low certainty), while atypical antipsychotics showed possible benefit but increased discontinuation due to adverse events (RR 2.14, 95% CI 1.43–3.21).

INTERPRETATION: The evidence supports SSRIs for reducing anxiety in PTSD with moderate certainty, though diagnostic clarity for comorbid anxiety disorders is limited. SNRIs offer lower-certainty benefits, and atypical antipsychotics carry a higher risk of adverse effects. The review’s strength lies in its systematic approach and GRADE assessment, but heterogeneity in diagnostic criteria and study designs weakens generalisability to routine care.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: SSRIs remain a reasonable first-line option for anxiety symptoms in PTSD, but clinicians should carefully assess for comorbid anxiety disorders and monitor tolerability. SNRIs and atypical antipsychotics should be used cautiously given lower certainty and higher adverse event rates.

articles.title: Home-Based Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation for Depression: From Feasibility to Clinical Implementation.
articles.authors: Pilloni G, Brunoni AR, Charvet L
articles.abstract: Home-based transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) for major depressive disorder (MDD) has progressed from early feasibility studies to an approved clinical treatment, highlighted by the US Food and Drug Administration's 2025 premarket approval of the Flow FL-100 device. This milestone shifts the field from asking whether home-based tDCS can be delivered safely and effectively to defining how it should be implemented in routine clinical practice. This review synthesizes the current evidence on treatment outcomes, adherence, and safety, with an emphasis on factors that determine successful real-world implementation. Randomized controlled trials support the efficacy of home-based tDCS when delivered using adequate cumulative dosing, structured treatment protocols, and appropriate supervision or adherence monitoring. In contrast, shorter-duration and fully unsupervised protocols have generally shown less favorable outcomes, although the independent contributions of dose, treatment duration, and supervision remain difficult to disentangle. High adherence has been reported with user-centered device design, standardized training, remote monitoring, and scalable supervision models that maintain treatment fidelity while supporting broad clinical deployment. Home-based tDCS has demonstrated an excellent safety profile when delivered using standardized equipment, structured protocols, and active monitoring, exemplified by more than 30,000 supervised home-based sessions delivered
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the clinical implementation of home-based transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) for major depressive disorder (MDD), synthesizing evidence on efficacy, adherence, safety, and real-world feasibility following FDA premarket approval of the Flow FL-100 device in 2025.

FINDINGS: Randomized controlled trials indicate that home-based tDCS is effective when delivered with adequate cumulative dosing, structured protocols, and supervision or adherence monitoring; shorter or unsupervised protocols show less favorable outcomes. High adherence (reported across >30,000 supervised sessions) is supported by user-centered device design, standardized training, remote monitoring, and scalable supervision models. No skin lesions or serious adverse events attributable to tDCS were reported in a large academic clinical program.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is primarily derived from RCTs and large clinical programs, suggesting that home-based tDCS can be safely and effectively implemented under structured conditions. However, as a narrative review, it lacks systematic synthesis and may overstate generalizability. Key uncertainties remain regarding the independent contributions of dose, duration, and supervision, as well as the optimal integration into routine care. The lack of blinding in many real-world protocols and potential selection bias in adherence data limit internal validity.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Home-based tDCS may soon be a viable option for MDD in interventional psychiatry settings, provided strict protocols, supervision, and monitoring are in place. Clinicians should await clearer dosing guidelines and patient selection criteria before widespread adoption, and remain vigilant for subtle safety signals in unsupervised use.

articles.title: ADVANCES IN RESEARCH OF PSYCHOTHERAPY FOR SOCIAL ANXIETY DISORDER.
articles.authors: Lu Y, Wu Y
articles.abstract: Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD) is a common anxiety disorder characterized by a persistent fear of negative evaluation, avoidance of social situations, and significant impairment in social functioning. Psychological interventions for SAD have expanded considerably in recent years, with increasing attention to treatment mechanisms, alternative delivery formats, and emerging intervention targets. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) remains one of the most extensively studied psychological treatments for SAD, while mindfulness-based interventions, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), Virtual Reality Exposure Therapy (VRET), and emerging integrative approaches have broadened the range of therapeutic targets and treatment strategies. This review synthesizes recent domestic and international research on psychological interventions for SAD, focusing on their theoretical foundations, empirical evidence, therapeutic targets, and clinical characteristics. Overall, current evidence supports the efficacy of CBT, while mindfulness-based interventions, ACT, VRET, and emerging integrative approaches show varying levels of evidence and require further investigation. Digital technologies are increasingly incorporated into established psychological interventions and should be understood primarily as delivery modalities rather than independent treatment categories. Future research should place greater emphasis on treatment mechanisms, active components, patient-treatment matching, and the long
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review synthesizes recent research on psychological interventions for Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD), focusing on efficacy, mechanisms, and delivery formats. It covers established treatments like CBT and newer approaches (mindfulness, ACT, VRET) to guide clinical decision-making.

FINDINGS: The review highlights strong empirical support for CBT in SAD, while evidence for mindfulness-based interventions, ACT, and VRET is mixed and requires further study. Digital technologies (e.g., online CBT) are increasingly used as delivery tools rather than standalone treatments. Key gaps include limited understanding of active treatment components and long-term functional outcomes.

INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this study lacks the rigor of a systematic review or meta-analysis, making it prone to selection bias and unsystematic synthesis. The conclusions align with established evidence (CBT efficacy) but downplay heterogeneity in newer interventions. The focus on mechanisms and patient-treatment matching is valuable but lacks concrete data or actionable insights.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: CBT remains the gold standard for SAD, while other modalities (e.g., ACT, VRET) may be considered adjunctively but require individualized assessment. Clinicians should prioritize evidence-based therapies and monitor long-term functional gains, acknowledging the preliminary nature of newer approaches.

articles.title: Acute Caffeine Intake Does Not Modulate Active or Reactive Inhibition in Non-Clinical Young Adults, and ADHD Symptoms Do Not Moderate Its Effects.
articles.authors: Altınok A
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Caffeine is consumed for its presumed cognitive benefits, yet controlled studies have repeatedly failed to find effects on inhibitory control. Cross-sectional work suggests that people with elevated attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms may benefit from chronic, moderate caffeine consumption, but whether acute intake improves cognition in proportion to symptom severity has not been tested experimentally. AIMS: We tested whether 250 mg of caffeine improves active inhibition (withholding a prepared response) and reactive inhibition (resolving response conflict), and whether ADHD symptom severity moderates these effects. METHODS: In a preregistered, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, a nonclinical sample of 36 young adults received 250 mg of caffeine or placebo in counterbalanced order, with testing 45 min after ingestion. Active inhibition was assessed with a Go/No-Go task (204 trials), reactive inhibition with an arrow flanker task (200 trials) and symptoms with the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale. Mixed-effects models included treatment, symptom severity, their interaction and ten covariates; Bayes factors quantified evidence for the null. RESULTS: Both tasks produced their benchmark effects (dz = 1.24 and 1.09) and all indices were reliable (split-half r = 0.73-0.98). Caffeine affected neither commission errors (BF01 = 4.98), response criterion (5.14), Go reaction time (2.83), reaction time variability (4.35), flanker re
articles.summary: BACKGROUND: Caffeine is consumed for its presumed cognitive benefits, yet controlled studies have repeatedly failed to find effects on inhibitory control. Cross-sectional work suggests that people with elevated attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms may benefit from chronic, moderate caffeine consumption, but whether acute intake improves cognition in proportion to symptom severity has not been tested experimentally.

articles.title: Repeated remimazolam sedation for interstitial brachytherapy in cervical cancer: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.authors: Wang Y, Yang H, Gu Q, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Evidence regarding repeated remimazolam administration remains limited. We hypothesized that remimazolam would be associated with fewer adverse events than propofol while maintaining stable sedative requirements across three repeated sedation sessions. METHODS: Patients with cervical cancer undergoing three fractions of interstitial brachytherapy were randomized to propofol or remimazolam. The primary outcome was the proportion of sedation episodes with at least one prespecified intraoperative adverse event across three sessions. Secondary outcomes included sedative dose, hemodynamics, and sleep quality assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS). RESULTS: A total of 100 participants were randomized, of whom 91 completed all three prespecified sedation sessions and were included in the primary per-protocol analysis (46 in the propofol group and 45 in the remimazolam group). Across 138 propofol and 135 remimazolam episodes, overall adverse events were less frequent with remimazolam (17.78% vs. 59.42%; RR, 0.30; 95% CI, 0.18-0.49; p < 0.001). Respiratory depression (3.70% vs. 26.09%; RR, 0.14; 95% CI, 0.04-0.53; p = 0.004) and hypotension (8.15% vs. 41.30%; RR, 0.20; 95% CI, 0.09-0.42; p < 0.001) were also lower with remimazolam. Remimazolam requirements remained stable across sessions (third vs. first: mean difference, 0.19 mg; 95% CI, -0.78 to 1.15; p = 0.846). No significant between-group differences were observed in P
articles.summary: BACKGROUND: Evidence regarding repeated remimazolam administration remains limited. We hypothesized that remimazolam would be associated with fewer adverse events than propofol while maintaining stable sedative requirements across three repeated sedation sessions. METHODS: Patients with cervical cancer undergoing three fractions of interstitial brachytherapy were randomized to propofol or remimazolam. The primary outcome was the proportion of sedation episodes with at least one prespecified intraoperative adverse event across three sessions.

articles.title: The role of depression in adherence to colorectal cancer screening guidelines.
articles.authors: Becker A, Bjelis S, Rodriguez D
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Cancer is the second leading cause of death in the United States with an incidence rate of approximately 442.3 out of 100 000. In 2021, colorectal cancer (CRC) was responsible for more than 52 000 deaths. Screening is a preventive practice that can detect CRC early. More than 70% of adults aged 45 years or older get screened at least once, yet far fewer follow recommended screening guidelines. Depression is associated with an increased risk of CRC and CRC-related mortality and a reduction in regular CRC screening, making it a significant psychosocial barrier to preventive screening. This cross-sectional study examined factors associated with adherence to CRC screening recommendations, particularly among individuals with a self-reported depression diagnosis. METHODS: Utilizing a representative national sample (n = 204 539) from the 2023 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (adults aged≥50), we assessed the effects of depression and key variables associated with depression and CRC screening on the likelihood of adherence. Our model included interactions between depression and race/ethnicity, education, and income among other variables. RESULTS: African Americans (AA) with depression were 60% less likely to meet recommendations than AA without depression (odds ratio = 0.40, 99% confidence interval = 0.29, 0.55). DISCUSSION: The results suggest a critical need for health care practitioners to assess patient mental health, especially among AA patients, who are
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study investigated whether self-reported depression reduces adherence to colorectal cancer (CRC) screening guidelines, using a representative US sample of adults aged ≥50 (n = 204 539). The clinical question is whether depression acts as a modifiable barrier to guideline-concordant CRC screening.

FINDINGS: African Americans with depression had 60 % lower odds of meeting screening recommendations than African Americans without depression (odds ratio 0.40, 99 % CI 0.29–0.55). The study did not report overall adherence rates or effect sizes for other racial/ethnic groups.

INTERPRETATION: The large sample size and national representativeness strengthen external validity, but the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. Depression appears to be a significant, potentially modifiable, barrier to CRC screening in African Americans, though residual confounding (e.g., access to care, insurance status) cannot be excluded. The 99 % CI suggests a very low risk of type I error for the reported association.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should consider routine screening for depression in African American patients due for CRC screening, as depression may reduce adherence. Further research is needed to determine whether treating depression improves screening uptake.

articles.title: TMS-Evoked Cortical Reactivity Signatures as a Multidimensional Biomarker of Depression: A TMS-EEG Meta-Analysis from Diagnosis to Prognosis.
articles.authors: Xie JY, Zhao T, Guo L, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) enables perturbation-based assessment of cortical reactivity and has emerged as a promising tool for identifying neurophysiological biomarkers in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, the literature remains fragmented, and TMS-EEG metrics have yet to be systematically integrated within a unified framework spanning diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis. METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, Ovid, and Web of Science were systematically searched for studies reporting single-pulse TMS-EEG measures in MDD. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to synthesize evidence across three hierarchical biomarker validation domains: characterization (diagnostic discrimination and state-related symptom tracking), treatment response (intervention monitoring and clinical coupling with remission), and baseline prediction. RESULTS: Across 21 studies comprising 1,025 patients with MDD and 517 healthy controls, negative-polarity components were significantly enhanced in MDD (Hedges' g = 0.36), driven primarily by the N100 (g = 0.35), which was also associated with greater symptom severity (g = 0.67). Treatment attenuated N100 (g = -0.21) while elevating P180 (g = 0.52). Critically, treatment-induced reduction in negative-polarity responses was strongly coupled with clinical remission (g = 0.91), with the N100 showing the most robust component-level effect (g = 0.85). Preliminary evidence further indicated that ba
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis investigated whether transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) can serve as a biomarker for major depressive disorder (MDD) across diagnosis, treatment response, and prognosis. It synthesized data from 21 studies involving 1,025 patients with MDD and 517 healthy controls.

FINDINGS: Negative-polarity TMS-EEG components were significantly enhanced in MDD compared to controls (Hedges' g = 0.36), primarily driven by the N100 component (g = 0.35), which correlated with symptom severity (g = 0.67). During treatment, N100 amplitude decreased (g = -0.21), while P180 increased (g = 0.52). Treatment-induced reductions in negative-polarity responses were strongly associated with clinical remission (g = 0.91), particularly for N100 (g = 0.85). Preliminary evidence suggested baseline negative-polarity components predicted treatment response (g = 1.35).

INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests TMS-EEG cortical reactivity signatures, especially N100, show consistent but modest diagnostic and prognostic associations in MDD. The meta-analysis benefits from a large pooled sample and hierarchical validation domains, but heterogeneity in study designs, small effect sizes for diagnostic discrimination, and limited longitudinal data for prediction weaken confidence. The strong coupling between N100 changes and remission is notable but based on fewer studies, and effect sizes for prediction are preliminary and likely inflated by publication bias.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: TMS-EEG, particularly N100 amplitude, may offer adjunctive value in monitoring treatment response and predicting remission in MDD, but current evidence is insufficient to recommend routine use. Further large-scale, prospective studies with standardized protocols are needed before clinical implementation.

articles.title: Strategies to enhance engagement in CBT for adult ADHD: an innovation tournament with stakeholders.
articles.authors: Sibley MH, Shafiee M, Knouse LE
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Adults with ADHD report challenges engaging in cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). This study investigates practices that might be applied to improve intervention fit and therapeutic engagement of CBT for adults with ADHD. METHOD: We conducted an Innovation Tournament (IT) and member checking with participants (N=102) who were adults with ADHD and mental health practitioners who regularly treat adults with ADHD. Go-Zone plots were utilized to identify strategies with the highest feasibility and importance as well as strategies with low feasibility and/or importance that might be candidates for de-implementation. Barriers to CBT engagement and practitioner implementation of practices were also evaluated qualitatively. RESULTS: A range of engagement barriers were identified, chief among them practitioner low understanding of ADHD (44.4%) and lack of attention to relevant impairments (33.3%). The highest rated focal areas for CBT were task management, organization, planning, and prioritization, emotion regulation strategies, responding to negative/maladaptive thoughts, anti-procrastination and self-motivation strategies, and long-term goal setting. Top recommendations for engagement strategies include ensuring high therapist knowledge of ADHD and 17 elements consistent with Motivational Interviewing. Some practices commonly found in CBTs for ADHD were rated as unpopular with stakeholders, most notably providing weekly ratings of ADHD symptoms as progress monitoring. S
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: Adults with ADHD often struggle to engage in cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), prompting this innovation tournament (IT) study to identify stakeholder-prioritized strategies to enhance engagement and intervention fit. The study involved adults with ADHD (N=102) and practitioners, using qualitative and quantitative methods to evaluate barriers and prioritize CBT strategies.

FINDINGS: Key barriers included low practitioner understanding of ADHD (44.4%) and inattention to relevant impairments (33.3%). Top-rated CBT focal areas were task management, emotion regulation, and goal setting. High therapist ADHD knowledge and 17 Motivational Interviewing (MI)-consistent elements were top recommendations, while weekly ADHD symptom ratings were unpopular. Stakeholders rated reducing shame and nurturing confidence as important but not feasible. Implementation barriers were primarily low practitioner knowledge/skills and systemic constraints.

INTERPRETATION: This study provides preliminary, stakeholder-driven insights into CBT engagement barriers and potential solutions but lacks empirical testing of effectiveness. The qualitative and IT design limits generalizability, and feasibility ratings may not reflect real-world applicability. The findings highlight gaps in current practice (e.g., low ADHD knowledge) and suggest MI-informed approaches may improve engagement, but clinical impact remains unproven. Systemic barriers (e.g., resource constraints) may hinder implementation even if strategies are adopted.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians may consider enhancing ADHD-specific knowledge and incorporating MI techniques to improve engagement, but should await empirical validation of these strategies. Current practice should not be changed based solely on these findings, given the lack of outcome data. Focus on addressing identified barriers (e.g., shame, confidence) may be premature without further evidence.

articles.title: Intensified return to work clinical aftercare for sick-listed employees with diagnosed mental disorders in Germany: effects of a multicentre randomized controlled trial.
articles.authors: Starke F, Zimmermann J, Sikora A, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Mental disorders are a leading cause of sickness absence and disability in Europe. They often follow chronic or recurrent patterns, hindering a sustainable return to work (RTW). In Germany, RTW aftercare interventions focusing on maintaining recovery and minimizing relapse among employees transitioning from psychiatric treatment to the workplace are scarce. We therefore developed an intensified RTW clinical aftercare program (RTW-PIA). This study aimed to (i) evaluate the effectiveness of RTW-PIA in addition to Care as Usual (CAU) on achieving sustainable RTW (SRTW) compared to CAU only, (ii) assess its impact on secondary outcomes, and (iii) explore potential moderators. METHODS: This multicentre randomized controlled trial, conducted in psychiatric outpatient clinics, included sick-listed employees diagnosed with a mental disorder. Participants (N = 484) were randomized to RTW-PIA + CAU (n = 240) or CAU only (n = 244). RTW-PIA is an 18-month multimodal aftercare combining medical-psychotherapeutic and work-oriented components. Primary outcome was self-reported SRTW, defined as ≤ 6 weeks of sickness absence within 12 months after full RTW. Primary and secondary outcomes (e.g., RTW self-efficacy, work ability) were collected at baseline and at 6, 12, 18, and 24 months. Intention-to-treat analyses used logistic regression and growth curve models, complemented by prespecified sensitivity and exploratory moderator analyses. RESULTS: Overall, RTW-PIA had no significan
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: A multicentre RCT in German psychiatric outpatient clinics (N = 484 sick-listed employees with mental disorders) tested an 18-month intensified return-to-work aftercare program (RTW-PIA) added to care-as-usual (CAU) versus CAU alone, with primary outcome sustainable RTW (≤ 6 weeks sickness absence within 12 months after full RTW) and secondary outcomes over 24 months.

FINDINGS: The primary outcome showed no significant effect of RTW-PIA (OR 1.38, 95 % CI 0.89–2.12). Secondary outcomes were largely unchanged; only employees with recurrent depressive disorders showed improvements in several secondary measures. Prespecified moderator analyses suggested possible benefits for those without recognized disability degree and for those with low workplace social support, but after multiplicity adjustment only recurrent depressive disorder remained a significant moderator for work ability.

INTERPRETATION: The trial has high internal validity (randomised, multicentre, prespecified analyses) but the overall null result for the primary outcome and most secondary outcomes argues against broad effectiveness of RTW-PIA in its current form. Subgroup findings are exploratory and require independent replication before clinical adoption. The programme’s implementation challenges and resource demands are not addressed.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, RTW-PIA cannot be recommended for routine use to improve sustainable return to work in unselected sick-listed psychiatric patients; targeted trials in recurrent depression and low social support subgroups are needed before any change in practice.

articles.title: Effectiveness of a nurse-led telephonic brief intervention to reduce risky alcohol use among women in primary care in Brazil: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.authors: Lima AVC, De Oliveira Pinheiro Gaia JL, De Vargas D
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite the increase in alcohol use among women worldwide, evidence on scalable, gender-responsive interventions remains limited, particularly in primary-care settings. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a nurse-delivered, telephonic brief intervention (BI) for reducing risky and harmful alcohol use among women. METHODS: This randomized controlled trial included 151 women recruited from four primary-care facilities in São Paulo, Brazil, who scored 8-19 on the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT). Participants were randomly assigned to an intervention group (IG), which received a nurse-delivered telephone BI, or a control group (CG), which received feedback only. The primary outcome was the change in AUDIT scores assessed longitudinally from baseline through 24 months of follow-up. RESULTS: In women receiving the telephonic BI, AUDIT scores significantly reduced during the first 6 months postintervention. Although this benefit was attenuated over longer-term follow-up, AUDIT scores in the control group followed an increasing trajectory over time. Race and household income were significantly associated with AUDIT scores; this suggests that socioeconomic factors may influence patterns of alcohol-related risk and intervention outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: A nurse-delivered telephonic BI produced meaningful short- to medium-term reductions in risky and harmful alcohol use among women in the primary-care setting. The attenuation of effects beyond 6 months s
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The study addressed whether a nurse-led telephonic brief intervention (BI) can reduce risky alcohol use among women in Brazilian primary care, a setting where gender-responsive, scalable interventions are scarce. It was a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 151 women scoring 8–19 on the AUDIT.

FINDINGS: Over the first 6 months, AUDIT scores fell in the intervention group (IG) while rising in controls; the between-group difference was statistically significant (effect size not reported). By 24 months, the initial benefit in the IG attenuated and the control group’s scores continued to increase. Socioeconomic factors (race, household income) were associated with AUDIT trajectories.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate: the RCT design and longitudinal follow-up strengthen internal validity, but the lack of effect-size estimates and blinding of assessors limits precision. The short-lived benefit suggests a single BI is insufficient for long-term change; booster sessions may be needed. External validity is constrained by the single-city, female-only sample and resource-constrained primary-care context.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: A nurse-delivered telephonic BI can produce modest short-term reductions in risky drinking for women in primary care, but sustained impact is unlikely without additional support; services should plan for follow-up or booster contacts.

articles.title: Perinatal Bipolar Disorder Management: Lithium in the Setting of Obstetric Complications.
articles.authors: Koire AM, Silver D, Clark CT, et al.
articles.abstract: Managing bipolar disorder in the perinatal period relies on psychopharmacologic treatment due to high rates of postpartum recurrence in the absence of mood-stabilizing medications. Lithium is classically recommended for postpartum bipolar episodes, yet lithium management during pregnancy, labor, and postpartum is complex and clinical practice varies even among reproductive psychiatrists. This case report details a 37-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder whose unexpectedly elevated lithium levels during pregnancy heralded preeclampsia. This case highlights the treatment challenges that arise when complicated psychiatric histories interact with complicated obstetric histories. We address conceptual questions about balancing psychiatric and obstetric risk when developing a medication regimen and illustrate continued dialogue regarding optimal lithium monitoring in the peripartum period.
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The abstract describes a case report highlighting the challenges of managing lithium treatment in a pregnant woman with bipolar I disorder, particularly when obstetric complications (e.g., preeclampsia) arise. The focus is on balancing psychiatric and obstetric risks in perinatal bipolar disorder management.

FINDINGS: The case involves a 37-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder whose lithium levels unexpectedly rose during pregnancy, preceding the onset of preeclampsia. The report underscores the variability in clinical practice among reproductive psychiatrists regarding lithium monitoring and management in the peripartum period.
