INTERPRETATION: As a case report, the evidence is anecdotal and lacks generalizability. The findings are preliminary and do not establish causality or provide quantitative data. The study highlights a potential association between elevated lithium levels and preeclampsia, but this requires further investigation in larger, controlled studies to confirm any clinical significance.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This case report serves as a reminder to monitor lithium levels closely in pregnant patients with bipolar disorder, particularly in the context of obstetric complications. However, it does not provide definitive guidance for practice changes, and clinicians should rely on broader evidence-based guidelines for now.

articles.title: Demographic, history, university and lifestyle factors associated with university student mental health: cross-sectional analysis across five UK universities.
articles.authors: Dooley J, Morse KF, Byrom N, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The whole-university approach to mental health emphasises that well-being should be a strategic priority across all aspects of higher education. However, there is limited evidence on which aspects of university life institutions should target to maximise well-being. AIM: To identify factors associated with student mental health and well-being and provide an evidence base for developing initiatives that protect and promote this. METHODS: The Nurture-U survey was conducted across five universities in the UK from 2022 to 2024. This cross-sectional sample of the survey data assessed student well-being and mental health at the start of the academic year. Hierarchical linear regression models examined the relative association between demographic, family history, university and lifestyle variables and self-reported depression, measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), anxiety, measured using the Generalised Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) and well-being, measured using the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale (SWEMWBS). RESULTS: A total of 14 172 students completed the survey. Over a quarter self-reported probable anxiety or depression based on established screening thresholds. Regression analysis indicated that younger age, identifying as female or lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer/questioning, intersex or asexual (LGBTQIA+) and reporting a disability were associated with poorer mental health. There was minimal evidence of mental health i
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study across five UK universities (2022–2024) examined demographic, university, and lifestyle factors associated with student mental health and well-being, aiming to inform whole-university mental health strategies.

FINDINGS: Of 14,172 students, >25% screened positive for probable anxiety or depression (PHQ-9/GAD-7 thresholds). Younger age, female/LGBTQIA+ identity, and disability were associated with worse mental health. University-specific factors (course or institution) showed minimal impact. Exercise and self-care were strongly associated with better well-being (SWEMWBS) and lower depression/anxiety.

INTERPRETATION: The large sample size strengthens precision, but the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. Self-reported data may introduce bias, and unmeasured confounders (e.g., socioeconomic status) could influence associations. The effect sizes for lifestyle factors (e.g., exercise) are modest but consistent, suggesting potential utility in interventions. However, the lack of university-specific impact limits actionable targets beyond general health promotion.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Universities may prioritize promoting exercise and self-care to support student mental health, but should avoid overemphasizing course/institution-level changes based on these findings. Further longitudinal or interventional research is needed to confirm causality.

articles.title: Integrating Wearable Technology in Digital Therapy for People With Psychosis (SloMo): Mixed Methods Co-Design and Feasibility Study.
articles.authors: Taylor KM, Ward T, Cella M, et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Digital health interventions for psychosis, like SloMo, leverage smartphone technology to help transfer learning from therapy to real-life situations. Usage relies on motivation, recall, and awareness. Wearable devices that track physiological signs of stress can boost engagement by encouraging the use of coping strategies when most needed. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to co-design an integrated user interface for wearable technology and the SloMo mobile app, and explore its usability, acceptability, engagement, and preliminary clinical outcomes for individuals with psychosis through a feasibility study. METHODS: A co-design team developed the wearable augmented SloMo app using the Double Diamond framework. The team included 10 experts by experience based across three UK National Health Service (NHS) mental health trusts, who had completed SloMo as part of a randomized controlled trial, and were purposively recruited to ensure a range of demographic backgrounds. Users tested the app for 8 consecutive weeks during a 5-month data collection period in 2018, providing feedback that guided iterative improvements. Self-reported engagement, usability, and acceptability were collected through quantitative ratings and interviews, evaluated through qualitative content analysis. Assessments of paranoia and well-being were completed pre- and post use, summarized descriptively, with change scores calculated and evaluated for reliable change. RESULTS: The Spire Stone clothing-adh
articles.summary: BACKGROUND: Digital health interventions for psychosis, like SloMo, leverage smartphone technology to help transfer learning from therapy to real-life situations. Usage relies on motivation, recall, and awareness. Wearable devices that track physiological signs of stress can boost engagement by encouraging the use of coping strategies when most needed.

articles.title: Unseen and underserved: A scoping review of perinatal mental health interventions in Sub-Saharan Africa.
articles.authors: Aboul-Enein BH, Ballout S, Kelly PJ
articles.abstract: Maternal mental health (MMH) remains a critical public health issue across Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Despite the high burden, access to culturally appropriate and evidence-based mental health interventions remains limited. This scoping review examines interventions targeting mental health outcomes for pregnant and postpartum women across SSA countries. Guided by PRISMA-ScR and Arksey and O'Malley's framework, a comprehensive search was conducted across 14 electronic databases for peer-reviewed intervention studies published in English between 2000 and March 2026. A total of 57 studies across 18 SSA countries were identified with interventions primarily focused on the individual or mother-infant level. The majority used strong research methods, with widely varying intervention content, including cognitive-behavioral therapy, problem-solving therapy, psychoeducation, and community-based programs, often delivered by community health workers, focusing on problem-solving skills, and involving cash transfers. While most studies reported reductions in depressive symptoms and improved psychosocial outcomes, few addressed scalability, health system integration, or cost-effectiveness. Few studies worked with health professionals or included technology interventions. A wide range of mental health interventions show promise in addressing perinatal mental health in SSA. However, gaps remain in scaling up sustainable, culturally relevant, and system-integrated interventions. Future efforts
articles.summary: Maternal mental health (MMH) remains a critical public health issue across Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Despite the high burden, access to culturally appropriate and evidence-based mental health interventions remains limited. This scoping review examines interventions targeting mental health outcomes for pregnant and postpartum women across SSA countries. Guided by PRISMA-ScR and Arksey and O'Malley's framework, a comprehensive search was conducted across 14 electronic databases for peer-reviewed intervention studies published in English between 2000 and March 2026.

articles.title: Flow and Similar Attentional States in Autism and ADHD: A Scoping Review of Similarities and Differences.
articles.authors: Pace-Tonna C, Murtaza M, Rodak T, et al.
articles.abstract: Flow is a state of optimal engagement. Autistic individuals and individuals with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) might have variations in flow-like experiences, such as hyperfocus, autistic inertia, and monotropism, that diverge from traditional or typical definitions. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines, we systematically reviewed 43 publications, including empirical studies, reviews, and other literature, to examine these constructs. Results showed that attentional experiences associated with neurodivergence overlap with, but also differ notably from, typical flow. Autistic inertia hinders task initiation and transitions, in contrast to flow's seamless engagement. Monotropism involves rigid, directed focus and repetitive, tenacious engagement, whereas flow allows for flexible adaptations to challenges. Hyperfocus is like flow regarding intense concentration and immersion but is often involuntary, lacks clear goals, and is associated with emotional dysregulation. Although commonalities exist across these attentional experiences, the greatest overlap occurs within autistic inertia, monotropism, and hyperfocus. Attention in autistic and ADHD individuals might be more dynamic than previously believed, with potential for transitions between these experiences. This fluidity can enhance focus and productivity but may also lead to negative outcomes, such as overly rigi
articles.summary:
BACKGROUND: The review asks whether attentional states such as hyperfocus, autistic inertia, and monotropism in autistic individuals and those with ADHD resemble or differ from the construct of “flow” (optimal engagement). Using PRISMA-ScR methods, it synthesises 43 publications to map similarities and distinctions.

FINDINGS: Across studies, autistic inertia is described as a barrier to starting or switching tasks, whereas monotropism denotes rigid, narrow focus with repetitive persistence; both diverge from the flexible adaptation seen in typical flow. Hyperfocus shows overlap with flow in intensity and immersion but is often involuntary, lacks clear goals, and is linked to emotional dysregulation. The greatest overlap is between autistic inertia, monotropism, and hyperfocus, suggesting a spectrum of attentional experiences that can shift over time.

INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is heterogeneous (empirical studies, reviews, conceptual papers) and largely qualitative, so conclusions are suggestive rather than definitive. The review highlights nuanced differences that may inform personalised supports, but effect sizes and quantitative comparisons are not reported. Funding sources and risk of bias assessments are not provided, limiting certainty about internal validity. External validity depends on the representativeness of included samples, which are not clearly described.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians may use these distinctions to tailor psychoeducation and environmental adaptations (e.g., clear goals, structured transitions) for autistic individuals and those with ADHD, while recognising that attentional states can fluctuate and may yield both productivity gains and risks of rigidity or overload.
